Applies after it restarts. modify_prompt Rewrite its own system prompt (full replacement; recorded in Config → Revisions under the agent's name). restart_self Restart itself so saved changes take effect — scheduled just after its reply, so the answer isn't cut off. add_subagents Add specialist subagents to itself, from scratch or drafted from a template. connect_mcps Connect services (MCP servers and built-in toolkits). Find every supported way to reach a service (self_find_integration), add or remove an MCP server or a built-in toolkit on itself, and start the sign-in. OAuth and sign-in codes happen in the user's own browser; API keys go through the vault. Also lets it read an outside project's documentation before anyone installs it (self_inspect_external). connect_platforms Wire messaging channels onto itself — token platforms (Telegram, Discord, Slack) and WhatsApp by a QR code shown right in the chat. manage_skills List the skills it has and switch individual ones on or off for itself — the same switches on its Skills tab, writing the same disabled_skills list. It can never install, edit or delete a skill this way, and switching off a common skill leaves every other agent's copy alone. Applies after it restarts. magic_links Send magic links — the magic_link_* tools: sign a person in to a service or MCP server, collect an API key straight into the vault, connect messengers by QR or token, let someone edit its instructions or a file, open the dashboard on their phone. The default way a bot connects itself to anything, so it ships on. Off removes the whole family from the bot; a single link tool can also be switched off on its Tools tab. Owners only, group chats refused, and an approval card on the stricter profiles; Config → Magic links stays the hard off switch for the whole deployment and separately gates the dashboard link. external_access Publish itself for outside callers (MCP / A2A) and mint access tokens — self_set_external_access and magic_link_mint_access_token. The tools additionally refuse anyone who is not an administrator, so this only decides whether a bot holds them at all. Off removes them from the bot; the External access tab still works for admins.

Four guardrails apply regardless of these switches. Only people who own the bot can make it change itself (see below). Every change is written through the same validated path the dashboard uses, so a broken edit is refused rather than half-saved. Every agent.json5 change lands in Config → Revisions attributed to the acting agent, so it can be reviewed and rolled back. And on the stricter security profiles each self-change first raises a human approval card. These switches govern the agent acting on itself only — they grant nothing to humans and nothing over other agents.

Who may ask is a separate question from what the bot may change. The switches above decide what the bot is capable of; ownership decides who is allowed to trigger it. Anything that writes — model, instructions, subagents, MCP services, messaging channels, restart, sending a magic link — is limited to:

  • an owner of that bot (whoever creates a bot owns it; more owners are granted under Admin → Access, where the roles are Owner and User),
  • any deployment admin, and
  • on a messaging channel, a sender on that channel's allowed users list — which is what keeps "pair yourself with WhatsApp" workable from a phone.

Everyone else who may chat with the bot gets a plain refusal naming the remedy, and keeps the read-only half: it can still list the models it could switch to, the services it could connect, and the templates it could draw from. So a colleague you shared a bot with can explore what it could become and then ask you to approve it, rather than silently reconfiguring your bot.

Two cases are refused outright, with no way to grant them: an agent asking another agent to reconfigure it, and a scheduled or background run trying to reconfigure the agent while nobody is watching.

One built-in exception: an agent in customer-service mode (per-customer isolation — a support bot serving strangers on a shared channel) inherits off for every capability, whatever the deployment default says. A stranger must not be able to talk a support bot into rewiring itself. You can still enable an individual capability for such an agent deliberately, with an explicit On in its own Chat self-configuration card.

docs.title: groups: — multi-bot conversations
docs.text:
On by default, and editable from the dashboard at Config → Group chats — no file editing needed. While it is off, group threads do not exist and every group address on the API answers "not found"; turning it off never deletes a group, and turning it back on restores every group and transcript untouched.

Key Type Default Meaning enabled boolean true Group threads: one conversation several bots share, where you can address any member. Replies stream in word by word, the same as a one-to-one chat. Whether the bots then answer each other is the separate autonomous switch below. min_members integer 2 Fewest bots in a group. max_members integer 6 Most bots in a group. autonomous boolean true A second, separate switch, also on by default. With it on, a bot whose reply names another member by @name hands that member the next turn — so the bots carry on with each other without you in between, inside the two limits below. With it off, you post, the bots you named answer, and the thread waits for you. max_hops integer 3 How many bot-to-bot turns one message of yours may set off. Clamped to 1–10. When it runs out the thread stops and says so in the conversation. cascade_timeout_seconds integer 180 How long the whole chain may run before it stops itself, in seconds. Clamped to 10–1800.

autonomous is the one to think about. It is what makes a group a conversation rather than a switchboard, and it is also the setting that spends model calls nobody is watching, because one message from you can start a chain of bots answering each other. That is why the two limits exist, why the switch is separate from enabled, and why every stop — hop limit, timeout, or two bots going back and forth — is written into the conversation instead of the thread just going quiet. If you would rather relay every hand-off yourself, turn it off at Config → Group chats; the group surface stays exactly as it is. Raise max_hops only once you have watched a few chains and know what they cost you, and raise cascade_timeout_seconds with it — more turns under the same time limit only converts "out of turns" into "out of time".

If you are upgrading from a release where this switch was off by default and your config.yaml never mentioned it, your groups start doing this after the upgrade. Set autonomous: false there, or switch it off in the dashboard, to keep the old behaviour.

Using groups. A Group chats section appears in the agent list of both interfaces — in the full dashboard, under your agents in the sidebar. Click a group to open it; right-click it to rename it; use New group chat… at the foot of the section (or right-click its heading) to start one, picking the agents in the order you want them to answer. Each group has a details panel — the ⓘ button in its header — for renaming it, adding an agent, removing one, or deleting the whole group; on a phone the panel fills the screen. Order matters: the first agent in the roster answers anything that doesn't name someone. The Add an agent button in a one-to-one chat's header is the other way in: it turns that conversation into a group (see the Chat section).

Sharing a group with a teammate. With team accounts on, the person who created a group (or an admin) can let other team accounts into it from the group's details panel, under People: pick a person from Share with a teammate and they see the group in their own sidebar, marked Shared, can read everything in it and post into it. The list offers only people who already have access to every agent in the group, because sharing never grants access to an agent; grant that first on the Admin page if the person you want is missing. For the same reason an agent can only be added to a shared group when everyone shared into it already has access to that agent. A shared person is a guest: they can leave from the details panel, and what they posted stays in the conversation under their name, but only the creator and admins can rename the group, add or remove agents, share it with more people, remove someone, or delete it. Admins see every group whether or not they are listed.

The People section lists everyone in the room who is not an agent: the creator, the people it is shared with, and any admin who has posted. Each person's messages are labelled with their handle, and every agent in the group is told who is in the room on every turn, so it answers the person who asked and knows the others are reading. Once more than one person is in a group, one rule changes: a message that names no agent is for the other people, is saved, and wakes no agent, so "thanks Maria, I'll take it" does not cost a model call. The line under the message box says so, and typing @ and an agent's name asks that agent exactly as before. A group with one person in it keeps answering with its first agent.

Addressing one agent, or several. Start a message with @ and an agent's name to put it to that agent; typing @ opens a list of the members to pick from. You can name more than one — "@ana @luis @ravi what would each of you do here?" — and then each of them takes its own turn, in the order you named them, and each one can see what the ones before it said, so they add to each other instead of writing the same answer three times. Name nobody and the group's first agent answers. A line under the message box says which of those is about to happen — "ana answers", "ana, luis answer, each in turn" — and it changes as you type, so there is nothing to set before sending.

Agents you did not name still read everything. They stay out of the way unless they are named — and any agent can bring a teammate in by writing @their-name in its own reply, which is what turns a group into a conversation rather than a switchboard. With autonomous on (the default) that mention wakes the other agent for the next turn; with it off, the mention marks who should pick the work up and the thread waits for you. When an agent answers a teammate that called on it, its message carries a small "↩ name" tag beside the "→ name" one, so you can always tell who is answering whom — and answering is not handing over: the chain only continues when a reply names somebody else.

Every agent in a group is told, on every turn, who else is in the room and what each of them does (their description from the agent's own profile), that a message naming somebody else is context to read rather than a cue to answer, and which ways it has of reaching the others — so the group behaves like a room of colleagues rather than several agents that happen to share a page.

Watching them work. The group header has the same Quiet / Normal / Verbose control as a one-to-one chat, and it starts on Normal rather than Quiet: Normal shows one line per tool an agent uses — including it calling another agent or handing work to one of its own helpers — and Verbose adds each tool's full input and result plus the helper transcripts. In a group that activity is usually the point, which is why the starting level differs. The choice is remembered in your browser and applies to every group.

The reply is laid out in the order it happened: what the agent said before it went to work, then what it did, then what it said afterwards — rather than a pile of tool lines above one block of text. That order is kept, so reopening the group later shows the same conversation you watched.

Files an agent makes. When an agent saves a file and names it in its reply, the group shows it: a picture appears inline, anything else gets a card with Download and Open in Files, and the file's name in the text becomes a link. Each agent has its own workspace, so a link goes to the files of the agent that made it. A file the agent later deletes stops being offered rather than leaving a dead link behind.

When one agent asks another one directly, the transcript says so while it waits: a line reading "maria is thinking…", with that agent's own face beside it, appears under the member doing the asking and clears the moment the answer comes back. It shows at every level, Quiet included, because it is about who is talking rather than about tools — and without it a group looks frozen for as long as the other agent takes. What that agent says comes back inside the asking agent's reply, not as its own message in the group; an agent pulled in with @their name is the other route, and that one does post its own message.

Renaming a group. Right-click a group in the sidebar and choose Rename, or open the group's info panel and use the pencil beside its name (that is the route on a phone, which has no right-click). One-to-one conversations rename the same way in both views: right-click the chat under its agent in the sidebar (or in the simple view's rail), use the pencil on a row of the chat page's conversation list, or type /rename followed by the name you want. A name is only a label — renaming changes nothing about the conversation, who is in it, or what the agents remember of it. The name shows everywhere the conversation is listed the moment it is saved.

Turning a one-to-one chat into a group. In any conversation, Add an agent in the header brings other agents in. The agent you were already talking to leads the new group, so it keeps answering by default, and the recent history is copied across labelled with who said what — so the agents you add can read what was discussed instead of starting blind. Long conversations are trimmed to the most recent messages and the group says so in the transcript. You can switch that copying off if you would rather start clean. Two things are worth knowing: your original one-to-one chat is left exactly as it was (this creates a separate conversation), and what an agent privately remembers of that chat does not transfer — every member, including the original one, starts the group with only what the transcript shows.

Letting bots use groups themselves. Adding "groups" to an agent's tools: list gives it four abilities: list the groups it belongs to, read a group's recent messages, post into a group (optionally addressing one member with @name), and create a new group for the person it is talking to. A bot does not need these to take part in a group it is already in — replying and @mentioning a teammate work with no tools at all; these are for reaching a group it is not currently being spoken to in. A bot can only see and speak in groups it is a member of, its own name is always stamped as the author, and whether an addressed member replies on its own still follows autonomous and its limits — a bot's post starts exactly the same bounded exchange a message of yours would, never more. Creating a group works only in a live conversation with a signed-in person (the group becomes theirs, in their sidebar); from a scheduled run the bot is told to ask a human instead.

docs.title: Olano Cloud
docs.text:
Deploy an instance on cloud.olano.ai, open the dashboard address it gives you, and the setup wizard below takes over. Nothing to install and nothing to keep running yourself — see Olano Cloud. Your sign-in is created on the instance before it is reachable, so the first screen you see is Sign in: use the email you signed up with and the temporary password from your welcome email (also copyable from the deployment card in the cloud console). The dashboard address carries no credential — nothing signs you in by itself, and a Create your account screen on a fresh cloud instance means its setup has not finished; wait a minute and reload rather than creating an account.

While the instance still has that temporary password, the sign-in screen says so itself: it greets you as a new instance and shows a First sign-in note that the password is in the email we just sent you, with a link that opens your deployment's Security tab in the cloud console, where the password stays copyable. Forgot password? points to the same place. Once you have set a password of your own (the setup wizard's profile panel, or a password change), the note is gone for good and the screen is the ordinary sign-in form. The note never shows your email or the password; it only says where to find them.

docs.title: Self-hosted
docs.text:
The quickest install is the Docker Compose stack in the Olano repository (deploy/self-host/): three containers from the public images, set up and started by one line on a Linux server, a Mac with Docker Desktop, or Windows with Docker Desktop and WSL 2:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/olano-ai/olano/main/install.sh | bash

The installer checks for Docker with the Compose plugin (on Linux it offers to install it, and asks first), downloads the stack's files into ~/olano, and runs its setup script, which writes the generated settings into .env, pulls the images and starts the stack. Options for the setup script go after bash -s --, for example curl -fsSL …/install.sh | bash -s -- --host olano.example.com --sandbox. If you would rather download the files yourself, the README beside the compose file lists them and the same script runs as bash setup.sh.

Everything the install keeps lives in a data directory next to the compose file; backing that directory up backs up the install. Updating is docker compose pull && docker compose up -d; the README covers pinning a version, moving the data directory and the day-to-day commands.

docs.title: The address
docs.text:
Unless you say otherwise, the setup script picks the address on its first run:

  • A server with a public IP address on its own network interface (a typical VPS): it serves https on <your-ip-with-dashes>.sslip.io, for example https://203-0-113-7.sslip.io. sslip.io is a public service whose names point at the IP address written in them, which lets the dashboard get a Let's Encrypt certificate with no domain of your own.
  • Anything else (a laptop, a home server, a cloud VM behind NAT such as AWS EC2): http://localhost:3200, reachable on that machine only.

Choose explicitly with an option:

Option Address --host olano.example.com https on your own domain; point its DNS record at the machine first. The reliable route for anything long-lived --host auto https on <your-ip>.sslip.io, also on a NAT'd cloud VM whose ports 80 and 443 are forwarded to it --local http://localhost:3200 only

For either https mode, ports 80 and 443 must be reachable from the internet: in a cloud firewall or security group, open 22 (SSH), 80 and 443, and nothing else. The certificate is obtained on the first visit and renewed on its own. sslip.io names share Let's Encrypt's rate limit with every other sslip.io user, so issuance can occasionally be refused for a while; a domain of your own avoids that. Whatever the mode, the plain-http port 3200 is published on the machine's loopback only, never to the network, so from another computer it is reached through an SSH tunnel (ssh -L 3200:localhost:3200 you@server, then http://localhost:3200), which also works while a certificate is still pending.

docs.title: The setup code
docs.text:
A fresh install has no accounts, and the first person to create one becomes its admin. So that this is you and not someone who found the address first, the dashboard asks for a one-time setup code before it creates that first account. It is three groups of four letters and digits, like ABCD-EFGH-JKMN, and you will find it:

  • in the setup script's output, printed next to the address;
  • in the .env file beside the compose file, on the OLANO_SETUP_CODE line;
  • in the runtime's log (docker compose logs olano), under FIRST-RUN SETUP CODE.

Case, spaces and dashes do not matter. A wrong code is refused with a message saying where to look, and after ten wrong tries the form waits fifteen minutes before accepting another. The code stops working the moment the first account exists; from then on the dashboard asks for that account's email and password. An instance on Olano Cloud never asks for it: its account is created before the instance is reachable.

docs.title: Sandbox mode
docs.text:
By default an agent's shell commands (and the Terminal) run inside the runtime's own container. --sandbox gives every agent its own sandbox container instead, the way an Olano Cloud instance runs them: a non-root container per agent with only that agent's workspace in it and resource limits, so one agent's commands cannot read another agent's files or the runtime's. If an agent's sandbox cannot start, that agent has no shell rather than falling back to the runtime container.

The cost is on the host: to start those containers the runtime is given the host's Docker socket, and access to the Docker socket is equivalent to root on the machine. Agents never get it, but a flaw in the runtime would reach the whole host. Use sandbox mode on a machine you alone control. --no-sandbox turns it off again; both are remembered across runs of the setup script.

Running from source (the Python package, with the dashboard on port 3200 and the runtime API on 8765, both configurable in config.yaml) is described in the repository's README. Either way, from then on everything happens in the dashboard and in conversation with your agents, exactly as on the cloud.

Models are paid for either way you like: paste your own provider keys, or run on Olano credits with an Olano API key from cloud.olano.ai (see Models and credits). The wizard offers both.

docs.title: The setup wizard
docs.text:
The first time an admin opens the dashboard on a fresh deployment, a full-screen wizard walks through four short panels, then drops you straight into a conversation with Agent Father:

flowchart LR
    A["Sign in"] --> B["Setup wizard<br/>four short panels"] --> C["Chat with<br/>Agent Father"] --> D["Describe your<br/>first agent"]
The Welcome panel. Your profile, on an instance with no accounts yet: the handle is generated from your name as you type.
  1. Welcome.
  2. Your profile. A deployed instance ships with one account: the email you signed up with and a temporary password from your welcome email. You signed in with that password a moment ago; this panel is where you create your own user on it — it keeps your email and asks for your name, a password of your own, and the passphrase that protects the vault. Your handle (the permanent @name agents and the issue tracker refer to you by, like carlos-rivera) is generated from your name and shown as you type; it is not editable, here or later, while the name always is. Saving replaces the temporary password everywhere — it stops working at once, and any other browser still using it is signed out — while this browser stays signed in as the user you just created: the rest of the tour, and Agent Father's chat at the end of it, run as you, not as the provisioned sign-in. On an instance with no accounts yet the same panel also asks for your email (and, on a self-hosted install, the setup code) and creates the admin account, and signs you in as it. On a managed cloud deployment this panel is required, because the instance was provisioned with temporary credentials that must be replaced; the vault half asks for the temporary passphrase only if the vault is locked, and then links to your deployment card where it is copyable.
  3. AI provider. On a managed deployment your plan's Olano Credits already cover the AI, so this panel just shows what is included; bringing your own keys stays optional. Self-hosted installs choose here: paste an Olano API key to run on Olano credits (the panel then lists what is included and your balance), paste a provider key, or both.
  4. Meet Agent Father. What Agent Father does for you — creating agents from a description, reconfiguring them, connecting messaging channels and services, inviting your team, keeping things running, and asking for your approval before it changes anything. The panel also tells you that Agent Father wakes up when you continue and greets you in the chat — usually within seconds, up to a minute on a brand-new instance — and offers starting points: things to try (create an agent from a description, change an agent's model, tools or channels, list the available providers and connectors) and things worth telling it about yourself (whether this is personal or business use, what your business or interests are, which systems and platforms you use, and which repetitive daily or weekly tasks you would like to hand to AI). Press Meet Agent Father and setup is over: the dashboard opens Agent Father's chat showing Agent Father is waking up… until its hello arrives, and it then asks what you would like to build first.

There is no separate step for a first agent, a messenger or web search: you ask Agent Father for those in the chat, and web search is already available on a managed deployment. Everything the wizard touches lives in the dashboard afterwards (your profile in the account menu, Providers, Vault).

docs.title: Three ways to do everything
docs.text:
Every task in this guide can be done from one of three places, and they never disagree:

Surface Good for The dashboard seeing everything at once; admin work; anything with a form Asking an agent connecting a service, a messenger or a key; changing the agent's model, instructions, subagents or skills — the agent uses its built-in self_* tools and sends a magic link when a browser is needed (Ask the agent: self-configuration, magic links and admin tools) Asking AgentFather anything about the deployment as a whole: new agents, teammates and access, diagnostics, settings, updates — with an approval card in front of every change (Building agents from a conversation)

There is no command line to learn: an agent never asks you to open a terminal, and nothing in this guide requires one.

Inside a chat session, slash commands control the conversation — /model to switch models, /new to start a fresh thread, /memory to inspect what the agent remembers, /verbosity to change how much it narrates. /help lists them — the ones that agent exposes on that surface, plus any custom commands you defined, so it never offers something it will then refuse.

docs.title: Two ways to pay, not two modes
docs.text:
Olano-managed Bring your own key (BYOK) What you pick olano:turbo, olano:pro, olano:max anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6, openai:gpt-5.5, … Who holds the provider account Olano you What you are billed in Olano credits your provider bills you directly Setup needed none on Olano Cloud; an Olano API key on a self-hosted install a provider API key in the vault 
flowchart LR
    A["The model an agent<br/>or a conversation uses"] --> T{"olano:turbo, olano:pro<br/>or olano:max?"}
    T -- yes --> O["Olano runs the call,<br/>billed in Olano credits"]
    T -- "no, provider:model" --> K["Your provider key from the vault,<br/>billed by your provider"]

A deployment can do both at once. Billing is a property of the model you choose, not a mode the whole box is in — one agent can run on credits while another runs on your own OpenAI key. Pick per agent, and per conversation with /model.

BYOK shows tokens and estimated dollars, because you own that provider bill and want to reconcile it. Olano-managed shows credits.

docs.title: The Olano tiers
docs.text:
Tier (what you see) Value to write in config Reasoning effort Use it for Olano Turbo (default) olano:turbo not applicable Everyday work. Fast, cheap, no knobs. Start here. Olano Pro olano:pro low / medium / high Harder analysis, longer chains of work, better judgement. Olano Max olano:max low / medium / high The most powerful frontier models, for genuinely hard problems.

The name you see and the value you write are the same word for every tier. They were not always: the top tier's id used to be olano:reasoning, which is why you may still find that string in an older agent.json5.

olano:reasoning no longer works. It was retired, not aliased, so an agent still configured with it fails to build, with an error naming olano:turbo, olano:pro, olano:max — and the model picker shows the raw olano:reasoning instead of a product name, which is how you spot one. The fix is to edit the value to olano:max. Nothing rewrites it for you, and the change is nothing more than the new spelling: same tier, same routing, same credit rate.

The word "reasoning" does still appear here, in the Reasoning effort column above and in a model's reasoning_effort setting. That is how hard a model thinks about a single request — an unrelated setting that happens to share the word, and it is not going anywhere.

Every tier offers a very large context window; the dashboard's model picker shows the exact figure for each, and the context bar in a conversation shows how much of it you are using.

What backs a tier is not fixed. Olano routes each tier to whatever currently serves that capability and speed point best, and re-routes as the model landscape changes. That is the value of a tier: you buy a capability level, and you get upgrades without changing a config. It also means you should choose a tier by the job, not by assumptions about a particular underlying model.

olano:turbo is the default and always available. When in doubt, start an agent on Turbo and move it up only when its work demonstrably needs more.

docs.title: Deployment default models (default:*)
docs.text:
Three aliases sit above every concrete model:

Alias Picker name Out of the box it points at default:turbo Default · Turbo olano:turbo on an Olano-managed deployment; a bring-your-own-key model elsewhere default:pro Default · Pro olano:pro on managed; a bring-your-own-key model elsewhere default:max Default · Max olano:max on managed; a bring-your-own-key model elsewhere

An alias is not a model — it is a pointer the whole deployment shares. Any agent, subagent, team member or chat conversation set to one follows whatever target is configured in Config → Default models (the default_models: block of config.yaml), and the target must be a concrete provider:model — never another alias. Change a target once and every agent on that alias switches the next time it boots or reloads, with no per-agent edits. The pickers show what an alias currently resolves to ("Default · Turbo — currently Olano Turbo"), and clearing a target in Config restores the deployment's own built-in default.

Use an alias when an agent should simply run on "the deployment's everyday/heavier/top brain"; pin a concrete model only when that one agent genuinely needs that one model. Catalog agents install on the aliases — experts on default:turbo, team supervisors on default:pro — which is what makes "move the whole fleet to a different model" a one-field change.

One caveat on a bring-your-own-key install: an alias is only as usable as its current target. If the target's provider has no key or connection, every agent on that alias fails at its next turn — the chat picker greys the alias out for the same reason.

docs.title: What brain a new agent starts on
docs.text:
You almost never have to pick one. Every agent you add — from the New agent dialog, from an integration, or asked for in plain language — starts on default:turbo, the deployment's everyday brain. On an Olano-managed deployment that resolves to olano:turbo, so it works on credits from its first turn with nothing to configure; on a bring-your-own-key install it resolves to the bring-your-own-key target shown in Config → Default models.

AgentFather starts on default:turbo as well. Its turns are conversation and tool calls — a catalog lookup, a config change behind an approval card, a log read — and the everyday brain answers those in a beat where the deeper tier made every one of them wait. It used to start on default:pro; an AgentFather still on that tier from an earlier version is moved to default:turbo on the next runtime start, unless you picked a different model for it yourself. If you want it on the deeper tier for a hard design session, change its model in the Overview tab or use /model for that one conversation — a choice you make is never rewritten.

Two things override this, in order:

  1. A model you name. Ask for an agent on a specific model, or set one in the New agent dialog, and that is what you get — even if its provider is not connected yet (you get a warning, not a substitution).
  2. A preferred_model in your home config, which applies to agents installed without naming a model.

Changing an agent's model later is one field — the Overview tab of the agent's page in the dashboard, model in agent.json5, or /model for a single conversation. Nothing rewrites a model you chose yourself.

docs.title: Utility models
docs.text:
Two Olano groups exist that are not tiers and never appear in a model picker:

  • olano:vision — backs image_describe, so an agent can see images.
  • the Olano image group — backs image_generate and image_edit.

The product calls these on the agent's behalf. They guarantee a capability (accepts images, produces images) rather than a speed-and-capability point, which is why they stay independent of the tiers. They cannot be an agent's brain — setting one as model, cognition.fast_model or cognition.deep_model makes the config fail to load.

On a managed deployment these run on credits automatically, so vision, image generation, image editing, speech-to-text and text-to-speech all work with zero configuration. To use your own provider instead, pin it in config.yaml under media: (vision, image) and speech: (voice) — see media: — vision and image generation.

docs.title: Credits
docs.text:
Credits are the unit for everything Olano-managed: model calls on the tiers, the utility models behind vision, image and speech, and managed services such as web search and LinkedIn outreach.

  • The dashboard shows your balance and what has been consumed; the Insights tab breaks usage down by agent, by model tier ("Credits by tier"), and by kind of work ("Where credits went": chat, Cortex, scheduled tasks, highlights, subagents…). Every model and service call records its charge on the deployment as it happens, so these figures are measured locally and include background work. Your account balance (Overview's "Credits left", and the cloud deployment page) is the billing-period view — a different window than the charts, so the totals need not match exactly.
  • credits.display in config.yaml switches cost displays between usd and credits. It is a display setting only.
  • Buy more from Olano Cloud (see Olano Cloud).
  • Per-agent budget caps (see Budgets) work alongside credits to stop one agent consuming everything.

docs.title: Olano credits on a self-hosted install
docs.text:
A self-hosted install can run on Olano credits too. It takes an Olano API key instead of a deployment:

  1. On cloud.olano.ai, open API keys and create a key. It is shown once; copy it whole (it starts with sk-olano-). You can create several, one per install, and revoke any of them there at any time.
  2. Buy account credits on the Billing page. They belong to your account, not to any deployment, and they never expire.
  3. Paste the key on the dashboard's Providers → Olano card, or in the AI provider panel of the setup wizard. The dashboard checks the key with your account before storing it in the vault.

From then on the install behaves like a managed one for billing: the Olano tiers, image generation and editing, vision, transcription, web search and page fetching run on your account's credits with no provider account; agents on the default:* tiers switch to the Olano tiers at their next start; the Overview and Insights pages show the credit book, and credits.display defaults to credits (you can still choose dollars). Everything else about the box is unchanged: it is still yours, with no plan, no cloud card and no hidden sections.

The same key also lets the install sign in to MCP servers through Olano's sign-in service, so a box without a domain or certificate of its own can still finish an MCP server's sign-in (MCP servers). That covers MCP servers only: the one-click Connect with Olano's app on the Connections tab stays an Olano Cloud feature, and a self-hosted install connects those services with its own OAuth app.

Removing the key (same card) reverses all of it: default-tier agents go back to your provider keys at their next start, and the managed image, speech and web services switch off until a key is connected again. A box with no key and no deployment has no credit balance; there BYOK is the only route, and cost tracking is in dollars against your own provider bills.

docs.title: When a managed service says it is temporarily unavailable
docs.text:
Sometimes an agent answers with something like "The turbo tier (Olano-managed) is temporarily unavailable — the request was refused upstream of this deployment." That is an Olano-side problem, not yours:

  • Your credits are untouched. Nothing was consumed, and the balance you see is still yours to spend.
  • Nothing on your deployment is misconfigured. There is no key to set and no setting to change — a message that asks you to fix a credential is a different error with different wording.
  • Your own provider keys keep working. If you have BYOK configured, pointing the agent at one of your own models (dashboard → the agent → Model, or /model in chat) keeps it running until the tier recovers.

The message names what is affected. It can be a tier you chose (the turbo tier, the pro tier) or one of the services Olano runs on the agent's behalf — image understanding, for instance, which is what reading an image uses. That distinction matters: if it names a single service, everything else keeps working, and only the requests that need that service fail.

You will not see it for a passing blip. Olano retries a request like this a few times on its own, waiting a little longer between attempts, before it gives up and tells you — so a message that does appear means the problem has already outlasted several tries.

Wait a few minutes and send the message again. If it still fails, write to support@olano.ai and say which service the message named. In dashboard chat the error carries an Email support button that opens a pre-filled message naming the service and your deployment.

Two nearby errors that read similarly but mean the opposite, because the fix is yours in both cases:

What it says What it means out of olano credits … buy more on your deployment card Your balance is spent. Buy credits (see Olano Cloud); BYOK models keep working meanwhile. Your Olano account is out of credits Same, on a self-hosted install running on an Olano API key: buy account credits on the Billing page at cloud.olano.ai. Your Olano API key was not accepted The key pasted on Providers → Olano was revoked on cloud.olano.ai or pasted incompletely. Create a new one under API keys and paste it whole; nothing retries on its own. No Olano API key is connected on this box A self-hosted install with no Olano API key (none pasted, or it was removed) still has an agent on an Olano tier. Connect a key on Providers → Olano, or switch that agent to a provider model. your <provider> account is out of balance A BYOK provider account of yours ran dry. Top it up with that provider.

docs.title: Olano Cloud
docs.text:
cloud.olano.ai is the managed service: instead of installing and maintaining Olano yourself, you deploy an instance there and Olano runs it for you.

What you can do there:

  • Deploy a dedicated Olano instance in a few minutes. You choose the size — instances come in a range of CPU, memory and disk configurations — and you get your own dashboard at your own address.
  • Scale an instance up as your workload grows, and buy additional disk space when you need it.
  • Stay current. New Olano releases are made available to your instance, and you are notified when an update is ready, so you decide when to take it rather than discovering a version drift months later.
  • Take snapshots of an instance, so you have a restore point before a risky change.
  • Encrypted at rest. New instances keep all of their data on an encrypted volume that unlocks itself at boot (standard custody, Privacy and security). The console's Security tab shows the state of the volume; the recovery key, the one part only you hold, is created from the instance's own dashboard under Config → Disk encryption.
  • Buy credit packs on top of what your subscription includes, for months where your agents do more.
  • Run a self-hosted install on credits. Create an API key and buy account credits: they belong to your account, never expire, and any install you paste the key into spends them (see Models and credits).
  • Watch usage — what your agents consumed, by agent and over time.
  • Manage billing and your subscription — plans, payment method, invoices.
  • Organizations. Deployments belong to an organization, so a team can share access to the same instances.

Everything in this guide applies identically to a cloud deployment: the same dashboard, the same agent.json5, the same features. The differences are that Olano handles the infrastructure, Olano-managed models are available out of the box on credits, and your plan's entitlements may hide dashboard sections your deployment does not include.

Current plans, sizes and pricing are on cloud.olano.ai — they change as the offering evolves, so check there rather than relying on a figure written down somewhere else.

docs.title: organization.yaml — the org chart
docs.text:
A deployment-wide file at ~/.olano/organization.yaml holding the reporting structure and messaging rules for every agent in one place. Once it exists it supersedes each agent's own org: block — the per-agent settings are seeded into it once, and after that this file is the source of truth.

Edit it from the dashboard's Org Chart tab rather than by hand. The chart enforces consistency for you: if you say A manages B, it makes B report to A, and it refuses structures that would create a management cycle.

Why it exists: reporting lines are inherently a statement about two agents, and keeping both halves in two separate files invites them to disagree. One file means one answer to "who can talk to whom".

docs.title: What Olano is
docs.text:
Olano runs agents: long-lived AI workers that hold their own memory, reach real systems through tools, and talk to people on the messaging platforms those people already use.

An agent is four things:

Piece What it is Configuration agent.json5 — the agent's name, model, prompt, tools, channels, schedule, permissions. Workspace A directory the agent owns: its memory, notes, files, skills, and scratch space. A model The reasoning engine. Either an Olano-managed tier billed in credits, or your own provider key. Surfaces How work reaches it: the dashboard, a messaging channel, a schedule, a webhook, or another agent.

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text:
• The runtime is one long-running process. It boots every agent, keeps the channels connected, runs the scheduler, and serves the dashboard API.
  • The dashboard is the web control panel — the primary way to operate a deployment. Everything in this guide that mentions a "tab" means a dashboard section.
  • The agents themselves. Every agent carries built-in tools to configure itself, connect services, and send magic links so a person can finish a sign-in or hand over a key from their own phone; AgentFather carries the tools to manage the whole deployment. Asking an agent is a first-class way to operate Olano, not a shortcut — see Ask the agent: self-configuration, magic links and admin tools.
  • The vault is the encrypted credential store. Every API key, bot token and service password lives there. Credentials never belong in a config file.

How the pieces fit together:

flowchart TB
    subgraph surfaces["Where work comes from"]
        direction LR
        D["Dashboard"] ~~~ M["Messengers"] ~~~ S["Schedules"] ~~~ W["Webhooks<br/>and email"] ~~~ X["Other agents,<br/>outside platforms"]
    end
    subgraph runtime["The Olano runtime"]
        direction LR
        AG["Your agents<br/>each with its own workspace,<br/>memory and tools"] ~~~ AF["AgentFather<br/>manages the deployment"] ~~~ V[("Vault<br/>every credential")]
    end
    subgraph reach["What agents use"]
        direction LR
        LLM["Models<br/>Olano tiers or your keys"] ~~~ T["Files, web,<br/>a sandboxed shell"] ~~~ C["Connected services"] ~~~ MCP["MCP servers"]
    end
    surfaces --> runtime --> reach

docs.title: Where things live on disk
docs.text:
Olano keeps everything under one home directory, ~/.olano/ by default (override with OLANO_HOME). An install made under an earlier default keeps the ~/olano/ or ~/.lionclaw/ it already has; nothing is moved.

About the name lionclaw. Olano was first called lionclaw: it was built in Singapore, the Lion City. The name survives in a few identifiers that are kept so existing installs keep working: the LIONCLAW_* environment variables (every one also accepts the OLANO_* spelling), the lionclaw_docker backend, the lionclaw_memory default collection, and the older home and state-folder names ~/.lionclaw/ and .lionclaw/. Wherever you see it, read it as Olano.

~/.olano/
  config.yaml                       # deployment-wide settings  (config.yaml reference)
  organization.yaml                 # the org chart             (organization.yaml)
  agents/<name>/
    agent.json5                     # that agent's config       (agent.json5 reference)
    workspace/                      # that agent's own files
      AGENTS.md                     # operating instructions
      SOUL.md                       # persona, tone, boundaries
      IDENTITY.md                   # who the agent is
      USER.md                       # who it works for
      TOOLS.md                      # notes on tool usage
      MEMORY.md                     # durable learned facts
      memories/YYYY-MM-DD.md        # daily logs
      notes/                        # the markdown wiki
      knowledgebase/                # documents indexed for search
      skills/                       # reusable procedures
      reports/                      # every file the agent produces for you
      uploads/                      # files you send it in chat
      downloads/  scratch/  trash/  # conventions the tools use
      system/                       # Olano-owned; replaced on upgrade
  sessions/                         # conversation transcripts
  vault/                            # encrypted credentials

The files under system/ are managed by Olano and overwritten when you upgrade. Everything else is yours — edit it freely, from the dashboard Files tab or a text editor. The agent reads AGENTS.md, SOUL.md, IDENTITY.md, USER.md, MEMORY.md, TOOLS.md and the recent daily logs at the start of every conversation, so editing them changes how the agent behaves on its next reply.

docs.title: Self-hosted or Olano Cloud
docs.text:
Olano runs the same either way:

  • Self-hosted — you install it on your own machine or server and bring your own model provider keys, or run on Olano credits with an Olano API key from cloud.olano.ai.
  • Olano Cloud (cloud.olano.ai) — a managed instance you deploy in a few minutes, kept up to date for you, with Olano-managed models billed in credits so you never need a provider account. See Olano Cloud.

You can mix: a cloud deployment can still use your own provider keys, and a self-hosted install can use whatever providers you have alongside Olano credits.

docs.title: Two interfaces: full dashboard and simple chat
docs.text:
Olano can show a person one of two entirely different screens after they sign in, chosen per account:

  • Full dashboard — the complete control panel described in the rest of this section: every agent, the scheduler, files, memory, tools, connectors, configuration and diagnostics. This is the default for every account, including all existing ones, so nothing changes for anyone unless you change it deliberately.
  • Simple chat — a stripped agent-chat app. A list of the agents that person has been given, the conversation with the selected one, attachments, voice, and the agent's profile. No settings, no diagnostics, no token counts, no model pickers. Suited to staff who only need to talk to an agent and would find the full console noisy.

People can also create agents of their own here: the New agent button in the agent list (and on the you-have-no-agents screen) builds one from a template or from a plain-words description. It asks for a name — a real name, like "Hillary" — and shows the permanent handle it will generate from it; a template's own label becomes the agent's title (shown under its name in the profile and chat header), never its name. A Model dropdown lists only the models this deployment can run right now — the deployment defaults, the Olano tiers and any provider connected with its own key — pre-selected to Default · Turbo; with a template picked, Template's own model keeps the one it was designed for. Admins always have the button; members have it while member bot creation is on, which it is by default — see the self_serve_agents: block in config.yaml reference and Config → Member bot creation.

By default the simple view shows replies only, with a single "working on it" line while the agent acts. A detail button in the chat header cycles three levels — Quiet, Normal (one compact line per tool the agent uses), Verbose (each tool's full input and result, the same rendering the full dashboard shows) — and typing /quiet, /normal or /verbose does the same. The choice is remembered per browser. Typing /context shows the same context-usage card the full dashboard's chat offers: how much of the agent's working memory this conversation and its setup are using.

When the agent asks another agent for something, that "working on it" line is replaced by a more specific one — "maria is thinking…", with that agent's own face beside it — and it clears the moment the answer comes back. It shows at every level, Quiet included, because it is about who is working rather than about tools. Without it the chat looks frozen for as long as the other agent takes, which can be a while. What that agent says comes back inside this agent's reply rather than as a message of its own.

The agent list is built for real fleets. The selected agent's chats unfold under its row, each labelled with where it came from — SCHEDULED, TELEGRAM, WHATSAPP, AGENT and so on, the same badges the full dashboard's conversation list uses; an ordinary chat typed here carries no badge. A row of filter chips (All · Chats · Telegram · Scheduled · Agents · …) narrows the list to one source — the way to hide a chatty schedule's runs — and the choice is remembered per agent on that browser. The list under an agent shows only the most recent handful; "Show all N chats" opens the full list in the right-hand panel, with a search box, the same filter chips, and paging ("Show more") so an agent with hundreds of conversations stays fast. Selecting an agent opens its latest conversation — the newest one a person is in, typed here or arrived over a messenger, then the newest of any kind, and a fresh chat only when there is nothing at all (a fresh chat is not saved until you send something, so reopening an agent never piles up empty ones); switching agents and back keeps the chat you had open. A chevron at the end of every agent row folds or unfolds its chats in place: on the selected agent it is the fold, on any other it selects that agent and unfolds its chats without leaving the list. It shows on hover on a desktop (always on the selected row) and is always visible on a phone, where it is how you browse an agent's chats from the drawer — tap the chevron, then the chat you want; tapping the agent's name goes to its latest chat and closes the drawer. On a desktop, clicking the selected agent's row also folds its chats away (click again to unfold); right-clicking any agent opens a quick menu — new chat, see all chats, its profile, pin/unpin, move the row up or down, mark its unread as read; right-clicking a chat offers to rename, open or delete it. On a wide screen the whole list can be resized by dragging its right edge (double-click the edge to reset); the width is remembered per browser.

Arranging it. Each of the three headings — Pinned, All agents, Group chats — folds away on a click and stays folded on that browser, so a long list can be cut down to the part you use. Agents can be dragged up and down to the order you want, and dragged across the divider between Pinned and All agents to pin or unpin them; that order is remembered per browser too, and an untouched list stays alphabetical. Dragging is off while the search box has something in it (the order it would write covers agents the filter is hiding) — use Move up / Move down on the right-click menu instead, which is also the way to do it from a phone or a keyboard.

Offline agents fold away. Under All agents, the agents that can answer come first. Agents that are paused (someone pressed Stop) or not running sit behind one N offline row at the foot of the list, closed until you click it; the choice is remembered on this browser. Opened, those rows are drawn dimmed. A few agents never fold: pinned ones, the agent you have open, and any with unread replies. When nothing under All agents is running (while the deployment starts up, say), the rows are listed flat instead, and while the search box has text in it every match shows, folded or not. The dot on each face says where an agent stands: green answers right away, amber is starting, stopping or not available on this deployment, red failed to start, and grey is paused or not running. For amber and red the reason is written on the row itself, under the name.

The button beside the Agents heading collapses the list to a strip of faces: names, previews, search and the open agent's chats go, the three headings stay, and clicking a face switches agents. Handy when a conversation wants the width; the same button brings the list back, at the width you had set.

Right-clicking the empty space below the list offers the two things this rail can create — New agent and New group — which is the fast way to either from anywhere in the list. (Right-clicking a row still offers that row's own actions; see above.)

A notification bell sits at the head of the list, the same one the full dashboard carries and fed by the same source: anything this deployment needs a person for — a channel that failed to start, a connector asking to be signed in, an action waiting on an approval — shows a count there and lists itself when you click it. View all opens the Overview panel below.

More. Below the group section, under a divider, a collapsible More group holds five of the full dashboard's pages — Overview, Insights, Issues, Cortex and Files — and opens them in place of the conversation. They are the same pages, not cut-down versions: Overview is the deployment snapshot with its notifications and approvals, Insights is usage and spend, Issues is the tracker, Cortex is what the agent has been thinking about, and Files is its workspace. Picking an agent, one of its chats, a group, or New chat while a page is open returns to the conversation (on a phone the drawer closes on it, as it does over a chat), and the browser's Back button brings the page back. A page a deployment has switched off in Config is not listed here either.

More starts closed on a browser that has never opened it, and after that it is whatever you left it — open it and it stays open across reloads, close it and it stays closed. Pages can also be dragged out of More into the space just above it, exactly as the full dashboard's own nav items can, so the one or two you actually use stay visible with More shut; drag them back in to undo it. Right-clicking a page offers the same move, which is how to do it from a phone or a keyboard. The arrangement is remembered per browser and is separate from the full dashboard's own — rearranging one does not disturb the other.

The account menu at the bottom of the agent list holds theme and language — one dropdown each — and, on a team install, Sign out; for an admin it also has the Simple view switch, which flips back to the full dashboard. It opens whole with the list collapsed to a strip too, hanging off the strip rather than being cut to its width.

Set it per person in Admin → Users, in the Interface column. On a single-user install (no team accounts) the equivalent switch is the ui_mode key in config.yaml — see config.yaml reference.

This is a display choice, not a permission. Moving someone to Simple chat does not restrict what they are allowed to do, and moving them to the full dashboard does not grant them anything. What a person may actually see and do is decided entirely by their role (admin or member) and by which agents they have been given access to, and those rules are enforced by the server whichever interface is on their screen. Use the Interface setting to reduce clutter; use Role and per-agent access to control access.

docs.title: The full dashboard
docs.text:
The dashboard is the control panel for the whole deployment. The sidebar lists every section; you can reorder it by dragging, and the search box (top left) jumps to a section, an agent, a task, or an individual setting by name.

Section What it is for Overview Which agents are online, notifications, and the Approvals inbox. Insights Token and cost usage over time, per agent and per model. Chat Talk to any agent you have access to, one thread per conversation. Agents The roster: create, start, stop and edit agents. Cortex The background work agents do between conversations. Scheduler Every scheduled job: what runs, when, and how it went. Issues A work tracker shared by agents and people. Revisions Version history of configuration and markdown files. Calendar Scheduled work laid out on a calendar. Files Browse and edit agent workspaces. Memory What each agent remembers, and where you correct it. Notes Each agent's linked markdown wiki. Knowledge Documents indexed so agents can search them by meaning. Tools Every tool on the deployment, and why a locked one is locked. Providers Model providers and which of them are usable here. Connections Sign agents in to GitHub, Google, Microsoft 365 and more. Vault Encrypted API keys, tokens and passwords. Admin only. Agent to Agent Messages between agents, and calls from outside the deployment. Org Chart Who manages whom, which also decides who may message whom. Logs Runtime logs by agent and severity. Admin only. Terminal A shell in an agent's workspace, in the browser. Playground Try prompts against an agent without touching a real conversation. Config Deployment-wide settings. Admin only. Admin Accounts, roles and per-agent access. Admin only.

docs.title: Addresses, reload and Back
docs.text:
Every page's address says where you are, so reloading the page, copying the link, or using the browser's Back and Forward buttons lands you in the same place. The address names:

  • The agent, on pages that are about one agent: /chat/<agent>, /memory/<agent>, /notes/<agent>, /knowledge/<agent>, /terminal/<agent>, /cortex/<agent> and /agents/<agent>. On pages that cover every agent (Files, Connections, Scheduler, Logs, Overview) the agent is optional and only narrows the page: /scheduler/<agent> shows that agent's jobs, /scheduler shows everyone's.
  • The tab inside a page: /agents/<agent>/tools, /cortex/<agent>/ideas, /knowledge/<agent>/sources, /insights/drill, /calendar/week.
  • What is open: the conversation (?thread=), the file in Files (?path=), the issue (?issue=), the note (?note=), the Cortex item, the scheduled task (?task=), the Agent to Agent conversation (?pair=), the revision, the Org Chart node.

Moving somewhere (another conversation, another agent, another tab, opening an item) is a step the Back button returns from. Filtering or searching is not: Back never replays your typing. Opening a page from the sidebar still returns you to the tab and item you were last on.

Older links keep working: an address in an earlier form (for example a notification that says ?tab=mcp, or a bookmark of /chat?thread=…) is rewritten to the current one when it opens. A link naming an agent that no longer exists, or that your account cannot see, opens the same page for your current agent instead, with a notice.

docs.title: Finding a setting by name
docs.text:
The search box — or ⌘K / Ctrl+K from anywhere — also searches the deployment's settings, not just the list of sections. Type what the setting is called ("voice replies", "sandbox memory", "link lifetime", "deep model") and the results list the matching controls under a Settings heading, each showing the section it lives in (for example Config › Speech). Choosing one opens that page and scrolls straight to the control, highlighting it for a moment so you can see which of the page's many fields you were sent to.

Searching matches a setting's name, the section it sits in, common synonyms, and its help text — so a word you remember from the description finds it even when you don't recall the exact label. Several words narrow the results rather than widening them: "telegram allowed" finds only settings matching both.

Settings you are not allowed to change never appear: the whole Config page is admin-only, so a member account searching for "sandbox memory" gets no result for it rather than a link that then refuses them.

The sidebar has three parts. At the top, the search box and, right under it, the New agent button. Then your agents, the same list the simple chat shell shows: a Pinned heading, any groups you have made, All agents and, when group chats are on, Group chats. There is no separate agent dropdown: clicking an agent here selects it everywhere (the pages that are about one agent — Memory, Notes, Knowledge, Terminal — also carry their own picker in their top bar). Hover an agent to reveal its pin button (always visible on a touch screen): pinning keeps it under Pinned, on this device; click again to unpin. Right-click an agent for the rest — new chat, all chats, its page, move up or down, move to a group — and right-click anywhere else on the sidebar (a heading, the empty space, even the bar's foot) to make a new group to sort agents into. Below the agents, under a rule, a collapsible More group holds every day-to-day section: Overview, Insights, Cortex and Issues lead it, then the rest. Drag any tab to reorder More; that order is saved to your account, so it follows you to any browser you sign in from.

The setup and administration pages are not tabs at all. They live in the account menu — click your name at the bottom-left of the sidebar — in two groups: Setup holds Providers, Connections and Tools; Administration (admins only) holds Vault, Logs, Config and Admin. While one of those pages is open, your avatar carries the highlight the tabs would otherwise show. Every one of them is also a keystroke away in the ⌘K search.

The same menu holds Theme and Language, one dropdown each; both apply the moment you pick and are remembered per browser. Thirteen themes. The two house themes lead the list, and the other eleven follow dark-first:

Theme Page Accent Olano Dark (the default) warm charcoal Olano orange Olano Light neutral off-white Olano orange Midnight deep navy azure Mocha espresso brown copper Cool Black pure black green Volt black, dark-grey cards electric chartreuse, with black type on buttons Black & White white black — no colour but the states Harbor cool slate deep teal Sepia warm parchment — nothing in it is pure white umber Sakura blush pink deep rose Pastel Green soft sage emerald Singapore red blush, white cards the flag's red High Contrast white deep blue, with visible hairlines everywhere

Cortex keeps its violet in every one of them. High Contrast is the accessibility choice rather than a taste one: body text is black on white and every status colour is pushed well past the usual readability floor. Sepia is the one to pick for long reading at night — no surface in it is pure white, so nothing on the page glares. Volt is the same theme the mobile app offers under that name, so a phone and a browser can match. The sun/moon button beside the bell at the top of the sidebar cycles through the same thirteen.

There is no separate Chat tab: click an agent to open the chat with it (the full chat, with its mode, detail, model and reasoning controls). An agent's row shows a pulsing dot while it is working on a reply and a count of replies that landed while you were elsewhere. Type "chat" into the search box if you want the chat page by name.

Clicking an agent opens its latest conversation, not an empty one: the most recent chat a person is in — typed in the dashboard or arrived over a messenger such as Telegram or WhatsApp — wins, then the most recent thread of any kind (a scheduled run, an exchange with another agent), and only an agent with no history at all starts a fresh chat. A fresh chat is not saved until you send something, so opening an agent again and again never litters its list with empty conversations. Switching agents and back keeps the conversation you had open. The address names both the agent and the conversation (/chat/<agent>?thread=…), so a reload, a copied link or the browser's Back button reopens exactly that conversation with that agent.

The selected agent unfolds into its recent chats right under its name, the way the simple view's rail does: a New chat row, a row of filter chips (All, Chats for conversations typed in the dashboard, Mobile for those had in the Olano mobile app, one chip per messaging app the agent talks on, Scheduled, Agents), the newest few conversations badged with where they came from, and Show all N chats — which opens the chat page's full list with search and multi-select delete. The chips only appear once the agent has more than one kind of chat, and the one you pick is remembered per agent on this device (the simple view reads the same choice). Click a chat to open it; right-click it for Open, Rename… (a name of your own, in place — Enter saves, Escape cancels; leave it empty to go back to the automatic title) and Delete chat (after a confirmation; admins of the agent only). The trash can on a hovered row deletes too. The chevron at the end of every agent row folds or unfolds its chats without leaving the page you are on — on a phone it is always visible, and it is how you browse an agent's chats from the drawer: tap the chevron, then the chat you want. Tapping the agent's name opens its latest chat instead.

Right-click an agent for its menu: New chat (a fresh conversation), Show / Hide its chats (the chevron's fold, for keyboards and long-presses), See all chats (the chat page with its conversation list open), About this agent (its page — profile, model, tools, channels), Pin / Unpin, Move up / Move down, Move to a group, and Mark N new as read when it has unread replies. Every item explains itself in its tooltip.

Groups are sections you make yourself to sort agents into — "Sales", "Personal". Right-click the empty space in the agent list (or any heading) and choose New group…, type a name and press Enter. Right-click a group's heading to Rename it or Delete it; only an empty group can be deleted — move its agents out first — and Pinned and All agents can never be. An agent is only ever in one place: pinning it takes it out of its group, and moving it into a group unpins it. Click any heading to fold that section away. Pins, groups and their order are remembered in this browser only; they change nothing about the agents themselves. With a row focused, the Up and Down arrow keys move through the list and Home and End jump to its ends.

Offline agents fold away here too. Under All agents, the agents that can answer come first, and the ones that are paused (someone pressed Stop on the agent's page) or not running sit behind one N offline row, closed until you click it and remembered on this browser. Opened, they are drawn dimmed. Pinned agents, agents in your own groups, the agent you have open and agents with unread replies always show, whatever their state, and when nothing under All agents is running the rows are listed flat. The dot on each face: green answers right away, amber is starting, stopping or not available on this deployment (for example over its agent limit), red failed to start, grey is paused or not running. Hover a row for what its dot means and, for amber and red, why. In the collapsed strip the row shows just the count.

Admins — and members, while Config → Member bot creation is on — also get a New agent button under the search box (or ⌘N / Ctrl+N). It is the same short flow as the simple shell's: a name, what the agent should be good at (a template, or from scratch), and which model it runs on. The model dropdown lists only what this deployment can run right now — the deployment defaults (Default · Turbo / Pro / Max), the Olano managed tiers (billed in credits, no key needed) and any provider you have connected with your own key — and comes pre-selected to Default · Turbo, the fast everyday tier. With a template picked, Template's own model keeps the model the template was designed for. The model can be changed later from the agent's page.

Four sections are admin-only and never appear for member accounts: Vault, Logs, Config, Admin. On a managed cloud deployment, other tabs can also be hidden by your plan's entitlements — if a section you expect is missing and you are an admin, that is why.

docs.title: Installing it on a phone or tablet
docs.text:
There is also an Olano app for iPhone, iPad, Android and Apple silicon Macs, from the App Store and Google Play: chats, Cortex and an inbox of approvals and alerts, built for the phone, with notifications; see The mobile app. Everything below is about the browser version, which needs no store at all.

The dashboard can be added to a phone's home screen and then behaves like an app: its own icon, full screen with no browser address bar, and the sign-in kept between launches. There is nothing to download — it is the same dashboard at the same address, and both interfaces (full dashboard and simple chat) work this way.

The same chat on a phone.
  • iPhone and iPad. Open the dashboard in Safari, tap the Share button in the toolbar, scroll down to Add to Home Screen, and tap Add. Safari is the only browser on iOS that can do this. A prompt at the bottom of the screen offers the same steps the first time you visit on a phone; dismissing it is remembered.
  • Android. Chrome shows an Install button in the same prompt, and also offers Install app in its own menu. Once installed, Olano appears in the Android share sheet: sharing a link or a note from another app opens the chat with that text already in the message box, waiting for you to add to it and send. Nothing is ever sent automatically.
  • Desktop. Chrome and Edge can install it too, from the icon at the right of the address bar. There is no prompt for this — a browser tab is a perfectly good home for the dashboard on a computer.

An installed copy keeps working well enough to read the last screen you were on when the network drops, but it is not an offline app: agents run on the deployment, so sending a message needs a connection. When a new version of the dashboard has been deployed, a small A new version of Olano is ready bar appears with a Reload button; the update is applied when you choose it, so it can never interrupt a message you are part-way through writing.

Installing requires the dashboard to be served over https, which cloud deployments always are. A self-hosted box reached over plain http (or by IP address on a home network) cannot be installed — it still works normally in the browser.

The installed app follows the phone's screen shape: on an iPhone it runs edge to edge, filling the screen from the top to the bottom edge, with the header clear of the status bar and the message box clear of the home indicator — no unused band at either end. It measures the screen it is actually on, so the same is true on every iPhone and Android size, on an iPad, and after rotating the device. Both the full dashboard and simple chat behave this way.

If a screen ever says "This view failed to load", press Reload on the card. That clears the app's stored copy of the old version and fetches the current one — it is the fix for a page that was left open across a deployment. If it keeps happening on the same screen, close the app entirely and open it again.

docs.title: Admin (admin only)
docs.text:
Opened, like Config, from the account menu at the bottom-left of the sidebar (under Administration) or from the ⌘K search.

User accounts and access. Invite people, set them as admin or member, and grant per-agent access. The access overview shows, for every agent, exactly who can reach it — including admins, who can administer every agent without holding an explicit grant. Bulk actions apply one role across many users and agents at once, which is what makes onboarding and offboarding a single step.

All of it is also available from an AgentFather conversation: ask it to invite someone (you get back a single-use set-password link plus a QR code image to forward — it never asks for or sets a password in chat), reset a password (a fresh link + QR; the person sets their own and is signed in), make someone admin or member, enable/disable an account, assign an owner or member to an agent, or show the whole access grid. Every change asks a human for approval first, and only admins can trigger these — a member chatting with AgentFather cannot see or manage accounts. If the link comes back without a QR or absolute address, the deployment doesn't know its public URL yet: open the dashboard once from a browser (or set the public URL) and ask again.

Each account carries two names, and neither is ever empty. Name is what everyone sees, and it can be changed at any time — but never erased (a blank edit is refused). Handle is a permanent public identifier — lowercase letters, digits and dashes, like carlos-m — and it cannot be changed once the account exists, because it is what identifies that person in the issue tracker (as human-<handle>). A third, optional field is the person's Title — their position, like Head of Sales — shown under their name in the account menu, on the org chart and in the access tables, the same way an agent's title is. Set it when inviting someone or edit it in the Users table at any time; it changes nothing about what they may do.

The Langfuse column decides whether an admin sees Langfuse links in the dashboard: one under each traced reply in the chat (in both interfaces) and the Open in Langfuse link on an Insights conversation. It is off for every account by default, existing ones included, so turning tracing on does not put a debugging link under everyone's replies; switch it on for the admins who debug with Langfuse. It only shows or hides the links: tracing itself is set in Config → Observability and keeps running either way. Members show Admins only there and never see the links, because trace data is admin-only. A single-user install has no Users table, so its owner always sees them.

The handle field appears everywhere an account is created: the first-run owner screen, this invite form, and the chat "secure your dashboard" link (the onboarding wizard's profile panel shows the handle it will generate from your name, read-only). It checks availability live as you type and shows exactly what will be saved. A handle you type that is already taken is refused with the next free one suggested — you are never silently given a variant of the identity you chose. Leave the field empty instead and one is generated automatically from the name (or the part of the email before the @); auto-generated handles quietly get a number on a clash, since nobody chose them. An account created with no name at all gets a presentable one derived from its handle (dana-ray → Dana Ray). A handle is not a login: people still sign in with their email address and password.

docs.title: Agent to Agent
docs.text:
A live view of messages passing between agents: who asked whom to do what, and what came back. The place to look when a delegation chain does not behave the way you expected.

Delegations between agents, grouped by pair, with each message and its reply.

Calls that cross the deployment boundary are listed here too, under the External segment, and never mixed in with peer conversations: an outside system asking one of your agents over MCP or A2A shows the caller by the label of the token or sign-in it used, with an MCP or A2A badge and a globe instead of an agent avatar; an agent calling a remote A2A agent shows the remote by its configured name with an A2A badge. Open a row to read the full exchange. The same conversations appear in the agent's Chat history carrying an External pill plus the protocol pill, and the agent's External access tab lists its most recent inbound calls with links to both views.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
The roster: every agent, online or offline, with its emoji, model, and status. From here you create agents (from a ready-made archetype or from scratch), start, stop and restart them, and open one for editing.

The roster. Each card shows the agent's title, model and status, with quick Chat, Restart and Stop buttons.

Stopping is not deleting. A stopped agent keeps its config, workspace, memory and history, and stays offline across runtime restarts until you start it again. Prefer stopping over deleting when you just want an agent out of the way.

Opening an agent gives you a detail page with these tabs:

Tab What you set there Overview Name, emoji, colour, avatar, description, model, system prompt, and the core behaviour switches. Subagents Specialists this agent can delegate to (see Agent-to-agent and the org chart). Tools Which tools the agent may use, by category, with a description of each. Connectors Messaging channels — Telegram, Slack, WhatsApp, email and the rest (see Channels and connectors). MCP External MCP servers this agent connects to, with live connection health (see MCP servers). Browser The agent's web browser: what it has open, who is in control, and whether it has saved sign-ins. Watching the screen and Take control happen in the browser window in the agent's chat; Open chat goes there, and Hand back to the agent shows here while you hold control. Close browser and Forget sign-ins are here too. Below them, When a site asks for a person (wait for you, hold with no time limit, or skip; empty uses Config → Browser, see Browser control) a Debug trace for a check that keeps coming back (see Browser control), and Actions that don't ask: the narrow rules (a site, and send / submit / sign up on it) that let the agent act there without an approval card; admins and the agent's owners edit them, everyone else sees them read-only (see Browser control). Webhooks Inbound and outbound webhooks (see Webhooks). Commands Which slash commands are exposed, plus your own custom ones. What you enable here is what the messengers' slash menus offer; changes apply without a restart. Monetization Paid subscriptions for this agent's end users (see Subscriptions and monetization).
