Multi-user Per-end-user isolation for a shared agent (see Multi-user: two different features), plus Message policy — message length caps, silence rules and a reply-length ceiling, which apply to any agent (see agent.json5 reference). Skills Reusable procedures the agent can follow. Every skill opens: see Reading a skill. Talk to Agent Who may message this agent and who it may message, plus its place in the org chart (see Agent-to-agent and the org chart). Pages Pages this agent publishes at /pages/<slug>/: each page's kind (files, static build or server), its state, last error and logs, with Restart and Stop, plus the viewer password that guards all of them. See Pages. Variables Per-agent environment values. Advanced Backend/sandbox, ACP, budgets, prompt mode, iteration limits. Config The raw agent.json5, when the raw editor is enabled. An agent's detail page, Overview tab: identity, model and reasoning effort.

The Overview tab also carries an Observability (Langfuse) card: whether this agent's turns are traced, what each trace contains and the share of turns traced. Each choice can be Follow Config, which keeps the deployment's setting from Config → Observability, or a value of this agent's own. The line at the bottom says what is in effect right now, including where the keys come from. Changes apply from the agent's next turn, with no restart. To send this agent's traces to a different Langfuse project, an admin saves keys for it; the card's settings and the Config card's keys are admin-only.

Most changes need a Restart of that agent to take effect. The UI tells you when one is pending.

docs.title: Reading a skill
docs.text:
The Skills tab lists every skill this agent can actually reach, and each row carries two labels that tell you what you are looking at before you open it:

  • Where it lives. Common skill — the shared set every agent on the box loads. Agent skill — this agent's own, in its workspace. Learned skill — one the agent wrote for itself. Configured skill — from an extra directory named in the agent's skills setting.
  • Whether you can change it here. Editable or Read-only. Common skills are read-only from an agent's page on purpose: they are shared, so editing one from a single agent would quietly change what every other agent loads. Change those in the shared skills folder on the box, or ask AgentFather (olano_install_skill for every agent, olano_create_skill for a new one).

docs.title: Switching a skill on or off
docs.text:
Every row also carries an on/off switch. It decides whether this agent loads that skill — nothing more:

  • Off means the skill is not described in the agent's prompt, cannot be delegated to, and is ignored by the agent's self-learning. The agent behaves as though it does not have it.
  • The skill is not deleted. It stays on disk and stays in this list, marked Off, so you can switch it back on whenever you want.
  • Turning off a common skill affects only this agent. Every other agent on the box keeps it. That is the whole reason the switch exists: common skills live in one shared folder, so before this the only way to take one away from a single agent was to delete it for everybody.
  • All skills are on by default.

Changes save immediately and apply the next time the agent restarts — the page reminds you when a restart is pending. Under the hood this writes the agent's disabled_skills list (see agent.json5 reference), so you can also set it by hand in the raw config.

A row marked Needs admin tools has no switch. That skill declares the tools it is written for (the AgentFather playbooks olano-admin and olano-agent-builder need the olano_* tools) and this agent does not have them, so it is never described in the agent's prompt whatever the switch would say. Granting the tools — the agent's Tools tab, or tools in its config — is what makes it appear; Turn all on leaves such rows alone.

An agent can work its own switches from a conversation too ("stop using the spreadsheet skill"), if Manage its own skills is on in its self-configuration settings — see Ask the agent: self-configuration, magic links and admin tools. It can list its skills and switch them on and off for itself; it can never install, edit or delete one that way.

Click any row to open the skill. The viewer takes most of the screen, because a SKILL.md is a document you are meant to read, not a summary to glance at. You get it rendered — the actual instructions the agent follows — with the YAML header folded away above it, and a list of everything bundled with the skill beside it: scripts, forms, reference documents, example images. Click a file to preview it; images render inline, and anything the browser cannot show offers a link to open it raw. On a phone the file list becomes a short index above the text.

Under the labels, every skill explains in a line where it lives and what that means for changing it. Editable ones also get an Open in Files button that jumps straight to the folder in the Files tab, which is where you edit it.

docs.title: Calendar
docs.text:
A time-based view of scheduled work and events — the schedule laid out on a calendar rather than as a list.

The same tasks laid out by month.

docs.title: Chat
docs.text:
Talk to any agent you have access to. Pick the agent in the header, and switch threads in the conversation list — each thread is a separate conversation with its own memory of what was said. The header also exposes a per-conversation model override and, for models that support it, a reasoning-effort control. Live progress shows what the agent is doing as it works.

The model chip belongs to the conversation you are in. A new conversation always opens on the agent's configured model; pick another in the chip and only that conversation changes, from its next reply on. Every reply records the model that wrote it, so when you reopen a conversation later, from any device, it continues on the model it last answered with rather than on whatever another chat was set to. You can switch as often as you like within one conversation and each reply is billed to the model that produced it. If that model is no longer available on the deployment, the conversation says so once and falls back to the agent's default. To change the model for every new conversation, change it on the agent itself.

Tool calls appear in the order they happened, and a file the agent names in its answer becomes a card with Download and Open in Files.

While the agent is still replying you have three choices for your next message. Press Enter and it waits: it is sent as your next message the moment the reply finishes. Press Steer (the ▸▸ button, or Cmd/Ctrl+Enter) and the agent gets it now, without stopping: it reads your message at its next step — as soon as the tool it is running finishes, before it decides what to do next — and adjusts the work in progress. Steering is for "not that file", "use blue", "also include Q3": corrections you would otherwise watch it finish a version without. If the reply finishes before the agent reaches its next step, the message is simply sent as your next one, so nothing is lost either way. Press Stop (■) to cancel the reply; whatever was waiting stays waiting. Every waiting message shows as a chip above the message box with its own Steer, Edit (take it back into the message box) and Cancel buttons, and Cancel all clears them. A message the agent read mid-reply is tagged Steered in in the conversation. Messages with files attached wait for the reply; they cannot be steered.

Attach any file with the paperclip, or by pasting or dropping it onto the conversation. Each file can be up to 10 MB. What happens next depends on what the file is, judged from its contents rather than its name:

You attach The agent gets A photo, screenshot or other image The file, saved in uploads/; it looks at it with its vision tool A voice note, audio or video The file, saved in uploads/, plus a transcript when speech-to-text is on A short text file of any kind (.txt, .md, .csv, .json, .yaml, .py, .sql, a Dockerfile, a log) The text itself, in your message A long text file (over about 60 KB) The file, saved in uploads/, so it can read every line rather than a cut-off copy PDF, Word, Excel or PowerPoint, including older .doc, .xls, .ppt and OpenDocument files The file, saved in uploads/; it reads it with its document reader, which converts older formats and reads scanned PDFs with OCR A .zip or any other file The file, saved in uploads/; an agent with a shell can unpack or inspect it

Agents open these files only with the tool made for each kind. If an agent tries to read a recording, a video, a document or an archive as a plain file, it is told which tool to use instead (speech-to-text for audio and video, the document reader for PDF and Office files, the shell for archives), so a voice note never enters the conversation as raw audio data. Images in PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP it can still look at directly, up to about 3.7 MB each; larger ones go through its vision tool.

Because saved files are the real files, the agent works on every row and formula of a spreadsheet, not a summary. A saved file shows as a card in your message with Download and Open in Files. Team members with read-only access cannot save into the agent's workspace, so for them the text of a document or text file is read once and added to the message instead, and other types arrive as a note that the file could not be read.

Add an agent sits in the same header row, beside the MCP status, whenever group chats are on and you have a second agent. It brings another agent into this conversation by turning it into a group chat: the agent you were talking to stays the one that answers anything that names nobody, the agents you add reply when you @mention them, and — unless you switch Bring the conversation along off in the dialog — the recent messages of this chat are copied in so nobody starts blind. Your one-to-one chat is left exactly as it is; the group is a separate conversation, listed under Group chats in the sidebar, and it opens as soon as it is made.

When the agent is using its live browser, you can watch it. A small window appears in the corner of the conversation with the agent's screen and a cursor that moves to whatever it clicks. Click the window to open it large and take control (to sign in, enter a code or finish a step yourself), hand back, and collapse it again. When the agent waits for your approval (to submit a form, buy or send), the window folds into a small Approval needed pill and the approval card is scrolled into view, in every approval mode. On a phone the window is always the pill; tap it to open the browser full screen. It appears only when browser control is set to live; see Browser control.

A conversation is live on every device, whichever surface the turn came from. Open the same thread on your laptop and your phone and both follow it as it happens: a message that arrives over Telegram, a scheduled run, a turn sent through the OpenAI-compatible connector, or something you type in another browser shows up in the open conversation without a reload — the agent's working indicator, its tool calls as they run, the reply forming, and the final answer. The indicator names the surface the turn is running from ("Working on this from Telegram…"). New conversations started elsewhere appear in the conversation list the same way, and one touched elsewhere moves to the top. If a device was asleep or offline, the thread catches up on its own when the tab comes back.

The agent keeps working when you put the device down. Closing the tab, locking your phone, switching apps or moving between Wi-Fi and mobile data does not stop a reply in progress: the turn runs on the deployment, not in your browser, and only the view of it goes away. Come back — the same tab, a new tab, or a different device — and it rejoins the reply exactly where you stopped seeing it, filling in the words, tool steps and files you missed, then carries on live. A reply that finished while you were away is simply there when you return, and a conversation the agent is still working on shows as busy in the conversation list even on a device that never saw the turn start.

This is why Stop (■) is the way to end a reply: it tells the deployment to stop, so it works from any device, and the agent stops whether or not the tab that started the reply is still open. Closing the tab is not a stop.

Two consequences worth knowing. Sending again while a reply is still running does not start a second one — a conversation runs one reply at a time, so the message either steers the reply in progress or waits its turn, exactly as described above. And "Connection lost while … was replying" now means what it says: the reply is genuinely gone (the deployment restarted, or it ended long enough ago to have been cleared), which is when Retry appears. While the reply is merely catching up you see Reconnecting instead, with no Retry — nothing was lost, so there is nothing to resend.

Everyone who can chat with an agent shares its whole conversation list, and can pick up any conversation in it. A scheduled run, a heartbeat, a conversation that arrived over Telegram or WhatsApp, a chat a colleague started here — open it from the list and reply, and the agent continues with everything that was said in it (ask "what did you just do?" under a scheduled run and it answers about that run). Messages show who wrote them, so a thread several people have typed into stays readable. Two things to know: a reply you type here into a messaging-platform conversation is recorded and badged in that thread but is not sent out to the platform, and deleting a conversation removes it for everyone, so that is reserved for admins and the agent's owner — anyone with access can still rename or compact it.

Three buttons in your theme's own colour frame the header row, laid out the way the simple view's chat header is. A filled pair leads it: a + that starts a new conversation and, right beside it, a clock that opens your past ones. An info button (ⓘ) closes the row at the right: it opens the agent's profile card — its face, name, title and description, an Edit profile button for those allowed to change them, and (for admins) doors into its settings, connections and keys — as a panel that slides in from the right, exactly where the simple view keeps the same card. Only one of the two panels, the conversation list or the profile card, is open at a time; pressing either button closes the other.

The conversation list is a panel that slides in from the right, not a column that sits there. The conversation itself always gets the full width of the window; press the clock and your past conversations slide in over the right-hand side. Pick one (or start a new one) and the panel closes again — so does clicking the page beside it, pressing Escape, or the ✕ in its corner. It opens closed every time you arrive, at every screen size, so the list is one click away without ever costing you room to read. On a desktop you can drag its left edge to make it wider or narrower, and that width is remembered; on a phone it is sized to always leave a strip of the page beside it to tap on.

Every conversation shows where it came from. A thread that arrived over a messaging platform carries a coloured badge with that platform's name beside its title — TELEGRAM, WHATSAPP, SLACK, DISCORD, WECHAT and so on, one colour each — and the person you are talking to on the line underneath. Conversations you start here in the dashboard carry no badge: they are the default that everything else is read against. The same badge appears in the header of the open conversation.

Inside a conversation, a badge appears on an individual message only when that message arrived by a different route than the thread itself. So a reply you type here inside a Telegram conversation is marked, and the Telegram messages around it are not — which is what makes a conversation that moved between surfaces readable at a glance, without putting the same label on every line.

Conversations that predate this all still get labelled: the agent already remembers every chat it has been messaged in, and the badge is recovered from that. A conversation that only ever existed here stays unbadged, as it should.

One badge is not about a messaging platform: a violet CORTEX marks a conversation you opened from the Cortex tab — pressing Chat on a Pulse card, a self-check finding, or a Cortex item brings the discussion here, and the badge is how you find it again among your other dashboard chats. It is an ordinary conversation in every other respect: reply to it, rename it, keep it, delete it.

docs.title: Rating a reply
docs.text:
Under each finished reply, beside Copy, are a thumbs up and a thumbs down. They are there for everyone who can read the conversation, in the dashboard chat and in the simple chat.

  • Thumbs up records that the reply was good. Thumbs down records that it was not, and opens a small box for an optional comment on what went wrong (up to 2000 characters). The vote counts as soon as you press the thumb; the comment is extra, and Skip closes the box without one.
  • The thumbs are the same plain colour as Copy until you vote. Your vote then turns green (up) or red (down) and stays lit, so you can see it later and after a reload. Press the other thumb to change it, or the lit one again to take it back.
  • Each person has one vote per reply, and only you see your own. Insights shows the totals per agent.
  • Votes are kept on this deployment, with or without Langfuse. When the agent's turns are traced to Langfuse (Config → Observability), the vote is also sent there as a user_feedback score on that reply's trace (1 for up, -1 for down; taking the vote back removes the score). The comment is sent only when traces include full content; with the default, metadata-only traces, it stays on the deployment. Votes cast while tracing is off are never sent later.
  • Replies from before this feature have no thumbs.
  • Deleting a conversation deletes its votes too.

docs.title: Opening a reply in Langfuse
docs.text: When tracing to Langfuse is on (Config → Observability) and the connection has been tested, an admin whose account has Langfuse links switched on (Admin → Users, off by default) sees a Langfuse link beside Copy under each traced reply. It opens that reply's trace in Langfuse in a new tab: the turn with every model call and tool call under it. Members never see the link, and a reply that was not traced (tracing off, or not chosen by the sampling rate) has none. Deleting a conversation also deletes its traces in Langfuse.

docs.title: Config (admin only)
docs.text:
Not a tab in the left navigation: open it from the account menu — your name at the bottom-left of the sidebar — under Administration, or type "Config" into the ⌘K search. Admins only; members do not see the entry.

Deployment-wide settings — everything in config.yaml with a form for each block: team accounts, member bot creation (whether non-admins may create their own bots, how many each may own, and which templates they may pick from), cognition defaults, heartbeat, disk monitoring, MCP connection health, deployed pages (the switch for page builds and servers, servers per agent, health checks and request limits; see Pages), browser control (mode, where it runs, how many agents may browse at once and the idle timeout, plus the live browser's install status; see Browser control), context window (what a compaction keeps and the MCP result cap), revisions, issues, speech, media, web search, rate limits, catalog sync, and the ports.

The General card: default agent, preferred model and the theme for this browser.

The Mobile app card decides what the Olano app on people's phones shows: the Cortex tab, the Inbox tab and each of its sections (Approvals, Alerts, Issues), and the Files, Credits and Usage, and Transcribe on this phone rows in the app's Settings, plus where voice notes are transcribed for people who have not chosen (on the deployment, by default). It is saved with the page's Save button, and phones pick it up the next time the app is opened or brought back to the foreground. The keys are in the config.yaml reference.

The Cloud catalogs card shows each synced catalog (model pricing, the MCP directory, credit rates, agent archetypes, official connector clients) with its revision and where it is being served from, and a Sync now button that re-fetches everything immediately instead of waiting for the hourly background check — useful right after a new official connector is enabled for your deployment, so its one-click Connect button appears without the wait.

The Observability (Langfuse) card sends each agent turn to a Langfuse project as one trace, so you can see every model call and tool call of a conversation with its timings, tokens and credits, and search them over time. It is off by default and agents cannot change it. The switches (on or off, the Langfuse address, what each trace contains, the share of turns traced, an environment name, whether Cortex background work is traced) are saved with the page's Save button, like the rest of the page; the field meanings are in the config.yaml reference. Choosing Full content puts a warning on the card before you save: traces then hold the conversations themselves. The keys and the connection test act at once instead:

  • Langfuse keys: paste the public key (pk-lf-…) and secret key (sk-lf-…) from Langfuse → Settings → API keys and press Save keys. They are stored in the vault, hidden from agents and from the Vault page, and never shown again. The line above the boxes says which keys are in use: the ones saved here, the server's LANGFUSE_* environment variables, or none.
  • Test connection checks the keys against the Langfuse address and remembers the project, which is what lets conversations link to their traces. A failure says why; a refusal on Langfuse Cloud is usually the wrong region.
  • Status shows how many steps were sent since the last restart, or the last problem, with a link to open the project in Langfuse, and Agents with their own setting lists the agents that override the card from their own Observability card (see Agents).

The Disk encryption card appears only on a managed instance whose data lives on an encrypted volume (see Privacy and security); a self-hosted install never shows it. It reads the state of that volume (the custody mode, the volume's identifier, whether a header backup exists and which generation is current, whether the instance's encryption service is answering) and holds the one action the volume asks of you: Create recovery key. The key is generated on the instance, shown to you once, and confirmed by typing it back, so a copy you never checked cannot be the one you rely on. A key that was shown and not confirmed stays pending for fifteen minutes (Confirm the shown key or Cancel pending key on the card), and Replace recovery key makes a new one that takes over only once it is confirmed. The Encryption service row names the version of the service on the instance that answers these actions; when it reads Unavailable, that service is not answering: your data stays encrypted and the instance keeps working, only the recovery-key actions pause (Refresh re-reads the state; if it stays unavailable after a restart of the instance from the cloud console, contact support). Every row's hint explains what the value means and what the buttons do.

Some fields (ports, team accounts) only take effect after a runtime restart; the form says so.

Saving. The page is long, so Save changes and Discard live in the bar at the top, which stays put while you scroll — you never have to scroll back up to save. While anything on the page differs from what is saved, an Unsaved changes badge sits beside the buttons. Three things then guard the edits: clicking anywhere that would leave the page (a sidebar entry, the ⌘K search, a link inside the page) asks Save and leave / Leave without saving / Stay on this page — Save and leave is greyed out while a field is invalid, and the dialog says which case you are in; closing or reloading the tab gets the browser's own "leave site?" prompt; and if the edits sit untouched for about a minute, one reminder toast says so. The browser's Back button is the one exit that is not intercepted, so use the sidebar or the dialog to leave. The Usage budgets card has its own Save button beside its fields and is not part of this — save it where you edit it.

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
Opened from the account menu (bottom-left) under Setup, or from ⌘K.

One card per service an agent can be signed in to — GitHub, Google, Microsoft 365, Salesforce, HubSpot, QuickBooks, Shopify, Slack, Notion, LinkedIn, X, Meta, Reddit, DocuSign and more. Each card shows whether it is connected, which sign-in methods it offers, and — when a connection has expired — a way to renew it. A connection made here is the credential for that service: the service's toolkit, any MCP server for it and the git tools all use it, with nothing else to configure and no restart.

One card per service, listing what that connection lets an agent do.

Each card also lists the tools that service brings. They turn green once the service is connected — those tools are live for your agents; while it is not connected they stay neutral, as a preview of what connecting would grant.

There are four ways to connect, and a card shows the ones its service offers:

  • Connect with Olano's app (shown when available): one click, nothing to configure. You approve access on the service's own consent screen — no developer account, no OAuth client, no redirect URI to register. The card shows via Olano's app on connections made this way, and tokens are stored only on your deployment. Which services offer this arrives via background sync: opening this page checks for updates within seconds, and Config → Cloud catalogs → Sync now forces an immediate refresh. This option is for Olano Cloud deployments: an Olano API key on a self-hosted install does not unlock it, so a self-hosted install uses its own OAuth app instead.
  • Use your own OAuth app: the classic Connect form — create an OAuth client in the service's developer console, register the shown redirect URI, and paste the Client ID and Secret. Your own client always takes precedence when both are configured.
  • Sign in with a code: for services that offer it (GitHub does), no app to create and no fields to fill. The panel shows a short one-time code and a button to the service's device page; enter the code there on any device — a phone is fine — approve, and the card turns Connected on its own. This is the route to use when you have no OAuth app and do not want to create one.
  • Paste a key: store the service's API key or personal access token in the Vault under the name the service's toolkit reads. The reference list is on each card's setup guide. A key still works for every service — it is simply the last resort, since it never expires on its own and has to be rotated by hand.

Scopes. Every card works at two scopes: System (one connection every agent uses) and Per agent (that agent's own account, optionally shared with the others as a fallback). Inside a tool call the agent's own connection wins, then a shared one, then the system one — which is how three agents can post from three accounts of the same service. The Vault page (account menu → Administration) remains the place to see and manage stored keys.

An agent can hand you any of these from a chat: ask it to connect a service and it sends a magic link (Ask the agent: self-configuration, magic links and admin tools) for the best method the card offers — Olano's app if there is one, otherwise your own app, otherwise a code, and a secure form for a key. Nothing is ever pasted into the conversation.

When a connection stops working. Any service on this page, Google included, can refuse a saved sign-in while its card still says Connected: an admin revoked the session, the grant died with a password change, or the token outlived what was stored. The card cannot see that; the agent's tools can, because they are the ones handed the 401 Unauthorized. The first refusal is repaired silently when it can be (the token is refreshed and the call retried once), whichever service and whichever tool. When that fails, the card turns Needs reconnecting with the service's own words under the badge, its button reads Reconnect, and the agent does not stop at the error: it tells you the sign-in has expired, offers the routes this deployment has (a reconnect link, a sign-in code or a pasted personal token where the service allows one, the card's Disconnect then Connect as the manual route), suggests what else can reach the same service if you cannot reconnect right now, and finishes your request once you have signed in again. A reconnect replaces the broken connection in place; you never have to disconnect first. A token you pasted into the Vault by hand gets the same treatment with a different fix, since nothing renews it: connect the service through this page so its tokens refresh on their own, or store a fresh token when asked. MCP servers get the same care in the agent's MCP tab (see MCP servers).

docs.title: Cortex
docs.text:
Olano's autonomous cognition engine. When Cortex is on, the agent does useful background work between conversations: distilling what it learned into memory, tidying its own notes, expanding ideas, and generating proactive suggestions. This tab shows what it has been doing and what is scheduled. It is off until you turn it on: the Cortex engine switch is inside Cortex settings below, for the whole deployment or for one agent (see Cortex and Pulse).

Everything you can change about it sits in one card, Cortex settings, at the top of the tab. It is folded away by default — the line beside its title is the live state (on or off, the pace, and today's deep-run count), so you only open it when you want to change something. Inside are three parts: How it runs, the switches; Phases & schedule, what runs when; and Creative direction, what the agent should aim at when it thinks on its own. Fleet-wide defaults live in Config; per-agent overrides live here and in the agent's own settings (see Cortex and Pulse).

The Brainstorming, Ideas, Prototypes and Projects tabs are the four stages of one funnel (see the funnel). A card that the Rate & Promote phase has reviewed carries its score as a badge (7/10; hover for the recommendation and the reason), and the drawer shows the reason and the suggested next step under the status line. Create project on a card jumps the item straight to a project; the agent's own cortex_promote moves it one stage at a time. A promoted card shows a link to the folder it became. Open on a card (or clicking the card) shows the item's full write-up in a drawer, and the drawer carries the card's own buttons too: Create project, Discard, Explore more and Chat, with the same confirmation and the same busy state, so you can act on an item as you read it. Discarding from the drawer closes it; Create project hands over to the run's panel. The Phases & schedule list has a row for Rate & Promote like every other phase, with Run now to rate on demand.

Every button on a card answers the click itself. While its request is out, the button you pressed turns into a spinner with what it is doing (Discarding…, Starting…, Approving…) and the card waits dimmed, so a second click cannot start a second run; the moment the server agrees the card leaves the list (a discarded item to Discarded, an answered Pulse card out of Pending) and a short notice confirms it. Approving a Pulse card also puts an outcome card at the top of the tab that says exactly what happened and links to the file it changed; the page scrolls to it. A Pulse card about work the agent already applied on its own offers Keep and Undo rather than Approve and Reject: Keep accepts the change, Undo restores the backup the agent took first.

Everything Cortex does in the background keeps running when you look away. Create project, Think now, Optimize workspace, Optimize skills and a phase's Run now each start a run on the server and open a panel that follows it: what it is doing right now, how long it has been going, and every step it has taken (each tool it called, what came back, what the model said). Closing that panel, leaving the page, locking your phone or reloading does not stop the run. While a project is being created its card reads Creating project… with the step it is on, and its button opens the same run again rather than starting a second one; a phase that is running shows Running in its row for the same reason. Pressing a button for something already running (from another tab or another device) always joins that run. When it ends you get a short notice, the card moves on (a promoted idea goes to Promoted, the new project to Projects), and a run that failed within the last hour leaves a Last attempt failed line on its card with a View log link. Stop in the panel ends a run early.

Runs, next to Refresh at the top, lists every run for every agent you can see: what is running now (the button shows a count while anything is) and the history before it, including the phases Cortex runs on its own schedule and the tasks you approved in Pulse. All, Running and Failed narrow the list, the agents filter beside the tabs narrows it too, and opening a row shows that run's full step log. A run that was going when the service restarted shows as Interrupted. The most recent 200 runs per agent are kept.

Two things on this page have a different scope, on purpose. The buttons along the top — Think now, Optimize workspace, Optimize skills, Activity — and the settings card act on one agent: the one named under the title, which you change with the agent dropdown in the page's top bar (the same dropdown Notes and Memory carry). The tabs below — Pulse, Brainstorming, Ideas, Prototypes, Projects, Learned Skills, Self-Improve, Self-Checks — show every agent's items at once, so reviewing what the fleet has come up with no longer means switching the dropdown once per agent. Every card carries a small label with the agent's face and name it belongs to, and the buttons on that card act on that agent (a Chat switches you to it). The agents filter beside the tabs — a dropdown with a checkbox per agent, a search box, Select all and Clear — narrows the tabs to the agents you tick; the line next to it says what is showing ("Showing items from all agents", "from 2 of 8 agents"). Every agent is shown by default, an agent created later is shown too, and the choice is remembered on this device. The counts on the tabs follow the filter.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
A file browser for agent workspaces. Read, edit, download and delete files, including the identity and memory markdown files that shape the agent's behaviour. Deleting through the agent's own tools moves files to a recoverable trash/ folder rather than destroying them.

nova's workspace, with a report open in the preview.

The tree lists every agent you have access to, each as a collapsed row with a workspace folder under it, so you browse the whole team from one place without switching the agent picked elsewhere in the dashboard. Nothing is loaded until you open it: expand an agent, then its workspace, then the folders you want — each one lists on demand. Right-click an agent or its workspace row to create a file or folder there or refresh it; the toolbar's New file / New folder buttons land wherever the row you last clicked lives. The footer names the agent whose files you are looking at. Links from other tabs (a Cortex item's files, a skill's folder) open straight to the file under its agent.

Upload files from your computer or phone. Tap or click the folder you want the files in (or a file, to use its folder; or the agent or workspace row, for the workspace root), then press Upload in the toolbar, the arrow next to New folder, and pick one or more files. Right-clicking a folder, an agent or its workspace row offers Upload files… too. Each file can be up to 100 MB; larger ones are skipped with a message naming them. A line under the toolbar shows progress, and when the upload finishes the folder opens in the tree (a single file opens in the preview). If a file of the same name is already there, you are asked whether to replace it; Keep existing skips just that file. Files keep the names you gave them, and the agent can use them straight away: tell it in chat where you put them. Members with read-only access do not see the Upload button.

Files an agent produces. Every agent keeps one layout: reports/ holds everything it makes for you (charts, images, PDFs, spreadsheets, documents, exports — one canonical file per deliverable, revised in place), scratch/ holds its scripts and intermediate files, and uploads/ holds what you sent it in chat or on a messenger. When an agent names a file in its reply — its own Saved: line, a path in backticks, or a full path — the chat shows it: images, audio and video render inline, and every other file appears as a card with Download and Open in Files, which jumps to that file in this tab. The same works when you reopen an old conversation. On a messaging channel the agent's Saved: line attaches the file to the chat instead. Members see and download the files of the agents they have access to; editing and deleting stay with admins.

Only the agent's finished answer attaches files, and only the files it names there. A path that came up while it was working — a file it opened to read, a scratch file, a path quoted out of some document — is not attached, so you get the deliverables and not everything the agent touched on the way. If it names the same file more than once in one answer, you still get one card. Agents are told to list every file they made or changed for you, with its full path, so if one leaves something out, say so — and if you would rather it not attach a particular file, tell it that too.

What an agent can do with documents. Every box now carries the tools an office document actually needs, so an agent does not have to explain that it cannot: it can turn a Word file, a spreadsheet or a slide deck into a PDF (and open a legacy .doc), read a scanned PDF or photographed page with OCR, merge, split, rotate and unlock PDFs, and check its own work by looking at the pages it produced. Two limits worth knowing: OCR reads English — for another language the agent reads the page with its vision instead, which it will say — and a converted document uses substitute fonts for any typeface the box does not have, so the common ones (Arial, Times New Roman, Courier New) keep their layout and an unusual one may shift. Ask for the result you want ("turn this into a PDF", "what does this scan say") rather than naming a tool.

If an agent runs on your own machine rather than a hosted box, whoever installed Olano could have declined these packages — the agent checks before it relies on one, and tells you what it did instead.

On a hosted box every agent also has Olano's four document skills, docx, xlsx, pptx and pdf: step-by-step know-how for building, editing and checking Word files, spreadsheets, slide decks and PDFs. They arrive with the box's shared skills and update on their own; you see them on the agent's Skills tab as common skills. A self-hosted installation does not include those four skills. Its agents can still work with documents using the tools above, they just do it without that extra guidance.

The tree is fully keyboard-driven: ↑/↓ move, → opens a folder or steps into it, ← closes one or steps back to its parent, Home/End jump, Enter opens, F2 renames, ⌘⌫ / Ctrl+⌫ deletes, and typing a few letters jumps to the next row that starts with them. Very large folders show their first 2,000 entries and say how many more there are — use the filter box to narrow. A very large text file previews its beginning, says so, and offers the download for the rest; editing is switched off for it so a save can never lose the part you were not shown.

The Filter box searches by name across every workspace you can access, not just the folders you have opened: type memor and each agent's MEMORY.md appears under its agent row even with everything collapsed. Matching is case-insensitive and looks at the file or folder name and at its path, so memories/2026 finds a daily log by its folder. It starts from two characters, waits for you to pause typing, and searches everything at once — press Enter to search without the pause, Escape to clear. Version-control, dependency and cache folders are skipped, and dot-files only take part while the eye button shows them. Click a match to open it and reveal it in the tree; when there are more matches than it shows, it says so — keep typing to narrow.

Markdown and HTML files open in a rendered preview, with a Preview / Raw toggle in the preview header to switch to the source. An HTML page renders live in an isolated frame: stylesheets, scripts and images it references by relative path are pulled from the same workspace folder, so a small prototype site looks the way a browser would show it. The frame is sandboxed — the page runs cut off from your dashboard session and cannot read or change anything outside its own preview.

Images, audio, video and PDFs play or display inline. A file that is none of those and not text either (a .zip, an Office document, a database, a program) is never printed as text: the preview shows its type and size with a Download button, so you can open it in an app that understands it.

On a phone the tree and the preview are not side by side — whichever you are using gets the whole screen. The tree is what you browse; opening a file hands the screen to the preview, and the All files button at the left of its header hands it back. The Preview / Raw toggle and the file actions sit on their own row under the file's name, so the name stays readable however long it is.

Files whose name starts with a dot — .env, .olano/, .git/ — are left out of the tree by default, so a workspace opens on the files you work in. The eye button in the tree toolbar shows them; click it again to hide them. The button lights up while they are showing, and your choice is remembered the next time you open the dashboard. It only changes what the tree lists: a hidden file you open, edit or delete behaves like any other file, and a link that points at one turns the toggle on for you.

docs.title: Insights
docs.text:
Charts and numbers: token and cost usage over time, per agent and per model, thread counts, and activity trends. If your deployment displays costs in credits rather than dollars, this section follows that setting.

The figures cover everything your deployment runs, not just chat: Cortex background thinking, scheduled tasks, delegated skill workers, the daily highlights and periodic reports, post-turn PULSE curation, subagent calls, and the non-chat services (image generation and editing, vision, voice, web search) all count. A "Where credits went" card breaks the window down by kind of work — chat and channels, Cortex, scheduled tasks, and so on — which is the place to look when usage seems higher than your conversations alone explain, and a "Credits by tier" card splits managed model spend across the Turbo / Pro / Max tiers so you can see which tier is doing the work.

Every number here is measured on your own deployment: each model call and service call records its charge locally as it happens, so the charts, the breakdown cards, and the headline credits figure all come from the same local record and stay available even when the deployment is offline. That one record also backs every range button, so the ranges nest the way you would expect — 1 day is a rolling last-24-hours view and is always contained in 7 days, which is contained in 30 days and 90 days. A shorter range can never show more calls or more spend than a longer one; if it ever does, something is wrong and it is worth reporting. The range buttons mean the same thing on the Drill-down tab, which shares the selector — "1 day" is the last 24 hours there too, scoped to the conversations active in that time.

Drill-down's agent ranking and its chat-vs-autonomous cards read the same record as the Overview, so an agent's total is the same number on both tabs. What changes is when you open an agent: from there down, the figures are attributed from stored conversation history, the only record that ties a cost to a particular conversation or tool. Long conversations are compacted as they grow, which removes older calls from that history, so the conversations you can open account for part of an agent's total rather than all of it. The page says how much — "openable conversations account for $X of $Y" — so a short list under a large total reads as coverage rather than as a contradiction. One more difference follows from what it ranks: a conversation is counted whole, in the range its most recent activity falls into, so a long-running thread brings its entire cost with it. Take the Overview and the agent ranking as the totals, and the levels below as the answer to where inside a conversation the cost went.

Billing itself still lives with your Olano account — the Credits left balance shown on the Overview page and the usage bar on your cloud deployment page track the account's remaining balance for the billing period, which is a different window than the charts' last-N-days view, so the two totals are not expected to match digit for digit.

On deployments upgraded from an older version, the dashboard reconstructs past Cortex background spend from its stored history the first time it starts, so the charts show the full picture rather than beginning at the upgrade day. Reconstructed history is marked internally and never re-billed — your balance is unaffected.

The Reply feedback card, in the Fleet activity section, counts the thumbs up and thumbs down people gave agents' replies in the chat during the selected range, per agent (see Chat → Rating a reply). A vote counts once, as it stands now, in the range it was last changed in; a vote taken back does not count. It reads the votes kept on this deployment, so it works without Langfuse. Members see the counts for their own agents only.

When tracing to Langfuse is on, an admin with Langfuse links switched on (Admin → Users) drilling into a conversation sees an Open in Langfuse link beside its name, which opens all of that conversation's traces in Langfuse.

docs.title: Issues
docs.text:
A shared work tracker where agents and humans are both participants. An issue has a title, a body, a type, comments, an assignee and a status. You can assign an issue to an agent and it will pick it up on its next poll and work on it; agents can open issues for each other or for you. Search is hybrid — plain keyword matching plus meaning-based matching — so "the customer can't log in" finds an issue titled "authentication failure". See Issues.

Open issues, each assigned to an agent, with labels and a type.

The list's filters — search text, Open/Closed, type, assignee, label and sort — live in the page's address, so the URL in your browser always reopens the same list and can be sent to a teammate; Copy link (next to Clear filters, shown while any filter is active) puts it on the clipboard for you. Opening an issue keeps the filters, and coming back to Issues from another tab restores the last filters you used.

Inside an issue, Copy issue (top right, across from Back to list) puts the whole thread on the clipboard as Markdown: the title and number, a line with its state, type, author, assignee and labels, the description, then every comment with who wrote it and when (times in UTC). Assignment, label and close/reopen events are left out. To copy a single card instead, use the copy icon next to its time: it copies that description or comment exactly as it was written, so lists and code blocks paste intact, and turns into a check mark for a moment once copied.

docs.title: Knowledge
docs.text:
The searchable document library (RAG). Add files, folders or URLs and they are indexed so agents can search them by meaning. Documents you drop into an agent's knowledgebase/ folder are picked up automatically. Use this for manuals, policies, contracts and reference material you want agents to cite.

The page has no store of its own: it runs every search, listing and ingest through the knowledge-base tools of the selected agent — the agent picker in the page's top bar, the same selection the sidebar's agent list drives, so the agent named here is always the one named everywhere else. Those tools are not granted automatically, so an agent has them only when its tools list names them (see agent.json5 reference). When the selected agent is missing them the page says so, names exactly which are absent, and disables the controls it cannot serve — pick another agent, or add the tools to that one and restart it. A knowledge call needs a running agent: if the selected one is stopped, the page says so and answers through another agent that is running until you start it.

docs.title: Logs (admin only)
docs.text:
Opened from the account menu (bottom-left) under Administration, or from ⌘K.

Runtime logs, filterable by agent and severity. First stop when an agent will not boot or a connector is silent.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
What each agent remembers. The tab shows MEMORY.md (durable facts); edit it directly, which is the fastest way to correct something an agent has learned wrongly. The daily logs are files, one per day, under memories/ in the agent's workspace: open them from the Files tab. See Memory and self-learning.

nova's MEMORY.md as an outline of sections and facts, with Add a fact below.

The page names the agent whose memory it shows in its own top bar, with an agent picker — it is the same selection the sidebar's agent list drives, so picking an agent here or clicking one in the sidebar changes both. (On a phone the sidebar is a drawer, which is why the page carries a picker of its own.)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
The agent's markdown wiki: linked notes with backlinks, searchable, editable by both you and the agent. Good for structured knowledge that is neither a fleeting memory nor a document — project pages, contact sheets, running decisions. See Notes. Like Memory, the page carries the agent picker in its top bar.

A note with its tags and its links to other notes.

docs.title: Org Chart
docs.text:
A visual map of your agents: who manages whom, who reports to whom, and who counts as a peer. Editing the chart here changes what the agents are actually allowed to do — the hierarchy grants messaging permissions (see Agent-to-agent and the org chart).

A manager with three reports. The lines are also messaging permissions.

Connectors on each card. Every agent card shows a row of small icons, one per messaging connector the agent is set up with (WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, Slack, Signal, email, SMS and the rest), so you can see at a glance which agent answers where. A healthy connector shows just its icon. A corner dot means it needs a look:

What you see Meaning Icon only Connected and working. Amber dot Connecting: still starting, reconnecting, or waiting for you to finish pairing (for example a WhatsApp QR code that has not been scanned yet). Red dot and red ring Needs attention: the connector could not start (often a missing token or password) or the service refused it. Hover the icon to read the reason. Greyed out The agent itself is stopped, so none of its connectors are running. Pulsing ring The agent is answering a message that arrived on that connector right now.

When a card is too narrow for every icon, the last slot shows +N; hover it to list the rest. If any of the hidden connectors has a problem, the +N carries its dot. Click a card to open its details: the Connectors section lists each connector with its status and, for a failing one, the reason, and Manage connectors opens that agent's Connectors tab to fix it. Typing a connector name in the chart's search box (for example whatsapp) highlights every agent on it. The Connectors toggle above the chart hides or shows the icons; the chart refreshes their status on its own every half minute and whenever an agent starts or stops.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The landing page and the recovery surface: it is the one section that always renders, even when something else is broken. It shows which agents are online, recent activity, disk health, and — most importantly — the Approvals inbox.

Overview on a demo deployment with four agents and four scheduled tasks.

Four tiles head the page: Agents, Channels, Scheduled tasks and Status. Click or tap the Agents tile to jump straight to the Agents section. The Channels tile counts the connectors your agents are configured with, and the line beneath it says how many are actually connected right now — "2 active" when everything is up, or "1 of 2 active" when one is configured but did not come online. That second reading usually means an expired or wrong credential; open the agent's Connectors tab, where the connector reports what it is waiting for.

Above the tiles, a usage strip summarizes the last 30 days. On an Olano-managed deployment it leads with Credits left — your account balance, the same number the deployment page at cloud.olano.ai shows — followed by Credits used (30d), which is what the window consumed, not what remains. A freshly deployed box correctly reads "used: 0 credits" while the balance is full; that zero means nothing has been spent yet, not that the account is empty. The Olano credits card further down the page shows the same balance with the monthly-allowance meter and a top-up link. A self-hosted install running on an Olano API key (Models and credits) shows the same strip and card for the account's balance, without the monthly meter: account credits have no period.

Notifications is the section above Approvals: everything the deployment needs you to look at — a connector that did not start because its credential is missing, an issue assigned to you, a background run that failed, disk over threshold. A row that names something opens it, so following the row is how you act on it. Each row says how long ago it happened — "5 mins ago", "2 hours ago", "3 days ago" — which is what separates a problem that is still live from one that fixed itself overnight; on a desktop browser, hovering that age shows the exact date and time. When the same problem keeps recurring it collapses into a single row with a seen N times badge, and the age then tracks the most recent occurrence, with the first one named in the same hover. Dismiss rows one at a time, or use Mark all read and Clear read; a notification also disappears on its own once its condition clears. The bell in the sidebar (the topbar on a phone) carries the unread count and the newest few rows.

Approvals is a section on this page, not a separate tab. When an agent wants to run something that needs human sign-off (see HITL), the request appears here with the exact action described, and it waits for you to approve or reject. The sidebar shows a badge with the pending count.

Disk is a collapsible card on the same page, and it answers two different questions. Expand it and the first block, Where the space went, accounts for the whole machine in a few groups:

  • Container images — the software this deployment runs on: the agent runtime, the sandbox agents execute their commands in, the dashboard, and the database. Several gigabytes on any install, and re-downloaded whenever the deployment updates. The "reclaimable" note next to it is what Clean now would recover (superseded copies left behind by past updates).
  • Container volumes and containers — the database's stored data (threads, agent memory), TLS certificates, and the running containers' own working space and logs.
  • Olano home — your side of the machine: agent workspaces, conversation transcripts, memory, skills, the credentials vault and the shared tool layer agents install packages into.
  • Swap file — a file the machine uses as overflow memory. It takes its full size on disk whether or not it is being used.
  • System & other host files — the operating system, system logs, package caches and the deployment's own checkout. Measured as what is left over, because the runtime is sandboxed and cannot read those directories directly.

On a typical managed deployment the Olano home is the smallest of these — a box can be 60% full with only a few hundred megabytes of your own data on it. That is expected, and this card is how you confirm it rather than guess.

The second block, Largest directories in the Olano home, then breaks down just that home slice folder by folder; click any row to see one level deeper. Both blocks refresh on their own (the home is walked once a day); Scan now re-measures everything immediately.

docs.title: Playground
docs.text: A sandbox for trying prompts and configurations against an agent without touching a real conversation. Off by default; enable it in Config.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
Opened from the account menu (bottom-left) under Setup, or from ⌘K.

Model providers and their models. Shows which providers are genuinely usable here (a key in the vault, a live sign-in session, or a local model server), and lets you set the deployment's preferred model. Olano-managed tiers appear at the top (see Models and credits).

Providers with their install and sign-in state, and the models each one offers.

A provider's model chips turn green once everything it needs is in place — the package installed and its key present or its sign-in live — so you can see at a glance which models you can actually run. Chips stay neutral while a requirement is missing, while a connected provider is reporting that it is not currently working, and on models the provider has deprecated (shown struck through). Click any chip to copy its provider:model identifier.

docs.title: The Olano card on a self-hosted install
docs.text:
On a self-hosted install the Olano card carries a Run on Olano credits form. Paste an Olano API key created under API keys on cloud.olano.ai (it starts with sk-olano-); the dashboard checks it with your account, stores it in the vault and hands it to every running model. The card then shows the key's prefix, Buy credits and Manage keys links to your account, and Replace key / Remove. Removing it returns the install to your own provider keys at the agents' next start. On an Olano Cloud deployment the card has no form: the deployment bills its own credits.

If the card says the key was refused, it was revoked on cloud.olano.ai or pasted incompletely; paste a valid one. If it says stored but not in use, another key outranks it on this box (a gateway key set in the environment, or an enrolled deployment key): the install keeps that key and the pasted one waits in the vault until the other is removed. A key that comes from the environment variable OLANO_CREDITS_KEY cannot be replaced or removed from the card; change it where it is set and restart the runtime.

Connecting a key on an account with no credits yet is fine: the card and the setup wizard say so, agents on the Olano tiers answer with an out-of-credits message until you buy some on the Billing page, and nothing else changes.

If the box's environment sets a gateway key directly, the card says so and that key wins over a pasted one.

docs.title: Revisions
docs.text:
Automatic version history for your deployment's configuration and markdown files. Every meaningful change is committed, attributed to the agent or human who made it, and browsable here — so you can see what an agent changed in MEMORY.md last Tuesday, and what a config looked like before an edit. See Revisions.

  • History: the list of commits, newest first, ten to a page. The arrows above and below the list go to the newest page, the previous page, the next page and the oldest page, and the label says which page you are on and how many there are. Type a path in the filter box to see only the commits that touched one file (the list starts again on its newest page), and View to read that file as it was at a commit. A merge badge marks a commit that joined GitHub's changes with this deployment's, and not on GitHub marks commits a push has not sent yet.
  • Select a commit to open its details: the full commit id, author, date and message, a summary (files changed, lines added and removed, how many files were added, modified and deleted), and the list of files. Select a file to see its diff, side by side (the default on a computer) or unified (the default on a phone); your choice is remembered. Whole file shows every line around the changes, and Open file at this commit shows the file as it was.
  • GitHub sync (admins only): connect a private GitHub repository, then Push, Pull and Check for updates, choose Automatic push, and resolve a pull whose changes collide with this deployment's. The card shows the repository, its branch, how the deployment signs in and the automatic push mode; a status line (up to date, commits to push, commits to pull, or GitHub has moved on); and when the last push, pull and check happened. While a connection, push or pull runs, the card shows each step as it happens, a progress bar, and while the history moves over the network how many objects and megabytes have been sent or received and at what speed. Everyone viewing the page sees it, including who started it.
  • Held back: a warning lists any tracked file whose current version is not being recorded (too large, looks like it holds a credential, or an agent configuration that does not parse), with the reason.
  • Documents, images, audio and video show as binary in a commit, with Download buttons for the version before and after; opening one at a commit offers a download instead of a text view.
  • Snapshot now records the current state immediately instead of waiting for the next automatic commit.

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text:
Every scheduled job across the deployment: what runs, when it runs next, and what happened last time. Create, edit, pause and delete jobs, and trigger one immediately to test it. Jobs are defined per agent (see Scheduler and heartbeat).

Each job has a Model field and, for models that advertise effort levels, a Reasoning effort field. "Agent default" (the first choice, and what an untouched job uses) follows whatever the agent is configured with; picking a specific model pins that one job to it without changing the agent, which is how the same agent can run a cheap nightly digest and a bigger weekly analysis. The card shows the job's model and effort, each run is billed to the model that ran, and a model whose provider is not connected is refused when you save.

Scheduled tasks with their schedule, the agent that runs them and their run history.

docs.title: The task form
docs.text:
Besides the name, the agent, the prompt and the schedule, a task carries two optional overrides. Both default to the agent's own settings, so a task that leaves them alone behaves exactly as the agent would in chat.

Field What it does Model The model this task runs on. Agent default follows whatever model the agent is configured with. Pick one to run only this task on it. The list holds the models this deployment can actually use. Changing the model changes which effort levels are offered below. Reasoning effort How much thinking the model does before answering on this task's runs. Shown only when the model the task runs on advertises effort levels, and every option is a level that model accepts, so a task can never be saved with an effort its model rejects. Agent default uses the agent's own setting. Higher levels cost more tokens and time per run.

The same two fields appear on the agent page's Schedule card for jobs defined in the agent's configuration, and an agent creating a task for itself can set them through its scheduler tools.

docs.title: Terminal
docs.text:
A shell in the agent's workspace, from the browser. Subject to the same boundaries the agent has — it reaches that workspace and the shared folders, not other agents' directories.

Every terminal belongs to one agent, because its shell runs in that agent's workspace: on a managed deployment, or a self-hosted install set up in sandbox mode, inside that agent's own sandbox. The Workspace agent picker at the top of the page says whose shells you are looking at: switch it and the tabs swap to that agent's terminals (its first one opens on its own if it has none), while the other agents' shells keep running out of sight. Each row of the picker shows how many terminals that agent has open, and a hint beside it says whether the shell runs inside the agent's sandbox or on the host in its workspace. + opens another terminal for the selected agent; closing an agent's last tab leaves an Open terminal button rather than starting a shell you did not ask for. If the agent's sandbox is not running, the tab says so and waits — start the agent, then press Reconnect. When the runtime knows why there is no sandbox (for example the container failed to start), that reason is shown under the message.

The terminal does not depend on the agent's Access level. On a managed deployment every running agent has a sandbox container, whether its Access is Read, Read & Write, Read, Write & Execute or Virtual Files — the container is started with the agent. For an agent without Execute the container is yours, not the agent's: it is where the Terminal, the chat ! shell and the agent's own media/CLI tools run in isolation, while the agent itself still has no shell tool and keeps exactly the file permissions its Access level grants. Switching that agent to Read, Write & Execute later reuses the same container, so anything you installed in it from the Terminal is still there.

It is a real shell, so it behaves like one: Tab completes file and directory names as you type a path, ↑ and ↓ walk back through what you have run, and tmux is installed if you want a session that survives closing the tab.

Two additions on top of the shell itself:

  • Command suggestions. Once you have typed a couple of characters, commands you have run here before appear next to the line you are typing. Press → (right arrow, at the end of the line) to accept the first one, or tap any of them. They are remembered in this browser only, they are never sent anywhere, and a command typed with a leading space is not remembered at all — the same convention the shell itself uses for keeping a secret out of history. Tab still does file completion; the suggestions never take it over.
  • A key bar on phones and tablets. A touch keyboard has no Tab, arrows, Esc or Ctrl, and a browser terminal has no right-click menu, so those live in a row under the terminal: Copy (the selection, or the visible screen when nothing is selected), Paste, Tab, ↑, ↓, Esc, Ctrl+C and Enter. If your browser refuses clipboard access, Paste falls back to asking for the text.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Opened from the account menu (bottom-left) under Setup, or from ⌘K.

Browse every tool available on the deployment, grouped by category, each with a description of what it does. Tools that exist but are switched off show as locked with the reason — for example a tool that needs a credential you have not set yet — so you can find out a capability exists instead of it being invisible.

The tool catalog, filterable by status and toolkit.

You do not have to come here to give an agent a toolkit. Ask the agent — "connect yourself to GitHub" — and it adds the toolkit to itself (self_add_toolkit), tells you which sign-in it needs and sends the link for it, then restarts when you say so; self_remove_toolkit takes one away again. AgentFather does the same for any agent (olano_add_toolkit). A toolkit added this way is the same as one you tick on the agent's Tools tab: it applies after the agent restarts.

Fleet-wide tools. A few tools are badged fleet-wide, with a note under the row explaining what that means. They act across the whole deployment rather than only for the agent holding them: reading the shared runtime log, another agent's chat transcripts or workspace, the credentials vault, or running a command as a different agent. Anyone who can chat with an agent can ask it to use the tools it holds — so a fleet-wide tool belongs only on an operations agent you trust with the entire deployment. AgentFather ships with them; nothing else gets them unless you tick them yourself.

Two rules back the badge up. Agents cannot hand these to each other or to themselves — a bot asked to "give yourself the log reader" is refused, and so is AgentFather doing it on a scheduled run or on another agent's behalf; adding one is a decision an administrator makes here, in the dashboard. And holding the tool is not enough to use it: these tools answer only when an administrator is the person on the turn, so an ordinary member chatting with an agent that holds them still cannot read another agent's logs or transcripts. Ordinary tools are unaffected — the badge is the whole list.

docs.title: Vault (admin only)
docs.text:
Opened from the account menu (bottom-left) under Administration, or from ⌘K.

The encrypted credential store: every API key, bot token and service password. You can add, rename and delete entries, and set per-agent overrides so two agents using the same credential name authenticate as different identities.

A locked vault: agents cannot read secrets until it is unlocked.

Who can see a stored value. An admin can reveal one here in the dashboard. An agent cannot, by default: asking the vault for a credential returns a masked preview (PKBM************), enough to confirm which key is stored without putting the secret in the conversation. The full value is an explicit, owner-only request that needs human approval before it reaches the agent. So an agent can list names and use a credential freely, and only a person can turn one back into plaintext.

Entries the runtime keeps for itself are not listed. The deployment's own connection credentials (the key it uses to reach Olano-managed models, the signing key for its link to Olano Cloud) live in the same encrypted store, but they are created and renewed by the runtime, never by you. They do not appear on this page, cannot be revealed, changed, removed or overridden from the dashboard, and agents cannot read or use them. Whether the deployment is connected is shown on the Overview provider card instead.

Rekey changes the vault passphrase and re-encrypts every stored secret under the new one. Use it if the passphrase may have been exposed.

The vault re-locks whenever the server or dashboard restarts, and the dashboard prompts you to unlock it before anything that needs a credential can run.

docs.title: Feature guides
docs.text:
The reference pages say what every field and tab does. These guides say how the pieces fit together for one job at a time: what to turn on, in which order, and what to expect once it runs. Each one points back at the exact fields in agent.json5 and config.yaml.

  • Agent-to-agent and the org chart: who may ask whom for work, and how the org chart and the allow-lists combine.
  • Human in the loop and approvals: which actions wait for a person, and where the approval cards appear.
  • Privacy and security: what an agent may read, reach and run, and how to tighten it.
  • Multi-user: team accounts on one deployment, and per-customer isolation for a public-facing agent. Two different features.
  • Subscriptions and monetization: charging for access to an agent.
  • MCP servers: giving an agent external tools, with or without a sign-in.
  • Webhooks: letting outside systems trigger an agent.
  • Pages, sites and web apps: publishing reports, npm-built apps and small web apps with their own server, behind a password you set.
  • Scheduler and heartbeat: recurring work, and the agent's own periodic check-in.
  • Memory and self-learning: what an agent keeps between conversations and how it distils it.
  • Notes: the agent's linked wiki.
  • Issues: the shared tracker between people and agents.
  • Revisions: the automatic history of configuration and markdown changes.
  • Channels and connectors: WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, email and the rest, including the OpenAI-compatible API.
  • Cortex and Pulse: the background reasoning engine and the proactive suggestions it produces.
  • The mobile app: the Olano app for phones, tablets and Macs, and the notifications it receives.
  • Budgets: token ceilings and spending warnings.
  • Ask the agent: self-configuration, magic links and the AgentFather admin tools.
  • Beyond the deployment, A2A and MCP: talking to outside agents, and letting outside platforms reach yours.

docs.title: Beyond the deployment, A2A and MCP
Beyond the deployment: A2A and MCP
docs.text:
Everything in Agent-to-agent and the org chart is about agents on this deployment talking to each other. Two further doors connect them to the world outside, each built on an open protocol so the other side can be anyone's software:

  • Outbound — A2A. Your agent hands work to an agent hosted elsewhere (another company's, another Olano deployment's) using the Agent2Agent protocol.
  • Inbound — MCP. An outside platform that speaks the Model Context Protocol (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, an agent framework, an automation tool) sends your agent a message and reads the reply.

Both are off until you switch them on, both are audited in the Agent to Agent tab, and neither changes how your own agents talk to each other.

flowchart TB
    EX["Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, an automation tool,<br/>or another agent over A2A"] -- "inbound, MCP or A2A,<br/>with a token you issued" --> B["Your agent with External access on"]
    B <-- "talk_to_agent, inside the deployment" --> A["Your agent with Remote Agents listed"]
    A -- "outbound A2A,<br/>only to names on its list" --> RA["An agent hosted elsewhere"]

docs.title: Talking to an outside agent (A2A)
docs.text:
1. Ask the remote party for their agent's base URL and, if it requires one, a credential. Store the credential in the vault (Config → Credentials, or ask your agent to send you a magic link for it).
  2. On your agent's Advanced tab, add an entry under Remote Agents (agent.json5 reference): a short name, the url, the auth mode and the credential as a vault reference.
  3. Restart the agent. It now has a2a_list_agents (what it may talk to), a2a_discover_agent (read the remote Agent Card: skills, endpoints, authentication), a2a_send_message (send a request and get the reply) and a2a_get_task (poll a long-running remote task).

What the agent can and cannot do: it can only address names on its list — there is no URL parameter, and it cannot add entries itself. Each reply is treated as input from another organisation: your agent reports it rather than following instructions embedded in it, and it is told not to forward secrets or private data you did not ask it to share. Multi-turn exchanges continue automatically within one of your conversations (the remote context_id is remembered), or explicitly by passing the context_id back.

What the platform enforces on every call: https:// only; the configured URL and the endpoint the remote Agent Card advertises are checked against the same outbound-request policy as every other web tool (no private networks, no cloud metadata addresses, your agent's own allow/deny lists); the card's endpoint must live on the same origin as the URL you configured unless you opt out per entry; credentials are read from the vault at call time and sent only to that vetted endpoint; replies are capped in length; and every send and reply appears in Agent to Agent under the External segment, as a conversation between your agent and the remote agent's configured name with an A2A badge. a2a_send_message counts as an external write for approval purposes, so an agent in Supervised or Locked-down mode asks before sending. Fleet-wide rules live in config.yaml → remote_agents (remote_agents: — fleet rules for talking to outside agents (A2A)).

docs.title: Letting an outside platform reach your agent (MCP and A2A)
docs.text:
1. Switch the doors on home-wide. Config → External access: turn on MCP endpoint, A2A endpoints, or both. The deployment must have an https:// public URL; a plain-http public endpoint is refused.
  2. Publish the agent. Open the agent → External access tab (clearly labelled as the opposite of its MCP tab), switch on Reachable over MCP and/or Reachable over A2A, and write the public description — what the agent can do for an outside caller, what it needs, what it will not do. It is required, it is what every remote caller sees, and it is not the system prompt. Save and restart the agent. The tab then shows the exact endpoints: the MCP endpoint and the agent's tool name ask_<agent>, and the A2A Agent Card and JSON-RPC address.
  3. Give the caller a credential. Either
  4. mint a token on the same tab (or on Config → External access for the fleet view): a label, the agents it may reach (or every exposed agent), a lifetime. The token is shown once; only a hash is kept. Revoke it from the same list at any time. An agent can also send an administrator a token-minting page with magic_link_mint_access_token — the token appears on that page, never in the chat; or
  5. let the client sign in with OAuth. Clients that cannot paste a header (a Claude.ai custom connector, an A2A client following the card) discover the deployment's own authorization server, register themselves, and send you to the dashboard's consent page. There an administrator sees who is asking and which agents they requested, ticks the agents to grant (or every exposed agent), and allows or declines. The client then receives a short-lived access token and a rotating refresh token; both appear in the token list tagged OAuth, and Config → External access → OAuth clients lists the applications, each with a Forget button that revokes everything it holds.
  6. Point the client at it. For MCP: a server of type Streamable HTTP at <public URL>/api/mcp with the header Authorization: Bearer <token> (or the OAuth sign-in). Its tool list shows olano_list_agents plus one ask_<agent> tool per exposed agent; thread_id on a call continues a conversation. For A2A: the agent's card URL <public URL>/api/a2a/agents/<agent>/.well-known/agent-card.json; the card declares both the bearer scheme and the OAuth flow. A client that calls an agent without a token is pointed at that agent's own sign-in details, so an OAuth-capable client can find the sign-in by itself. Applications that cannot keep a secret (command-line and desktop tools) can register and sign in as public clients.

From chat, only an administrator can do any of this. AgentFather (or any agent holding the admin tools) has olano_set_agent_external_access to flip an agent's flags and set its description, and every agent has self_set_external_access for itself plus magic_link_mint_access_token; all three refuse unless the person on the turn is an administrator (a peer agent, a scheduled run, an inbound MCP or A2A caller, or a non-admin member is refused with an explanation). The per-agent switch that decides whether an agent even holds those tools is the external_access self-configuration capability (agent_autonomy:).
