docs.title: LinkedIn outreach: profile visits, connection requests, inbox and posts
docs.text:
The LinkedIn connection on the Connections page can post as you, but LinkedIn does not let ordinary apps send connection requests, follow people, read messages or comment. The LinkedIn outreach toolkit does those things on your own LinkedIn account, in one of two ways: through Olano Cloud, as a paid add-on (of a managed deployment, or of your account for a self-hosted install running on an Olano API key), or through your own Unipile workspace (below), on any install. With neither, the tools say what is missing and do nothing.

Turning it on. First switch the LinkedIn outreach add-on on, in the place that matches your install:

  • An Olano Cloud deployment: in the Olano Cloud console, on the instance's page, open the Plan tab, and under LinkedIn outreach choose how many LinkedIn accounts to pay for (one seat per account, so one per agent that will do outreach). You can also pick it while deploying a new instance, in the Add-ons step. It takes effect right away.
  • A self-hosted install on an Olano API key (Models and credits): on cloud.olano.ai, under Billing, the LinkedIn outreach for your API keys card. The seats are bought for your account on their own monthly subscription and shared by every install using your API keys; the first switch-on opens a checkout, and the seats appear once the payment is confirmed.

Either way you can add seats, disconnect an account or switch the add-on off from the same place later. See cloud.olano.ai for the current price. Without the add-on the tools answer that it is not switched on, and say which of the two places to go.

Then add the LinkedIn outreach toolkit to an agent (Tools tab, or ask the agent to add it with self_add_toolkit) and ask the agent to connect LinkedIn: it calls linkedin_connect_account and gives you a secure link. Open it, sign in to LinkedIn on that page (two-step verification, if you use it, happens there too) and approve. Your password never passes through the chat or the agent. The link expires after about an hour; ask for a new one if it lapses. Each agent has its own LinkedIn account, so two agents can work two different accounts (each uses one seat), and connecting a different account replaces the agent's current one. When every seat is taken, the agent says which agents hold them; add a seat or disconnect one first.

Using your own Unipile workspace instead. If you already have a Unipile account, put its API key and DSN in the Vault as UNIPILE_API_KEY and UNIPILE_DSN (the DSN is shown in the Unipile dashboard, for example api1.unipile.com:13111; with or without https://). An agent can ask you for them with a secure link (magic_link_request_secret), so they never pass through the chat. As soon as both resolve for an agent, its LinkedIn tools talk to your workspace directly: no add-on and no credits, Unipile bills you, and it works on self-hosted installs too. Set them on one agent (its Vault override or env) to use them for that agent only. Which LinkedIn account of the workspace an agent uses:

How When UNIPILE_ACCOUNT_ID in the Vault Always wins: the Unipile account id of the LinkedIn account this agent must use The sign-in link Ask the agent to connect LinkedIn: the account the link adds to your workspace becomes this agent's Automatic A workspace with exactly one LinkedIn account that no other agent uses is picked up without asking

The same daily limits and the same approvals apply as on the managed service. Disconnecting deletes the account from your workspace only when it was added through the agent's sign-in link; an account you connected in the Unipile dashboard yourself is left there.

What the agent can then do:

Tool What it does Needs your approval Charged linkedin_account_status Is LinkedIn connected, did the last sign-in link finish, what are the daily limits No No linkedin_visit_profile Opens a member's profile, so they see the visit in "Who viewed your profile", and reads it No Yes linkedin_follow_profile Follows a member Yes Yes linkedin_send_invitation Sends a connection request, with a personal note (up to 300 characters) or without one Yes Yes linkedin_list_sent_invitations / linkedin_withdraw_invitation Lists pending requests you sent, and withdraws one. LinkedIn shows how long ago a pending request was sent only in its own words ("Sent today", "Sent 1 week ago"), never an exact time, so that is what the list shows No No linkedin_list_conversations / linkedin_read_conversation Lists your inbox and reads one conversation, oldest message first No No linkedin_send_message Replies in a conversation, or sends a first message to someone you are already connected with Yes Yes linkedin_list_posts Lists a member's recent posts (does not notify them) No No linkedin_comment_on_post Comments on a post, publicly, under your name Yes Yes linkedin_react_to_post Reacts to a post (like, celebrate, support, love, insightful, funny) No Yes linkedin_disconnect_account Disconnects the account, which frees its seat for another agent Yes No

"Needs your approval" follows your approval settings: with the default settings, anything that speaks for you to another person waits for a yes on the Approvals page or in chat first.

What it costs. The add-on is billed with your subscription, per seat; adding a seat charges the rest of the current billing period right away, and removing one or switching the add-on off credits the unused part to your balance. Switching it off disconnects every LinkedIn account at once. On top of the seats, each charged action above costs a small amount of credits. Nothing is charged when LinkedIn refuses an action, or when nothing was sent (for example a connection request to someone you are already connected with). The agent tells you what each action cost; the Insights tab shows the total as LinkedIn outreach.

Daily limits. LinkedIn restricts accounts that act too fast, so each account has a rolling 24-hour limit per kind of action (visits, follows, connection requests, messages, comments, reactions). The agent can tell you the current limits with linkedin_account_status. When one is reached the agent stops and continues the next day. LinkedIn has limits of its own on top: a weekly cap on connection requests, and, on free accounts, only a few requests with a personal note per month. When LinkedIn refuses, the agent passes on LinkedIn's reason and can offer to send the request without a note.

Messages and posts are other people's words. What the agent reads in your inbox or in someone's posts is treated as information, never as instructions to the agent, so a message that says "ignore your instructions" changes nothing.

When LinkedIn signs you out. LinkedIn ends sessions on its own schedule. The agent then says the account needs reconnecting and offers a new sign-in link.

LinkedIn's terms do not allow automating an account, and LinkedIn may restrict accounts it believes are automated. The limits above keep the pace well below what LinkedIn tolerates, but the risk stays with the account owner: keep the outreach personal and relevant.

docs.title: Cortex and Pulse
docs.text:
Cortex is the autonomous cognition engine: the work an agent does between conversations. Distilling learnings into memory, tidying its notes and workspace, refining its skills, expanding ideas, and generating suggestions. Watch it in the Cortex tab.

It runs on two model tiers — a fast_model for light passes and a deep_model for heavy ones — with max_deep_runs_per_day (default 12) as the cost ceiling. intensity (relaxed by default, or balanced / aggressive) sets the overall pace.

flowchart TB
    IN["Conversations, scheduled runs, the workspace"] --> CX["Cortex phases<br/>a fast model for light passes, a deep model for heavy ones"]
    CX --> MEM["Memory and notes<br/>distilled, tidied"]
    CX --> SK["Skills<br/>refined"]
    CX --> ID["Ideas, brainstorms,<br/>prototypes"]
    CX --> PU["Pulse<br/>suggestions"]
    PU --> YOU["You: at the start of a session,<br/>on a channel or in a daily digest"]
    CX -. "outward, irreversible<br/>or identity-changing" .-> AP["Waits in Cortex, Self-Improve"]

Cortex is off until you turn it on. On a new deployment the Cortex engine row in Cortex → Autonomy reads Off in the "All agents" column, so no agent does background cognition: no scheduled phases, no distilling of conversations into memory, and no cortex_* tools in chat (an agent can still read and write its memory when you ask it to). Switch the "All agents" column on to start it for every agent, at the relaxed cadence unless you pick another; or leave the fleet off and set one agent's own column to On to pilot it there first. An agent that was set Off on its own stays off either way.

Settings resolve with one rule in both directions: the agent wins when it has an opinion, the deployment applies when it doesn't. Every per-agent toggle is three-state, including the master switch, so "off for the fleet, on for one agent" works as well as the reverse.

docs.title: The funnel: brainstorms, ideas, prototypes, projects
docs.text:
Everything creative Cortex produces lives in one staged funnel, brainstorm → idea → prototype → project. Each item is a folder in the agent's workspace (brainstorming/, ideas/, prototypes/, projects/) tracked by a single index, and the Cortex tab shows all four stages for every agent. Items move down the funnel by promotion: a brainstorm's strongest angle becomes an idea, an idea becomes a small runnable prototype (run on the spot when it is safe to, with the output kept in its RESULTS.md), and a prototype that has proved itself becomes a project with a README, a phased PLAN.md of checkboxes, a STATUS.md and a JOURNAL.md. A promoted item stays where it was, marked promoted and linked to what it became; the new item links back. Create project on a card still jumps straight to a project, for the case where you have already decided.

You can also review the funnel from a conversation with AgentFather: ask it what an agent (or every agent) has been brainstorming, which ideas score below 4, to discard all of an agent's brainstorms, or to promote a specific idea to a prototype. It reads the items and their ratings, recommends what to keep, and does the same discard, restore and promote the cards do, each behind an approval card. See Asking the agent.

flowchart LR
    B["Brainstorm"] -- "strongest angle" --> I["Idea"]
    I -- "small build, run" --> P["Prototype"]
    P -- "proved itself" --> J["Project: PLAN, STATUS, JOURNAL"]
    R["Rate & Promote<br/>scores every item 1-10"] -.-> B & I & P & J
    J --> X["Advance Work: executes steps,<br/>schedules its own follow-ups,<br/>publishes results"]

Ratings. The Rate & Promote phase reads every active item's folder and gives it a score from 1 to 10 with a one-line reason, a recommendation (promote, execute, explore, keep or discard) and the single most useful next step. The score shows on the card and in the item's drawer, and the agent reports it when you ask about an item in chat. Ratings are always written, whatever the autonomy posture; what happens next depends on it.

With Fully Autonomous on (the default once Cortex is on), the funnel runs itself:

  • An item recommended for promotion and scored at or above the promotion threshold (cognition.promote_threshold, default 8) is promoted to the next stage, at most max_promotions_per_run (default 1) per run and never past the daily deep-run cap. An item recommended for discarding and scored 3 or lower is discarded; its folder stays and Restore brings it back (cognition.auto_discard, default on, turns this half off).
  • Advance Work then executes. It takes the highest-rated prototype or project with a doable next step and finishes one real step end to end: builds, runs, verifies, ticks the PLAN.md box it genuinely completed and records the result in the item's folder. When the work continues past the run, it schedules a follow-up step for itself (a check tomorrow, a daily pull, the next phase); those appear in the Scheduler tab named Cortex: <item>, bounded to a few pending steps per agent (cognition.max_self_scheduled_tasks, default 6), two per item and at most hourly, and each runs as a normal turn of the agent inside the item's folder. It writes procedures it will need again as learned skills, publishes results as a page from the item's folder when they are worth showing (you set the viewer password under the agent's Pages), asks another agent on the deployment when that agent has a capability it lacks (sending an email, say), and sends you a notification when something is ready to look at.
  • It works as a team. Every background run that executes, rates or plans is handed the same roster the agent sees in chat, with what each teammate can do: the services its tools reach (email, calendar, Slack, GitHub, a CRM, a trading account), whether it has a shell, and the MCP servers it is connected to with their tool counts. When a step needs one of those, the run asks that agent for exactly that piece and records the reply in the item's folder, so a project whose plan says "post the summary to Slack" or "pull the open tickets from Linear" gets done by the agent that holds the connection. Who an agent may see and message is still yours to set: the agent's Agent visibility and the org chart apply to background runs exactly as they do in chat.
  • cognition.approval_required still holds on every one of those runs, the self-scheduled steps included: by default an email, a payment or an identity edit waits in Cortex → Self-Improve (the tab that lists everything Cortex is holding for your approval), and the item's STATUS.md says so.

With Fully Autonomous off, ratings are advice. Each promotion candidate becomes a card in Cortex → Self-Improve whose Approve does exactly what the autonomous run would have done; nothing is discarded, and Advance Work develops items without scheduling, publishing or reaching out.

Nothing is generated twice. Every generating run (brainstorming, ideas, prototyping, a brainstorm promoted to an idea) is handed the whole portfolio: every brainstorm, idea, prototype and project, including the ones already promoted and the ones discarded, and is told that a rewording, a narrower or wider cut, or a recombination of existing items is not new. What the model returns is then checked against all of it on content, not just title: a candidate that restates an item at any stage or status is dropped and named in the run's summary ("Skipped 2 near-duplicates: ..."), a candidate that matches an active item of the same kind improves that item instead of adding a copy, and two candidates from the same run that repeat each other keep only the first. A discarded item stays discarded; it is never recreated under a new name. The Rate & Promote reviewer looks for duplicates among what already exists too, and marks the weaker copy discard with a link to the one to keep, so the pair is visible in the item's details rather than silently merged.

Steer all of it with Creative direction (CORTEX.md): the reviewer reads your goals and your Avoid list and rates against them.

When a background run fails. A run that a provider refuses with a temporary condition — a rate limit, an overloaded model — is not lost: the scheduler runs that phase again about 15 minutes later with a fresh start, and once more an hour after that if needed, before waiting for the next scheduled time. Runs across the deployment also never all start in the same minute (each agent's scheduled minute is spread out) and no more than worker_max_concurrency of them talk to a model at once, so the deployment does not bring a rate limit on itself. A failure the deployment can heal on its own reaches the notification bell and the Pulse Ops lane only once the same run has failed twice in a row; a failure that needs you — an expired sign-in, a locked vault, an empty balance — rings immediately, with the fix-it button. A success clears the streak.

Where intensity and max_deep_runs_per_day govern how many runs happen, two settings bound what a single run may spend: the Step budget (how many internal steps of thinking and tool use it may take, default 100 ≈ 25 rounds) and the Time limit (wall-clock seconds, default 1200). A run that exceeds either stops and its work for that run is discarded. Both follow the same two-tier rule as everything else and are edited side by side in Cortex → Autonomy — the "All agents" column for the whole deployment, the per-agent column for one, Inherit to follow the deployment. Raise them together: a larger step budget behind the old time limit just fails on time instead. The Step budget is the recursion limit — there is no second control by that name, and none for ordinary chat, which is not bounded this way. Each field's help text names the config key it writes, so a value you have read about in a config file can be traced back to the row that sets it.

Phases & schedule, the second part of the settings card, is one row per phase: what it is, when it next runs, how the last run went, the same two columns of on/off, and Log / Run now. On a phone each phase becomes a small block instead of a line — the phase's full name, then its schedule, then the two scopes each behind an "All agents" / agent-name label, then the two buttons — so it is always clear which phase you are about to run and which scope a switch belongs to.

Background work has no one watching it, so a run that fails, times out or needs setup raises a notification — the sidebar bell and the Overview Notifications section — naming the agent, the run and the fix, and clearing itself when that run next succeeds. You do not have to open Cortex to find out something went wrong. Runs stopped by a guard rail you configured (over budget, nested too deep) stay quiet: they are working as intended.

Talking about any of it happens in Chat. Every button in Cortex that asks the agent to do something — "Chat" on a Pulse card, an idea, brainstorm, prototype or project; "Explore more" on an idea, brainstorm or prototype; "Send to Agent" on a prototype; "Fix with agent" on a self-check finding — takes you to the Chat tab on that item's own conversation, switching to the agent the item belongs to. The first time, the message box arrives pre-filled, not sent: a short framing that says what you are there to do ("The user wants to explore more about this idea …") and gives the agent the full workspace path to the item's files, ending in User: so you type what you actually want and press Send yourself. Nothing goes to the agent until you do. Each item keeps one conversation, so coming back opens its history with an empty message box and continues where you left off rather than starting over; it is a normal chat, with attachments, the model override, tool approvals and the full history. The conversation carries a violet CORTEX badge in your conversation list so you can find it later. The same hand-off works from the simple shell's Cortex page.

Pulse is the output you actually see: short, proactive suggestions surfaced at the start of a session, optionally pushed to channels or emailed as a daily digest. quiet_hours_start / quiet_hours_end keep it from interrupting, and the per-session and per-day caps keep it from becoming noise.

docs.title: Human in the loop and approvals
Human in the loop (HITL) and approvals
docs.text:
When an agent wants to do something consequential, it can stop and ask. The request appears in the Approvals section of the dashboard Overview with the exact action described, and the agent waits for your decision (up to security.hitl_timeout_seconds, default 300).

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as Agent
    participant O as Olano
    participant P as Person
    A->>O: wants to run a gated action
    O->>P: the action and its details, in Overview, Approvals<br/>(an owner on WhatsApp gets a YES/NO code instead)
    Note over A: the agent waits,<br/>up to hitl_timeout_seconds (300 by default)
    alt approved
        P->>O: Approve
        O->>A: the action runs
    else rejected, or no answer in time
        P-->>O: Reject
        O->>A: the action does not run
    end
    O->>O: the decision goes into the approval record

Approval is decided in three layers, each overriding the one before:

1. The profile (security.profile) sets the baseline:

Profile Meaning Always asks before developer (default) Trusted — act freely money, writing secrets, running commands in another agent's workspace safe Supervised — ask before writes the above, plus external writes, shell commands, reading secrets production Locked down — strictest the above, plus filesystem writes and delegating to subagents

2. Toggles add categories on top: security.hitl_write_tools: true adds external writes; security.hitl_shell: true adds shell commands.

3. Per-tool overrides win over everything: security.tools.<tool_name>.approval set to "always" or "never".

security.hitl_enabled: false is the master off switch — full autonomy, no approvals at all. All three profiles enable it by default.

Two things are always individually approved, in every profile: running a command in another agent's workspace, and a browser action that submits a form, buys, pays, sends, posts or deletes. There is no configuration that turns either off, and neither the chat's Auto mode nor Accept all, a remembered "always allow", a scheduled run or a background run approves one on a person's behalf.

security.hitl_auto_approve_low_risk (default true) lets clearly-safe actions through without asking, so the queue stays meaningful.

Cortex has its own approval setting. cognition.auto_approve decides whether background work skips the queue, but cognition.approval_required — default ["external_send", "irreversible", "identity_edit"] — always needs a human, whatever auto_approve says. Anything that sends something outside, cannot be undone, or rewrites who the agent is, gets a person in the loop: the item waits in Cortex → Self-Improve instead of being applied, and a background run that tries such a step pauses on it the same way. So does a step the agent scheduled for itself from a background run (cortex_schedule, shown in Scheduler as Cortex: <item>): it runs under the same rule as the run that booked it, not with the free hand a task you scheduled yourself gets. Fully Autonomous still handles everything else on its own: new skills, memory, procedures, tidy-ups, promotions down the funnel and the execution of prototypes and projects. An owner who really wants an agent to act unattended on all of it sets approval_required: [] for that agent; one who wants only identity protected lists just ["identity_edit"].

Approvals from WhatsApp. When someone talks to an agent on any of the three WhatsApp connectors, the outcome of a risky action depends on who they are:

  • An owner has risky actions approved without being asked, unless Ask owners in chat before risky actions is on in the connector's Behavior section (chat_approvals: true). Owners are the numbers in Owner numbers; on the QR connector the numbers in Allowed phone numbers count as owners too, while on the Twilio and Meta connectors Allowed sender numbers is a list of customers and makes nobody an owner. Then the agent posts the action and its details in the chat with a four-character code and waits; the owner replies YES 4F2A to let it run or NO 4F2A to stop it. Only the owner whose message started the request can answer, and a reply without the code does nothing. With no answer before security.hitl_timeout_seconds the action is rejected, and so is one whose prompt could not be delivered.
  • Anyone else never decides: their risky actions wait in the dashboard's Approvals list for someone with access to the agent.

The approval record. Every approval decision is written to an append-only file, audit/approvals.jsonl in the Olano home: the action and its details, when it was asked, the outcome (approved, rejected, timed out, or abandoned when the server stopped before anyone answered), who decided (a dashboard user as human-<username>, a messenger sender as <platform>:<id>) and through which surface. Actions an owner's messages had approved without asking are recorded too. Read it on the Overview page under Approvals → Approval history, which can be narrowed to one agent. Admins see the whole record; a member sees the rows for agents they have access to.

docs.title: Issues
docs.text:
A work tracker where agents and humans are both first-class participants. An issue has a title, body, type, status, comments and an assignee, and every change is recorded in an audit trail.

Participants are identified by kind: agents as ai-<name>, dashboard humans as human-<handle>. You never pass an actor as a parameter — the tracker knows who is acting from the surface being used, so an agent cannot file an issue as someone else.

Both halves of those names are permanent: an agent's name and a person's Handle (set once when their account is created, in Admin → Users). That is deliberate — an issue assigned last month has to keep pointing at the same participant after someone edits their display name. So renaming an agent's Display name, or a person's Name, never moves their issues. You can assign by either form: carlos-m or Carlos M. both resolve, and if two people match you get an error naming both rather than a guess.

Delivery differs by kind. Assign an issue to an agent and it picks it up on its own poll (default every 15 minutes) and starts working. Assign one to a person and they get a dashboard notification — click the row, in the bell or in the Overview list, and it opens that issue's own page. Set issues.auto_process: false on an agent for manual mode, where issues wait until a human prompts the agent or a scheduled job runs.

Search is hybrid — keyword matching plus meaning-based matching — so "customer can't log in" finds an issue titled "authentication failure". Creating an issue that closely duplicates an open one is refused, with the existing issue shown; pass allow_duplicate if you meant it.

Surfaces: the Issues tab and seven issue_* tools every agent has (issue_create, issue_list, issue_show, issue_comment, issue_assign, issue_close, issue_reopen).

docs.title: MCP servers
docs.text:
MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers give an agent tools that Olano does not ship — a vendor's own integration, an internal service, a community server.

Add one from the agent's MCP tab, or ask the agent — "connect yourself to Notion" — and it finds every supported way to reach the service, adds the one you pick and starts the sign-in (self_find_integration → self_add_mcp_server → sign-in). AgentFather does the same for any agent (olano_find_integration, olano_add_mcp_server). Both read the Olano MCP directory — a curated catalog of add-able servers with verified endpoints and ready-made presets — so nobody has to type a server URL from memory.

Supported integrations come first. When you ask an agent to connect a service, it offers the supported ways to reach it, in this order: (1) a messaging channel, when the service is a place people talk; (2) an MCP server from the directory — it usually carries its own sign-in, so you click a consent screen you recognise; (3) a built-in toolkit, signed in through the Connections card's best method — Olano's app, your own OAuth app, a code typed on a phone, or as a last resort a key entered on a secure form. All three run inside Olano, are authenticated by Olano and appear in Connections. Anything the agent cannot find in a catalog is external: it may be installed in the agent's sandbox, Olano never authenticates it, and it is at your risk — the agent says so before doing it, and reads the project's documentation first (self_inspect_external) to tell you what it is, what it needs and whether a built-in integration already covers it. A small purpose-built MCP server is the answer only when the platform matters and nothing supported covers it. Whichever route: add the server or toolkit first, then sign in — in that order.

Transports:

  • sse (default) and http — the server runs somewhere and you connect to a URL.
  • stdio — Olano launches the server as a process (command + args + env). On a managed deployment each stdio server runs inside an isolated, throwaway container with access to the agent's workspace but not to the platform itself, so npx/uvx-style servers work there too. That container receives only the env the server declares — write each credential as ${vault:NAME} there and it resolves for that agent, a GitHub connection included — never the rest of the vault. It requires sandboxed execution to be enabled for the deployment (it is by default), and if the sandbox is unavailable the server is skipped with a message naming the reason — remote (http/sse) servers are always available. If a catalog entry's command is itself docker run …, use its remote preset instead on a managed deployment.

Authentication — a server that signs you in. Set auth: "oauth" for a server that requires a sign-in; the Authorize button on the MCP tab walks through it, and the grant is stored for you. From a chat, an agent can start the same flow: in the dashboard chat the sign-in appears as a Connect button card — the service's name and logo with one button to click, never a wall of URL text — while on messaging channels the agent sends the link (and PIN, when one applies) as a plain message you tap. Either way you sign in with the provider in your own browser and the agent's new tools come online on their own, without anyone touching the dashboard.

Add the server to the agent before signing in. Authorizing a URL the agent does not have stores a grant for a server it will never load — the sign-in looks successful and nothing works. If a sign-in does complete for a server that was never added, Olano now registers it using the transport the sign-in itself connected over; adding it first, with the settings you actually want, is still the right order.

Where the sign-in comes back to. A provider sends you back after you sign in, and it insists on a secure (https) address it can trust. Olano picks that address for you, in this order:

  • Olano Cloud deployments use Olano's sign-in service at auth.olano.ai. Nothing to set up.
  • A self-hosted install with an Olano API key (the one you pasted on Providers → Olano for credits; see Models and credits) uses the same sign-in service, even with no domain or certificate of its own: a box on a home network or a bare IP address can sign in to MCP servers. The box registers itself in the background a few seconds after the key is pasted or after a restart, and stays registered while the key is live. The sign-in service only ever passes back a one-time code that is useless without a secret that never leaves your box; the tokens are exchanged and kept on your box, as always. Revoking the key on cloud.olano.ai stops this at once. An account can have up to five self-hosted installs using it at a time; an install that has not been used for 30 days gives up its place on its own.
  • A self-hosted install with its own https address (a domain with a certificate, set as the deployment's public address) keeps using that address, key or no key.
  • A self-hosted install with neither has nowhere for the provider to send you back: the Authorize button and the agent explain that, and the fix is to paste an Olano API key or give the box a public https address.

This sign-in service is only for MCP servers. The built-in Connect with Olano's app option on the Connections tab (for example Google or Microsoft 365) is offered on Olano Cloud deployments only; on a self-hosted install, use Use your own OAuth app with an OAuth client you create in that service's developer console (see Connections).

A server that wants an OAuth app of your own. A few servers — HubSpot is the common one — do not register clients automatically and only accept an OAuth app you created in their developer console. (For HubSpot this is only the MCP server: the built-in hubspot toolkit connects from Connections → HubSpot, with Olano's app where your deployment offers it.) The directory knows which ones, so the magic link opens straight on a form asking for the app's Client ID and Client secret: it shows the exact redirect URL to register on the app, links to the provider's console, and continues the sign-in from the same page once the two values are saved. A server nobody had catalogued that turns out to want the same thing comes back to that form instead of failing the link. The Client ID stays on the agent's server entry (visible on its MCP tab); the Client secret goes into the Vault as that agent's own value, under a key named after the server (MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET_…), and the entry keeps a ${vault:…} reference to it — the same way a bot token or an API-key header is kept out of the config file. A later reconnect never asks again. The same form offers Composio as the route that needs no app of your own: one Composio sign-in reaches hundreds of platforms, and the page gives you a message to paste back to the agent — it connects the Composio MCP first, then the platform through it.

Authentication — a server that wants an API key. Ask for the key over a secure link rather than typing it into a chat, then point the server entry at the stored value instead of pasting the key into the config:

{
  url: "https://mcp.example.com/mcp",
  transport: "http",
  headers: { Authorization: "Bearer ${vault:EXAMPLE_API_KEY}" },
}

${vault:NAME} works in both headers (for http/sse servers) and env (for stdio ones), and resolves per agent — two agents can use the same server with their own keys. Write the key as a literal only if you are content for it to live in the config file.

Olano renews grants before they expire — see the mcp_health: settings in mcp_health: — keeping MCP connections alive. This matters more than it sounds: a token that lapses while an agent is idle can become unrecoverable, so leave refresh_tokens on.

Health. The MCP tab shows each server's live status, and Config → MCP connection health shows the fleet. Servers that time out or error are retried with backoff. A server that needs a sign-in you have never given is not retried — reconnecting cannot invent consent, so you have to authorize it. AgentFather reports the same with olano_mcp_status.

Narrowing a server. disabled_tools on the server entry hides specific tools it offers — useful when a server exposes fifty tools and your agent needs three. Only the enabled tools are bound to the agent and named in its prompt, so a hidden tool costs nothing per turn. The agent still knows the hidden ones exist: self_list_mcp_tools lists every tool a server offers with the switched-off ones marked, so when a task would need one the agent can say so and suggest enabling it here rather than routing the task through another service. Its prompt tells it how many tools are switched off per server.

In the dashboard this is the row of switches on the server's card, one per tool, with Enable all and Disable all above them. Those two are the fast route to "this agent only needs three of these": disable all, then switch the three back on. Each switch takes effect the moment you click it, and a burst of clicks is saved together, so working through a long list stays responsive.

Two things to know:

  • Disable all needs to know the server's full tool list, so it stays greyed out until the card has actually connected — press Refresh status first if it is. Enable all always works, since "nothing disabled" needs no list.
  • The switches change the configuration. A running agent keeps the toolset it booted with until you press Reload agent on the same tab (or restart it).

A tool you disable on one server stays available on any other server that offers a tool by the same name — the list belongs to the server it is set on.

When a server stops accepting the authorization. An OAuth server can revoke a grant after the agent connected to it, so the MCP tab still reads Connected while every call fails. The agent's tools are the first to learn it: the runtime renews the token and retries the call once, and when that fails the server's row turns Needs authorization, the bell rings on the next health check, and the agent tells you the authorization has expired and offers the fix in the same message: a sign-in link (the same one it uses to connect a server the first time; the tools reload on their own when you finish), or Authorize on the server's row in this tab, plus what else can reach the same service meanwhile. Reconnecting never needs a Disconnect first.

docs.title: Memory and self-learning
docs.text:
Memory is markdown files in the agent's workspace, which means you can read and correct it directly — in the dashboard's Memory tab, the Files tab, or a text editor.

  • MEMORY.md — durable facts the agent has learned and should keep.
  • memories/YYYY-MM-DD.md — a daily log. Today's and yesterday's are loaded into every conversation.
flowchart LR
    subgraph ws["The agent's workspace"]
        M["MEMORY.md<br/>durable facts"]
        D["memories/YYYY-MM-DD.md<br/>daily logs and the Activity block"]
    end
    C["Every conversation"] -. "loaded at the start" .-> M
    C -. "today's and yesterday's" .-> D
    SL["Self-learning<br/>with Cortex on"] -- "distils recent conversations" --> D
    SL -- "keeps what lasts" --> M
    Y["You, in Memory or Files"] -- "edit to correct" --> M

Self-learning (memory.self_learning, on by default) is part of the Cortex engine, so it runs only for an agent Cortex is on for, and Cortex is off until you turn it on (Cortex and Pulse). While it runs it reads recent conversations, distils what is worth keeping, and writes it into the daily log and MEMORY.md. A weekly pass consolidates. self_learning_interval (default 3600 seconds) sets the pace.

The same background pass (so, again, only with Cortex on for the agent) also keeps an Activity record in the daily log — what the agent did, as opposed to what it learned: each scheduled run, heartbeat finding, request from another agent, and Cortex phase, one line each with the time and a short excerpt of the request and the reply. It is written deterministically (no model call, no credits) on every cycle, so it is there even on days when the distillation itself is skipped, and it is bounded — one block per day, capped in length — so a busy day cannot crowd out the rest of the prompt. Ordinary conversations with people are not copied into it; those go through distillation only. Ask the agent what it did yesterday and it reads this block; the dashboard Overview → Daily highlights shows the fleet-wide version of the same day.

Turning on memory.rag also indexes memory for meaning-based search, so the agent can find something it learned months ago without it being in the prompt.

Per-customer memory (memory.per_customer) is the multi-user variant — see Multi-user: two different features.

If an agent has learned something wrong, editing MEMORY.md is the fix, and it takes effect on the next reply.

docs.title: The mobile app
docs.text:
The Olano app puts your agents on your phone: conversations with them, what Cortex is working on, the approvals and alerts waiting for you, and notifications when an agent needs you. It runs on iPhone, iPad and Android phones and tablets, and on Apple silicon Macs as the iPad app, and comes from the App Store and Google Play.

The app is built for the phone: a tab bar along the bottom, a back button and the swipe back gesture on every screen, pull down to refresh, and the look of the platform it runs on (iOS on an iPhone, Material on Android), in light or dark (see Appearance). It talks to your own deployment, with the same agents, conversations and permissions as the dashboard. Nothing about your agents is stored by Olano on the way.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
The first screen asks for your Olano address: the address you open your dashboard at in a browser, such as acme.olano.run. A bare name like acme means acme.olano.run; a full address (https://agents.example.com) works for a deployment on its own domain. The app checks that the address answers as an Olano deployment before it continues, and says so if it does not (no such address, a website that is not Olano, no network).

You then sign in with the email and password you use for the dashboard. The sign-in is kept on the phone for two weeks of inactivity, so you sign in again only when it expires or you sign out. A deployment with no accounts yet asks you to finish setting it up in its dashboard first. A single-user deployment (no accounts at all) opens straight away.

The app remembers the last few addresses you opened, so someone with more than one deployment switches between them with one tap. Settings, Switch deployment goes back to that screen.

docs.title: Trying the app without a deployment
docs.text:
Under the address field, Try the demo opens a demo deployment Olano runs, with sample agents, already signed in: no address, email or password to type. Each visitor gets a demo account of their own, and no other visitor sees your conversations, but the agents themselves are shared with other visitors, so type nothing private there. Your demo account and its conversations are deleted after a day; after that, Enter the demo again on the sign-in screen opens a fresh one. Settings says when you are in the demo, and Switch deployment takes you back to connect your own. Olano may remove the demo entry at any time; it never changes anything about your own deployment.

If the deployment cannot be reached when the app opens, it shows Can't connect with Try again and Use a different deployment. The usual causes are no connection, or the deployment restarting or stopped.

docs.title: The four tabs
docs.text:
Your administrator may have hidden some of what is described here; see What your administrator chooses.

Chats lists the agents you have access to, each with its latest conversation. A green dot means the agent is running. The list is arranged the way the dashboard's sidebar is: Pinned at the top, then your own folders, then All agents, then group chats. Tap a section's name to fold it shut. To arrange it:

  • Pin an agent by swiping its row to the right, or press and hold it and choose Pin. Pinned agents stay at the top in the order you pinned them.
  • Folders: the + button at the top makes a new folder. Move an agent into one by swiping its row to the left (Move), or press and hold it and choose Move to. An agent is in one place at a time: pinned, in one folder, or under All agents. The ... button beside a folder's name renames or deletes it; deleting a folder moves its agents back under All agents.
  • Move Up and Move Down (press and hold an agent) change the order within a section.

The arrangement is yours: it is kept on the deployment for your account, so it follows you to another phone or a reinstall, and it is separate from how the dashboard's sidebar is arranged in your browser. Searching shows matches in every section, folded or not.

Tap an agent to go straight back to the last conversation you had with it, like the dashboard's chat does: one you had in the app, the dashboard or a messenger. Scheduled runs, conversations with other agents, Cortex threads and calls from other systems never open this way. If you have no conversation with the agent yet, a new one opens. The agent's row shows that conversation's title.

Every other thread is one step away: the ... button at the top of a conversation, All Conversations. That list has every thread the agent has, newest first, twenty at a time: scrolling down loads the next twenty, so an agent with months of history opens as fast as a new one. The search bar at the top looks through the messages of the agent's conversations on the deployment, not just their titles, and lists the ones that mention the words with a line showing where; Search older conversations keeps looking further back when the history is long. The pencil button starts a new conversation. Each thread carries the same coloured badge the dashboard shows for where it came from: Mobile for a conversation had in this app, Dashboard for one in the dashboard, the messenger it arrived on (Telegram, WhatsApp, Email...), or how it started (Scheduled, Agent for a conversation between two agents, Cortex, External for a call from another system). Chips above the list show one source at a time (All, Dashboard, Mobile, each messenger, Scheduled, Agents), with how many threads each holds; the app remembers your choice for each agent. Swipe a thread to rename it, or to delete it if you are an administrator of that agent.

In a conversation, the agent's reply streams in as it is written. What the agent did on the way (searched the web, read a file, asked another agent) shows as one line per step while it works and folds into "N steps" when it is done; tap that line to see the steps. A plan the agent made shows as a checklist. While the agent works and the message box is empty, the send button becomes a stop button; see While the agent works for adding to what it is doing. If the agent needs your approval before an action, a card with Approve and Decline appears in the conversation.

The message box is one card at the bottom of the screen: what you type on top, and under it +, the conversation's model, the microphone and the send button. On a phone the keyboard's return key starts a new line, and only the send button sends, so a message never goes out half written. With a hardware keyboard (an iPad's, or a keyboard paired with the phone) Enter sends and Shift+Enter starts a new line. + sends photos and files, and images the agent produces show in the conversation (see Photos and Files). The microphone beside the send button dictates (tap it: your words appear in the box as you speak, see Dictation) or records a voice note (hold it, see Voice notes). On a phone that cannot dictate, the microphone shows while the message box is empty and only records voice notes.

Other files the agent hands you (a report it saved, a data file, a PDF) appear as cards under its reply; tap one to open it in the app. Markdown documents open formatted, data and code files (JSON, CSV, logs, scripts) open as text, and a PDF opens as a document on an iPhone. Files the app cannot show itself, such as Word or Excel documents, and PDFs on Android, open with Open in another app, which offers the phone's own choices (save to Files, mail it, open it in Word). The share button in the corner does the same for any file.

When an agent asks you for an API key or a model provider's key, the form is drawn under its reply: paste the value and press Save to vault. It goes to the vault without becoming a message, and the agent is told the name once it is saved. When an agent needs you to sign in to a service, connect a messenger or edit a file, it sends a magic link: after you approve it, a card appears under its reply with Open and, usually, a six-digit PIN. Open copies the PIN and opens a secure page of your deployment in a browser over the app; paste the PIN there and follow the page. That page needs no sign-in of its own (the link and its PIN are the key), and the link expires after a while (fifteen minutes unless your deployment says otherwise). When you finish, the conversation shows Connected (or Didn't complete), and offers to restart the agent when the change needs one and you are an administrator. See Magic links.

A new conversation offers a few ways to start, such as "What can you help me with?"; tap one to send it. Messages are grouped under the day they were sent (Today, Yesterday, then the date). A long conversation opens on its newest messages and fetches earlier ones as you scroll up, a little ahead of where you are, so they are usually in place by the time you get there; Start of conversation marks the first message. If they could not be fetched (no signal), a line at the top says so and a tap tries again. If you have scrolled up to read earlier messages, a round button with a down arrow takes you back to the latest one, with a dot on it when something new arrived.

Next to + in the message box is the model the conversation runs on, with its reasoning level in grey when the model has one (for example "Olano Pro High"); the name turns orange when this conversation uses a model of its own choosing. Tap it to pick another model, or how hard the model thinks (Low, Medium, High and so on, as that model offers them; Default leaves it to the model). The choice applies to that conversation only, the same as the model picker in the dashboard's chat: every message you send in it uses that model, reopening the conversation continues on it, and a new conversation starts on the agent's own model again. The list offers the models your deployment can run: its default models, the Olano models, and those of any provider an administrator has added a key for. Agent default goes back to the agent's own model. If a conversation last used a model the deployment no longer offers, it continues on the agent's model and the app says so.

Web addresses in a conversation are links, in the agent's replies and in your own messages, including an address in code formatting and one written as www.example.com. Tap one to open it in a browser over the app; press and hold one to Copy Link or Share Link. Anything in a reply that looks like web page markup is shown as text.

Under each finished reply are buttons to copy it, hear it (see Hearing replies) and share it to another app. Under your latest message are copy and edit: edit puts your words back in the message box to correct, and sending them sends a new message (the conversation's history is not rewritten, so the agent sees both). When a reply fails, Try again under it sends your message again. Pressing and holding any message offers the same choices, plus copying a voice note's transcript.

To flag a reply that is offensive, harmful or wrong, press and hold it and choose Report, then a reason. The report is recorded on the deployment as negative feedback on that reply, with the reason kept beside it, and counted for the administrators in the dashboard's Insights; nothing leaves the deployment.

A conversation keeps going on your deployment if you leave it, lock the phone or switch apps: come back and the app picks up where the reply has got to.

Cortex is what the agents have been working on by themselves. At the top, the Pulse card says how many findings the agents posted for you, the same news, research and ideas as the dashboard's Cortex Pulse; tap it for the cards. On each, Do it carries out the suggested next step, Later brings the card back in a day, Dismiss drops it. A card about work the agent already did on its own offers Keep and Undo instead: Keep accepts it, Undo restores the backup the agent took first. Later and Dismiss take the card away the moment you tap; Do it, Keep and Undo spin on the button while the agent answers, then the card goes and a short notice, above the tab bar, says what happened (when the step is a longer piece of work, the agent runs it in the background and posts the result here when it is done).

Under it, the four stages in the order things move through them: Brainstorms, Ideas, Prototypes and Projects, each with how many items it holds. The list shows every stage; tap a stage to show only that one, and tap it again (or Show all) to see everything. Chips narrow the list to one agent when more than one has items. An item this phone has not opened yet is lightly tinted; opening it clears the tint.

Triage happens on the list. Swipe a row to the right to approve it (move it to the next stage) and to the left to discard it: the word shows as the row slides, a full swipe does it, and a shorter swipe leaves the button there to tap. An approved item moves to the next stage straight away, marked as on its way while the agent writes it up; a discarded one leaves the list. To discard several at once, tap Select, tap the rows (or Select all), then Discard in the bar at the bottom and confirm.

Open an item for its write-up and Cortex's rating, then Make it a (the next stage) to move it forward, Talk it over to discuss it with the agent, or Discard. Moving an item forward is a piece of writing the agent does, and it takes a minute or two: the button turns into Making it an idea… as soon as you tap, then a banner under the title follows the run (with the step the agent is on, when it reports one) and you can leave the page, since the list already shows the item under its new stage. When it is done the banner reads Now an idea with a button that opens the new item's page; if the run failed, the banner says why and the button offers the tap again. The first time, Talk it over opens a conversation with the item already described in the message box (what it is, its title and where its files are), so you only add your thoughts or questions after it; nothing is sent until you send it. Later it reopens that conversation where you left it. See Cortex and Pulse.

Inbox has three parts:

  • Approvals: actions agents are waiting to take until someone approves them, from a scheduled run, Cortex or a request from another agent, and Pulse cards that need an approval. Answer each with Approve or Decline.
  • Alerts: the deployment's notifications, the same list as the bell in the dashboard. The line under an alert says what tapping it does; swipe one to dismiss it. See Alerts.
  • Issues: the issue tracker, every issue you can see, not only those an alert pointed at. Open (the default), Assigned to me or All, closed ones included; tap one to read it, comment, hand it to an agent or close it (see Alerts for what an issue screen offers).

The agents' Pulse findings are in the Cortex tab.

The tab's badge counts approvals waiting plus unread alerts.

Settings shows who you are signed in as and where, the agents' scheduled tasks, the app's appearance, voice, the phone's notifications, Switch deployment and Sign out. What the app does not do (agent configuration, tools, files, connections and the rest) stays in the dashboard, in a browser.

The app grants and removes no permission: a member sees the agents they have access to, an administrator sees all of them, exactly as in a browser.

docs.title: While the agent works
docs.text:
You do not have to wait for a reply to finish before saying more. While the agent is working, type in the message box and a bar above it says the agent is working:

  • Send (the arrow) hands your message to the agent while it works. It reads it at its next step, after the action it is in the middle of, and carries on with it in mind; nothing is stopped or started over. Your message appears in the conversation where the agent read it, marked Added while it worked.
  • Send after keeps the message until the reply is done, then sends it as your next message.
  • Stop stops the agent.

Messages waiting to be read show above the message box. Edit takes one back into the message box to change it, the cross cancels it; either works until the agent has read it. A message sent with the arrow just as the reply finishes goes out as your next message instead, so nothing is lost.

docs.title: The conversation menu
docs.text:
The ... button at the top of a conversation opens a sheet that names the agent and its model at the top, then groups what you can do. Rows with an arrow open another screen; the others act right away or ask one more question.

Conversation

  • New Conversation starts a new one with the same agent.
  • Mode is how the agent goes about your requests in this conversation; the current one shows on the right. Auto (the default) does the work, running tools without asking. Plan first has the agent write a plan and wait: under the plan are Approve & run, which tells it to carry the plan out, and the message box, to ask for changes instead. Ask before each step asks for your approval before every tool the agent runs. A bar above the message box shows the setting when it is not Auto. The app remembers the choice for each agent on this phone; approving a plan goes back to Auto.
  • Rename gives the conversation a name of your own.
  • Compact replaces the conversation's older messages with a summary the agent keeps, so a long conversation takes less of the agent's memory. It is the same as /compact in the dashboard's chat.

Agent

  • All Conversations lists this agent's conversations.
  • Files opens the agent's files.
  • Scheduled Tasks lists this agent's scheduled tasks.
  • Agent Info opens the agent's page. Tapping the agent's picture at the top of the conversation opens it too.

More

  • Hands-Free Mode lets you talk with the agent without touching the phone (see Hands-free).
  • Add an Agent turns the conversation into a group chat with a second agent you pick. The conversation so far is copied into the group, so the new agent can read it, and the agent you were talking to keeps answering messages that name nobody. It appears when the deployment has group chats turned on.

docs.title: When an agent is stopped
docs.text: An agent an administrator stopped (or that could not start, or that the deployment's plan holds back) is marked Stopped, Could not start or Held back in Chats. Its conversations still open and show everything said so far, but where the message box would be, the app says why it will not reply. An administrator sees a Start button there; anyone else is told to ask an administrator.

docs.title: An agent's page
docs.text:
The agent's page says whether it is running and, when it is not answering, why: Could not start with the error it stopped on (a missing key, a model that cannot be reached), Held back with what holds it (a plan limit, for example), or Stopped when someone stopped it. Administrators also get:

  • Start: starts a stopped agent, or tries again after an error.
  • Restart: stops the agent and starts it again, for example after changing one of its keys.
  • Stop: the agent stops answering messages, channels and scheduled tasks until someone starts it again, and it stays stopped if the deployment restarts.

Members see the status and the reason, without the buttons. The page also leads to the agent's conversations, files and scheduled tasks.

docs.title: Files and sharing into Olano
docs.text:
The + button next to the message box has Choose Files for documents: PDFs, Word, Excel and PowerPoint files, text and data files, up to 10 MB each. They wait above the message box with their size until you send; the cross removes one. You can send files with or without a message.

The agent gets them the way the dashboard's chat sends them. A text or data file (a .txt, .csv, .md, .json and so on) is read into your message, so the agent sees its contents directly. Any other document is saved in the agent's workspace, and the agent reads it with its document tools. In the conversation your message shows the files by name, never their contents.

Sharing into Olano. From another app (a link from Safari, a photo, a PDF from Mail or Files, some text), choose Olano in the share menu: the app opens, asks which agent it is for, and puts it in a new conversation with that agent, ready to send with a message of your own. Nothing is sent until you send it. A link or text arrives in the message box, a photo or a file above it. If the app does not open by itself after sharing, open it: what you shared is waiting.

docs.title: An agent's files
docs.text:
Settings, Files lists your agents; pick one to see its files, the same folders as the dashboard's Files page. The conversation menu's Files opens the agent's files directly. Tap a folder to open it (the back button goes up one folder) and a file to read it: photos open full screen, Markdown is laid out, text and code are shown as they are, a PDF is drawn, and anything else can be handed to another app with the share button.

The search box at the top finds files and folders by name across all of the agent's files, wherever you are. Folders the dashboard hides from its file list (version control, installed packages, caches) are left out here too.

Administrators can upload a file from the phone with the button at the top: it goes into the folder that is open. A file with the same name there can be replaced, or kept beside the new one under a new name. Members can open and search files but not upload.

docs.title: Scheduled tasks
docs.text:
A scheduled task is a message an agent gets on a timetable, such as "every weekday at 8, send me what is on my calendar". Each run is a conversation of its own, which you find in the agent's conversations with the Scheduled badge. Agents can set these up themselves when you ask them to; the app lets you see and manage them too.

Settings, Scheduled Tasks lists every agent's tasks, grouped by agent; Scheduled Tasks in a conversation's menu lists that agent's. Each row says when the task runs and when it runs next, or that it is paused. The switch on a row pauses or resumes it; swipe a row for Run now.

Tap a task for its details: when it runs, the agent it runs as, the time zone its times are in, its instructions and its recent runs (tap a run to read what it produced, or why it failed). Run Now runs it straight away, whatever its schedule. The pencil button changes it, and Delete Task at the bottom removes it; its past runs stay in the agent's conversations.

The + button adds a task: pick the agent, write what it should do (those words are the message the agent gets each time), optionally a name, and when it repeats: every day, week (on the days you pick) or month at a time, every few hours or minutes, or once on a date. The sentence under the choices reads the schedule back. A new task uses your phone's time zone; changing a task keeps the time zone it has. A task with a custom schedule made in the dashboard stays as it is unless you change it. Running more often than every five minutes shows a warning: each run is a full turn of the agent, which takes time and uses credits, and when a run is still going as the next one is due, that next run is skipped.

You can manage the tasks of the agents you have access to, as in the dashboard's Scheduler.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
The Alerts part of the Inbox lists the deployment's notifications. Most of them come with a fix, and the line under each one says what tapping it does:

  • Open issue: an issue assigned to you opens in the app. Read it and its comments, add a comment, or use the ... button to Hand to an Agent (it picks the issue up the next time it checks its issues, and comments as it works), Talk It Over with an Agent (a new conversation about it), or Close Issue and Reopen Issue.
  • Ask the agent to fix it: for problems an agent can fix with your help, such as a service that needs reconnecting or an MCP server that needs signing in again. Tapping opens a new conversation with that agent with a message about the alert ready to send; the agent usually answers with a magic link.
  • Repair the folders: when skills have folder names that do not match their names, an administrator can repair them from the phone. A folder is renamed to match a valid name; a name that is not valid (a title with spaces or capitals) is set to its folder's name. The app reports what it repaired and anything it left alone, and the alert clears once nothing is left.
  • Open Cortex, for a background run that failed.
  • Fixed on the dashboard: some problems, such as a locked vault, low disk space or a usage budget, are fixed in the dashboard. The alert says where.

Tapping an alert marks it read. Its menu always has Dismiss Alert.

docs.title: The agent's browser
docs.text:
When your deployment runs the browser in live mode (see Browser), an agent that opens its browser shows it in the conversation as a small floating window: the page it is on, live, and a line saying who has it (The agent is browsing, You have control, The agent needs you when it asked for help, or Waiting for your OK in the chat when a click needs your approval). Drag the window to any corner. Its x hides it until the agent opens a new browser or asks for you again; the globe button at the top of the conversation opens the browser at any time, with a dot on it when the agent asked for you.

Tap the window for the full view. While you watch, a dot shows where the agent is about to click or type, and two fingers (or a double tap) zoom in on the picture. Take control pauses the agent's browsing and lets you use the page yourself, for a sign-in, a security check or anything only a person should do:

  • tap to click (two or three quick taps for a double or triple click);
  • swipe to scroll;
  • rest your finger, then move it to press and drag;
  • the keyboard button opens a box to type into the page, with Backspace, Tab and Enter keys;
  • back, forward and reload, and tap the address to go somewhere else. When the page has several tabs, the tabs button switches between them.

The picture is sent at the size the phone shows it and only as fast as the phone draws it, so taps get through on any page, however much it redraws (a sign-in's verification step, a feed): on a slow connection it turns a little rougher for a moment and sharpens again as soon as the phone keeps up. If a page is too busy to take a tap for a few seconds, the view says so; tap again, or press reload.

Two buttons at the top of the full view keep what the screen shows, whether the agent is working or you are: Record makes a video of the browser (REC and a clock show while it runs, and Stop saves it in the agent's recordings/ folder, which the toast opens in Files), and the camera button saves a picture of the page under screenshots/. A recording ends on its own after 30 minutes or when the browser closes. The agent can record itself too: ask it to record a demo of what it does.

The page's own questions (a confirmation, a file to upload, a drop-down list, a date, time or colour to pick) come to you while you have control, as the phone's own pickers; and when a page asks the browser for something it does not have (your location, a camera, a microphone, leave to notify) you are told what it asked for and that it was declined, so a site that then behaves oddly is not a mystery. Hand back returns the browser to the agent; if it had asked for you, it is told you are done. Done closes the full view and leaves the browser as it is. With the browser in headless mode there is nothing to watch: the agent's screenshots arrive in its replies when it names them.

docs.title: Group chats
docs.text:
A group chat is one conversation with two to six agents, the same group chats as in the dashboard. They are listed under Group chats at the bottom of the Chats tab, with the last message in each. Start one with +, New Group Chat (or Start a group chat with several agents when you have none): pick the agents and, optionally, a name. The first agent you pick answers messages that do not name anyone.

To ask a particular agent, write @ and its name; typing @ suggests the members. Name several (@nova and @aria, what do you think?) and each answers in turn, in the order you named them, seeing the replies before its own. The line above the message box says who will answer. Each reply shows the agent's picture and name above it, and your own messages say who they went to.

Agents in a group can also hand the conversation to each other after replying. While they do, a line above the message box says so, with Stop to end it once the current reply is finished.

A one-to-one conversation becomes a group chat with Add an Agent in its ... menu: the conversation so far comes along, so nobody has to repeat it.

The i button at the top of a group chat opens its details: rename it, add an agent, remove one (swipe it to the left; a group keeps at least two), or delete the group chat. Group chats appear when the deployment has them turned on; an administrator turns them on or off, and decides whether agents may answer each other, at Config, Group chats in the dashboard (see groups:).

docs.title: Photos
docs.text:
The + button next to the message box adds photos: Take Photo opens the camera, Choose Photos opens your photo library, where you can pick up to ten at once. The photos wait above the message box until you send them: tap one to see it larger, or its x to leave it out. Add a few words about what you want done with them, or send them on their own.

Each photo is sent at a size suited to reading it (at most 2048 pixels on its longest side) and without its location or other details the camera recorded. For an administrator, each photo is saved in the agent's uploads/ folder (where it also shows in the dashboard's Files view) with a note telling the agent where, and the agent decides from your message what to do with it: look at it with its vision tool, pass it on, or keep it. A member's photos are shown to the agent with that message only and not saved, so they do not come back when the conversation is reopened.

In a conversation, one photo shows at its own shape and several as a grid. Tap a photo, yours or one the agent produced, to see it full screen: swipe sideways for the others in that message, pinch or double-tap to zoom, and swipe down (or tap the close button) to go back.

The first time you take or choose a photo, your phone may ask whether Olano may use the camera or your photos. If you declined, allow it again in the phone's Settings, under Olano.

docs.title: Dictation
docs.text:
Tap the microphone and talk: your words appear in the message box as you say them, and what you send is the text, never a recording. Your phone works the words out itself, so nothing you say leaves the phone until you send the message, and the agent gets text it can start on at once.

While you dictate, the message box shows what has been heard so far, with four controls under it:

  • x throws away what you dictated this time. Anything you had typed before stays in the box.
  • The waveform moves while the phone hears you (bars) and goes flat (dots) when you pause.
  • Stop (the square) stops listening and leaves the words in the box, so you can correct them, type more, or tap the microphone again to keep talking. Dictated words are added after whatever is already in the box.
  • Send (the arrow) stops listening and sends the message, the words still being worked out included. While the agent is working, it adds them to what the agent is doing, like a typed message.

Dictation keeps listening through pauses until you stop it, for up to five minutes. Switching away from the app, or a phone call, stops it and leaves what was heard in the box.

Dictation is offered where the phone can do it without sending your voice anywhere: an iPhone that recognizes your language on the phone itself, and an Android phone (Android 12 or later) with on-device speech recognition. It listens for the language your phone is set to; Android may need that language's speech recognition downloaded first (in the phone's settings for speech recognition, or by using voice typing once). On other phones a tap on the microphone records a voice note, as below. The first time you dictate, the phone asks whether Olano may use the microphone and, on an iPhone, speech recognition. To have a tap record a voice note instead, turn off Dictate with the microphone in the app's Settings.

docs.title: Voice notes
docs.text:
There are two ways to record a voice note:

  • Hold the microphone and talk, then let go to send. Slide your finger left to throw the recording away, or up to lock it, so it keeps recording without your finger on it.
  • Tap the microphone to record hands-free, on a phone that cannot dictate or with dictation turned off in Settings. A bin button throws the recording away and the send button sends it.

Where a tap dictates, a press becomes a voice note once it lasts longer than a tap, and the microphone is there whether or not you have typed anything.

The dot beside the timer is grey while the phone opens the microphone and turns red, with a small tick under your finger, the moment it is listening: what you say from then on is in the note. After a note the microphone stays ready for about twenty seconds, so the next one starts at once (the phone's microphone indicator stays on for that long); it closes when you leave the app. A recording shorter than about 0.7 seconds is not sent, and a recording sends itself when it reaches five minutes. Leaving the conversation, or switching away from the app, throws away a recording you have not sent.

By default the recording is sent to the deployment, which turns it into text (below). With Transcribe on this phone turned on in the app's Settings, an iPhone turns what you said into text itself, and the text is what is sent: the agent starts on your words at once, the recording stays on the phone, and nothing depends on the deployment's speech-to-text. Your administrator chooses the default, and may hide the switch. While the iPhone works it out, Transcribing… shows under the voice note, then your words (tap them to read all of them). The iPhone does this on the phone when it supports your language, and with Apple's speech recognition otherwise. It listens for the iPhone's own language (Settings, General, Language & Region): if you speak another language to your agents, turn off Transcribe on this phone in the app's Settings, and the deployment transcribes your voice notes instead. The first time, the iPhone asks whether Olano may use speech recognition.

Otherwise (on Android, with Transcribe on this phone turned off, when you declined speech recognition, or when the iPhone heard no words), the recording is sent to the deployment, which turns it into text with its speech-to-text service. The text appears under your voice note once the deployment has heard it. If speech-to-text is switched off or fails on your deployment, the voice note says it was not transcribed, and the agent is told it could not hear it. An administrator turns speech-to-text on in the dashboard, under Config, Speech.

A recording sent to the deployment by an administrator is saved in the agent's uploads/ folder, like a photo, and plays again when the conversation is reopened. A member's recording is used for its text only and not saved. When the recording was not sent (the iPhone transcribed it, or a member sent it), a reopened conversation shows what you said, marked as a voice note, without the recording.

Tap a voice note's play button to hear it, or tap or drag along its waveform to jump to a point. While it plays, the speed button switches between 1x, 1.5x and 2x. Starting another voice note pauses the first. Audio files an agent sends you play the same way.

The first time you record, your phone asks whether Olano may use the microphone. If you declined, allow it again in the phone's Settings, under Olano.

docs.title: What your administrator chooses
docs.text: An administrator can shape the app for everyone on the deployment, in the dashboard under Config, Mobile app: hide the Cortex tab, the whole Inbox or any of its sections (Approvals, Alerts, Issues), and the Files, Credits and Usage and Transcribe on this phone rows in Settings, and choose where voice notes are transcribed for people who have not picked. The app checks for changes every time you open it or come back to it, so a change shows up without updating the app. If you are on a screen that has just been hidden, the app takes you to Chats (or back to Settings). Hiding only removes it from the app; nothing is deleted.

docs.title: Hearing replies
docs.text:
The speaker button under a finished reply reads it aloud; tap it again to stop. Replies to your voice notes are read aloud as they arrive, so a conversation can go back and forth by voice. Read replies aloud in the app's Settings chooses when that happens:

  • After my voice notes (the default): a reply to a voice note is read aloud.
  • Always: every reply is read aloud as it arrives.
  • Never: replies are read only when you tap the speaker.

The voice depends on the deployment. When an administrator has turned on text to speech (Config, Speech in the dashboard), replies are read in the voice chosen there, and each reading is billed like the deployment's other speech use. Otherwise the phone reads them in its own voice, at no cost; an iPhone picks the best voice it has for the language the reply is written in (better voices can be downloaded in the iPhone's Settings, Accessibility, Spoken Content, Voices).

A reply is read the way a person would read it to you: code blocks are left out, a link is read as its text and a web address as the name of its site. Playing a voice note or starting a recording stops the reading, and so does leaving the app. These choices are kept on that phone only.

docs.title: Hands-free
docs.text:
Hands-Free Mode in a conversation's ... menu is for when your hands and eyes are busy, such as driving or cooking. The phone listens; when you stop talking it sends what you said, reads the reply aloud when it arrives, and listens again. On a phone that can dictate, your words appear under the button as you say them and go as a text message, worked out on the phone itself, so nothing waits on the deployment's speech-to-text; a pause of about two seconds after your last word sends them. On other phones, or with Dictate with the microphone turned off in the app's Settings, what you say goes as a voice note. If dictation cannot start (the phone's speech recognition is turned off for Olano, say), the app says so and sends voice notes for the rest of that hands-free conversation. The message box gives way to one large button:

  • While it listens, tapping it sends straight away instead of waiting for the pause.
  • While a reply is being read, tapping it stops the reading and listens.
  • After about fifteen seconds of silence it pauses; tap it to talk again.

End Hands-Free brings the message box back, and so does leaving the app. Every reply is read aloud while hands-free is on, whatever Read replies aloud is set to, in the voice described in Hearing replies, so a hands-free conversation costs nothing beyond the messages themselves.

docs.title: Siri, the Action button and Shortcuts
docs.text:
On an iPhone, two things can be asked of the app from outside it. Both name one of your agents, and Siri learns the agents' names from the app, so say them as they appear in Chats.

Ask an agent sends what you say and reads the reply back, without the app opening. It takes two breaths: name the agent, then answer Siri's question.

  • "Hey Siri, ask Jane in Olano". Siri asks "What do you want to ask?", and you say the question.
  • "Hey Siri, ask an agent in Olano" (or "Hey Siri, ask Olano"). Siri shows your agents and asks which, then asks for the question.

Keep the first sentence to the agent's name and the app's: words after it in the same breath ("...what is on my calendar") make Siri treat it as a text message to send, and it offers Messages instead. "Olano, ask Jane" and "ask Jane on Olano" work too. The two actions appear in the Shortcuts app under Olano once the app has been opened; if Siri still does not know an agent's name, open the app once so it learns the current names, or say "ask an agent in Olano" and choose.

Siri speaks the reply in its own voice. A reply that is mostly code or links is read the way the app reads one: code is left out and a link is read as its site. A few words from Siri follow soon after you speak; when the agent takes longer, Siri says the agent is still working and the reply comes to the app instead, and to the phone as a notification when those are on.
