A question asked within half an hour of the last one continues the same conversation, so "and tomorrow?" means what you think; after that a fresh one starts. These conversations appear in Chats like any other.

Talk to an agent opens the app straight into Hands-free with that agent, in a new conversation: it listens, sends what you say, reads the reply in the agent's voice when the deployment has one, and listens again.

  • "Hey Siri, talk to Hannah in Olano"
  • Settings, Action Button, Shortcut on an iPhone with an Action button: pick Talk to an Agent (or Ask an Agent) and the agent it should use, and a press opens the conversation listening.
  • The same two actions are in Control Center, on the Lock Screen, and in the Shortcuts app, where Ask an Agent can be a step of your own shortcut or automation: its reply is passed on as text (a morning briefing that is read to you at seven, say).

The actions need iOS 16.4 or later, the app signed in to a deployment, and work with whichever agents you can chat with. On Android, a long press on the app's icon offers Talk to ... for the first few agents, which opens the app the same way; those can be dragged to the home screen.

Settings, Siri and widgets, Default agent is the agent these reach when none is named: "Hey Siri, talk to Olano" suggests it first, the Action button and a Control Center control with no agent chosen open it, a widget shows it until you pick another, and on Android it is the first shortcut. Left at First in the list, it is whichever agent Chats lists first. The choice is kept on that phone.

docs.title: Widgets (iPhone)
docs.text:
Touch and hold the Home Screen, tap Edit, then Add Widget and choose Olano. The widgets read the deployment on their own, with the session the app signed in with, so they keep up while the app is closed; they refresh every few minutes, and at once when you do something in the app or on a widget. They need iOS 18 and the app opened once after signing in. A widget added while the app was closed fills in the next time the app is opened.

Every widget that shows one agent shows the default agent (Settings, Siri and widgets) until you pick another for it: touch and hold the widget and choose Edit Widget.

  • Ask (small, medium, Lock Screen): the simplest one, a way in. The small one is a single "Ask Anna" pill that opens a new conversation with the keyboard up. The medium one adds the composer's buttons: Message, Photo (the camera opens), Photos (the picker opens) and Talk (the conversation opens hands-free), so a question, a picture or a conversation is one tap from the Home Screen.
  • Agent (small, medium, and every Lock Screen shape): one agent's picture, its status, the last reply in your conversation with it, and how many approvals it is waiting on. Tap it to open that conversation, the same one a tap on the agent in Chats opens (a new one when you have none yet; scheduled runs and the agent's other threads stay in its conversation list). The medium one has Talk, which opens a new conversation hands-free, and for administrators Start or Stop.
  • Quick asks (medium, large): an agent and up to three questions you set when adding the widget, such as "Give me a short briefing of what matters right now". A tap sends one; the reply appears in the widget when it arrives (the large size keeps it in view). A widget cannot take typing, so the questions are fixed; tap the agent to open the conversation for anything else.
  • Approvals (small, medium, Lock Screen): what is waiting on you. The medium one shows the oldest approval with Approve and Decline and a countdown to when it expires; a high-risk action has no buttons, so you see in the app exactly what would run. Tap to open the Inbox.
  • Team (medium, large): every agent with its status and the last word in your conversation with it, each opening that conversation.
  • Pulse (small, medium, Lock Screen): the newest Pulse card from Cortex.
  • Next run (small, medium, Lock Screen): the next scheduled task, counting down, with the ones after it.

In Control Center (and the Lock Screen's two bottom buttons, and the Action button on an iPhone that has one), two controls can be added: Talk to an Agent, which opens the app listening to the chosen agent, and Message an Agent, which opens a new conversation with it. A control with no agent chosen reaches the default agent.

What a widget shows is the last thing the deployment answered, so a reply written seconds ago may take a moment to appear; the app itself always shows the latest. Signing out in the app clears the widgets.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text:
Settings, Appearance chooses how the app looks:

  • System (the default): light or dark following the phone's own setting, changing with it.
  • Light: always light, whatever the phone is set to.
  • Dark: always dark, whatever the phone is set to.
  • Volt: always a black page with an electric chartreuse accent, whatever the phone is set to. It is the dashboard's Volt theme, so a browser set to it and the phone look alike; the status bar and keyboard follow it as they do Dark.

The choice is kept on that phone only, for every deployment it opens.

docs.title: Locking the app
docs.text:
The app keeps you signed in for two weeks, and your agents can act on your accounts. Settings, Privacy, Lock with Face ID (Touch ID, or a fingerprint or face unlock on Android, depending on the phone) makes the app ask for it before anything shows: when the app opens, and when you come back to it. The phone's own passcode always works too. Turning it on asks once, to make sure the phone can unlock it.

Ask again chooses how long the app can be in the background before it asks again: Immediately (the default), or after 1, 5 or 15 minutes. While the app is in the background its screen is covered, so the phone's app switcher shows nothing either. The setting needs a passcode on the phone, and is kept on that phone only.

docs.title: Credits and usage
docs.text: On a deployment that runs on Olano credits, Settings, Credits and Usage shows the credits left, how much of this month's included credits are used and when they renew, any top-ups left, and what each Olano service (chat, images, speech and so on) used over the last 30 days. It is for reading only: buying credits is done from the dashboard. Deployments that use their own provider keys have no credits, and the row does not appear.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
Notifications reach you while the app is closed or in the background. While it is open on screen you see things happen live instead, so it does not also notify you.

Turn them on in Settings, Push notifications; your phone asks for permission once. There are four kinds, and each phone chooses its own:

Kind When it notifies Who receives it Replies An agent finished answering a message you sent, and you were not looking at that conversation (the app was in the background and no browser had it open). Not sent for a reply you stopped. You, the person who sent the message. Approvals An agent is waiting for you to approve or reject an action: in a conversation you started, or in the Approvals inbox for an agent you can act on (a scheduled run, Cortex, a request from another agent). The person who started the conversation; for the inbox, every administrator and every member with access to that agent. Cortex Cortex wants approval for a change to an agent, or found something urgent. Ordinary findings wait in the Cortex tab. Administrators and members with access to that agent. Alerts A warning or error appeared on the bell, such as a channel that cannot start. Each problem notifies at most once every six hours. Administrators only.

Tapping a notification opens what it is about: the conversation for a reply or an approval in a conversation, Pulse in the Cortex tab for a Cortex finding, and the Inbox for an inbox approval, a Cortex card that needs an approval, or an alert.

Answering from the notification. An approval notification has Approve and Decline buttons, and a reply notification has a Reply field: press and hold the notification (or pull it down) on an iPhone, or expand it on Android. The phone asks to be unlocked first, then the app answers without opening: the approval is decided, or your reply goes into that conversation as your next message, and the agent's answer arrives as another notification. An action marked high risk has no buttons, so that it is always looked at in the app first, and a reply that ran into a problem has no Reply field. If answering does not work (the deployment cannot be reached, or you need to sign in again), a notification says so; tap it to open the app. A reply sent while the agent is still working on your last message is not sent; the notification says so.

An approval nobody answers is rejected when the agent's approval timeout runs out, five minutes unless the agent sets security.hitl_timeout_seconds (see Human in the loop and approvals). Keep Approvals on if you rely on answering them from your phone.

docs.title: What a notification contains
docs.text:
By default a notification names the agent and the reason ("maria needs your approval", "Replied to your message.") and never contains what anyone wrote, or the details of the action awaiting approval beyond its name. An administrator can set push.previews: true in config.yaml to include the start of replies and Cortex finding titles; that text then passes through Apple's or Google's notification service on its way to the phone.

Signing out in the app, or switching deployment, stops that deployment's notifications on that phone. Deleting a person's account stops them on every phone they had.

docs.title: Who can have notifications
docs.text: Notifications are delivered through the Olano Cloud, so they work on deployments that run on Olano Cloud and are recent enough to send them. Any other deployment can still be used in the app for chat, Cortex and the inbox; Settings says why its notifications are unavailable. An administrator controls them for the whole deployment with the push: block in config.yaml: switching them off, the previews above, the lowest Cortex priority that notifies, and the lowest alert level that notifies.

docs.title: Multi-user: two different features
docs.text:
These have confusingly similar names. They are unrelated, and you may want either, both, or neither.

Team accounts — the humans who operate the deployment. Turned on with multi_user_enabled: true in config.yaml (labelled "Team accounts" in the dashboard), or automatically by creating the first admin. It gives you a login screen, invite-only accounts, admin and member roles, and per-agent access grants. Without it, Olano runs single-user: everyone who can reach the dashboard is the owner. Managed deployments have it on by default.

How access works: one or more admins configure everything and manage users. Each agent has an owner plus a flat list of members who may chat with it. Admins can reach every agent without holding an explicit grant — so the per-agent access list under-reports who can administer an agent, and the Admin page's access overview (account menu → Admin) is the complete picture. Bulk actions apply a role across many users and agents at once.

Access to an agent is access to all of its conversations: a member granted an agent sees the same conversation list an admin does — its scheduled runs, heartbeats, messaging-platform chats and everyone's dashboard chats — and can continue any of them. Only deleting a conversation is reserved for admins and the agent's owner.

Manage it in the dashboard's Admin page (account menu → Admin), or by asking AgentFather in chat — it can invite people (returning a single-use set-password link + QR image, never a password), reset passwords the same way, change admin/member roles, disable or delete accounts, and grant or revoke per-agent access, each behind a human approval card and admin-only.

Group chats follow the same grants and add one thing on top: the person who created a group (or an admin) can share it with other team accounts from the group's details panel, so several people and several agents sit in one conversation. Only people who already have access to every agent in the group can be shared in, a shared person can read, post and leave but not change the group, and in a room with more than one person a message that names no agent is for the other people and wakes none. The details are in the groups: section.

Multi-user mode / per-user isolation — the end users who chat with one shared agent. Turned on per agent with customer_service.enabled: true (equivalently memory.per_customer: true — the two mirror each other). This is for a support bot, a community assistant, a paid service: many people talk to the same agent, and each gets isolated memory, so the agent never mixes one person's context into another's conversation.

It swaps the shared memory tools for per-user ones (remember, recall, forget_me) and unlocks optional capabilities:

  • user_scheduling — end users can set their own reminders, capped by max_jobs_per_user and min_job_interval_minutes.
  • connections — end users can be introduced to each other, with consent, with their own caps and invite expiry.
  • user_credentials — end users store their own credentials for the agent to act on their behalf, restricted to the names in customer_credential_names.

These three, and per-customer schedule fan-out, require multi-user mode; a config that uses one without it fails to load rather than quietly ignoring it.

Configure it on the agent's Multi-user tab, which also lists end users and blocks or unblocks them.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
A markdown wiki in the agent's workspace, at the Notes tab. Notes link to each other, and every note shows its backlinks. Both you and the agent can read and write them (notes_add, notes_get, notes_search, notes_list, notes_backlinks).

Use notes for structured knowledge that is neither a passing memory nor a document you uploaded: project pages, contact sheets, decision records, runbooks the agent maintains itself.

docs.title: Pages: publishing sites and web apps
docs.text:
An agent can put its work on the web at /pages/<slug>/ on your deployment: a report, a dashboard, a single-page app built with npm, or a small web app with its own server and live data. Every page sits behind a password that only you set, per agent, on the agent's Pages tab. Until you set it, the agent's pages answer 503 and show nothing. Agents can neither see nor change that password.

There are three kinds of page, and the agent picks the tool that fits.

Kind Tool What runs Good for Files pages_start Nothing. The folder is served as it is. A report, an HTML export, a static site the agent wrote by hand. Static build pages_deploy with build and output A build command, once per deploy. React, Vue, Svelte, Astro or Vite apps: npm ci && npm run build, served from dist. Server pages_deploy with start A long-running HTTP server. Express, Fastify, Flask or FastAPI apps with an API, forms, or live data from a database.

A page can also have both a build and a server: the build runs first, then the server starts.

docs.title: Asking for a page
docs.text:
Tell the agent what you want, in plain words: "publish the weekly report as a page", "deploy the CRM dashboard so I can open it from my phone". The agent chooses the kind, runs it, and tells you the URL. Then:

  1. Open the agent's Pages tab and set the viewer password if it is not set.
  2. Open the URL and sign in with that username and password.

pages_deploy runs commands, so it goes through the same approval as the agent's shell: under the safe and production security profiles you approve each deploy before anything is recorded. An agent with no shell access cannot use it at all.

docs.title: Static builds
docs.text:
The agent gives a build command and the folder the build writes (output, usually dist for Vite or build for Create React App). Each successful build is copied into a fresh, read-only release and the page switches to it in one step, so a viewer never sees a half-written build. A failed build changes nothing: the previous release keeps serving, and the card says the build failed and why. The last three releases are kept.

For apps with client-side routing (React Router, Vue Router), the agent sets spa: any address that is not a file then loads the app's index.html, while a missing script or image still answers 404.

The app must load its files from under its own address. Relative paths (./assets/app.js) work everywhere; with Vite the agent sets base to /pages/<slug>/. pages_start and pages_deploy warn when an index.html links paths starting with / that would miss the page.

docs.title: Servers
docs.text:
The agent gives a start command, such as node server.js or python3 app.py. The server must listen on 127.0.0.1 and the port in the PORT environment variable (the agent can pin a port instead with port, for a server that cannot read PORT). Olano:

  • starts it in the agent's sandbox, the same isolated place its shell commands run, with no access to your credentials;
  • waits until its health path (/ unless the agent set another) answers, up to one minute by default, and shows "starting" to viewers meanwhile;
  • forwards every request for the page to it, including form posts, API calls, uploads and streamed responses;
  • watches it: a crash or three failed health checks in a row restarts it, waiting 1, 2, 4, 8… seconds between attempts;
  • gives up cleanly after five crashes without a stable run in between. The page then reads failed with the end of the server's output, and the agent is expected to fix the cause and restart it. Restarting, or deploying again, clears it.

A server that loses its connection for a reason that is not its own (the sandbox was rebuilt, the deployment restarted) is brought back at once and is not counted as a crash. Servers come back on their own after a restart of the deployment.

The page lives under /pages/<slug>/, and by default the server sees requests without that prefix: /pages/crm/api/people arrives as /api/people. Its own pages should therefore call fetch("api/people") (relative), not fetch("/api/people"). A framework configured with base path /pages/<slug> (Next.js basePath) sets strip_prefix: false to receive the full path. The prefix also arrives in the X-Forwarded-Prefix header.

docs.title: What a server can and cannot see
docs.text:
A page server is code the agent wrote, so Olano keeps it on a short leash:

  • It never receives the viewer's password or your dashboard sign-in. It learns who is viewing from the X-Olano-Viewer header (the username they signed in with), never how they proved it.
  • Its cookies are confined to its own page, and it cannot set cookies that belong to the dashboard, clear the browser's data for the whole site, or register a service worker outside its page.
  • Its redirects stay under its page.
  • A form post or API call from another website is refused, so a page cannot be driven by a link someone else sends you.
  • Viewers' requests are bounded: a request waits at most two minutes for the server, uploads are capped at 25 MB, and at most 64 requests run at once per page. All three are adjustable in Config → Deployed pages.

Each agent's sandbox is isolated on the network: no other agent's sandbox, and no other container on the machine, can open a connection to a server running in it, so the page password is the only way in. On the rare machine where that isolation is switched off or cannot be set up, a server listening on all network interfaces instead of 127.0.0.1 could be reached around the password, and the page card warns about it.

docs.title: Watching and fixing a page
docs.text:
Each card on the agent's Pages tab shows the page's kind and state:

State Meaning building The build is running. A page that already had a release keeps serving it. starting The server is up and Olano is waiting for its health path to answer. running The server answers and viewers reach it. live A static build's release is being served. restarting The server crashed or stopped answering; it is restarting after a short wait. waiting Something outside the page blocks it, such as the agent's sandbox being down or deployed pages being switched off. The card says what. failed The build failed with nothing earlier to serve, or the server crashed five times in a row. The card shows the last error.

Logs opens the server's output and the last build's output. Restart serves a stopped page again; for a deployed page it re-runs the build and restarts the server, which is also how to pick up code changes and clear a failed state. Stop stops serving the page and stops its server; the address stays reserved for the agent.

The agent has the same view through its own tools: pages_status reports the state and the last error, and pages_logs reads the server or build output. The same logs are in the agent's workspace under .olano/pages/<slug>/.

docs.title: Limits and switches
docs.text:
All of these live in Config → Deployed pages (the pages: block of config.yaml):

  • Run page builds and servers: the master switch. Off stops every page server within a few seconds and refuses new deploys; plain pages and static releases that were already built keep serving.
  • Servers per agent: how many server pages one agent may run at once (default 5).
  • Health check every, Request timeout, Largest upload and Requests at once, per page, as described above.

Not supported yet: WebSockets, custom domains, and pages without a password.

docs.title: Privacy and security
docs.text:
Several independent checks stand between what reaches an agent and what it does. The settings on this page switch them on, off or tighter:

flowchart TB
    subgraph inbound["On the way in"]
        direction LR
        IN["Message, email,<br/>web page, document"] --> RL["Rate limits<br/>external traffic only"] --> IS["Input scan<br/>injection, personal data"]
    end
    inbound --> AG["The agent"]
    AG --> acts
    AG --> outbound
    subgraph acts["When it acts"]
        direction LR
        AP["Approvals<br/>when the profile asks"] --> GD["Shell and<br/>network guards"] --> ACT["Action in its<br/>own workspace"]
    end
    subgraph outbound["On the way out"]
        direction LR
        OS["Output scan,<br/>credential scrub"] --> OUT["Reply"]
    end

Trust level (security.trust_level, 0–4) is the broad autonomy dial:

Level Name What it can do 0 Observer Read only; can suggest, not act 1 Assistant Write to memory and logs only 2 Collaborator (default) Create and edit workspace files; containerised shell 3 Autonomous Full workspace; auto-approves low-risk operations 4 Developer Local shell; auto-approves most things. Development and CI only

Personal data. pii_scan_input and pii_scan_output (both on by default) look for personal data moving in and out; pii_action decides what happens — warn (default), redact, or block. pii_scan_peer extends scanning to agent-to-agent traffic; it is off by default because internal traffic is usually already inside your boundary.

Prompt injection. input_scan (on) checks incoming text for attempts to hijack the agent's instructions — the classic risk when an agent reads email, web pages or documents from people you do not control. output_scan (on) screens what goes out. web_scan (off) extends the check to fetched web content; turn it on for agents that browse widely.

Credentials. credential_scrub (on) strips anything that looks like a secret from what the agent says, so a key that ends up in a log or an error message does not get repeated into a chat.

Network. ssrf_protection (on) blocks requests to internal network addresses — the defence against an agent being talked into fetching http://localhost/admin. Which public destinations an agent's tools may reach is a separate pair of lists, egress_allow / egress_deny, set for the whole deployment in Config → Outbound access and narrowed per agent in its Advanced tab; both empty (the default) allows everything. See agent.json5 reference for the format and exactly what they govern.

Shell. shell_guard (on) blocks dangerous command patterns. skill_audit (on, strict) reviews skills before running them.

Sandboxes are isolated from each other. An agent's shell commands, and any server it runs (such as the server behind a page), run in its own sandbox. No other agent's sandbox, and no other container on the machine, can open a network connection to it, so one agent cannot reach what another agent is serving. Sandboxes can still reach the internet, subject to the outbound lists above. The isolation is set up automatically; the agent's Terminal tab says when a machine could not set it up.

Disk encryption (managed instances). A managed instance created on Olano Cloud keeps everything it stores (agents, memory, files, conversations, the vault, the database) on an encrypted volume that is unlocked automatically when the instance boots. This is standard custody: it protects your data against disclosure from stolen disks, snapshots, backups and offline storage access; the instance decrypts at boot using Olano-operated key infrastructure, and Olano's production control plane retains the technical capability to authorize key release. What is yours alone is the recovery key: a second key that opens the volume without Olano's key service, for example to read your data from a disk image if the instance or Olano is gone. Create it from Config → Disk encryption in the instance's own dashboard: the instance generates it, shows it exactly once, and asks you to type it back before it counts. Olano never sees the key and cannot show it again; keep it in a password manager or printed somewhere safe. Losing it is not fatal while the instance runs (create a new one; the lost one stops working once the new one is confirmed), but without one your data can be opened by Olano's key service alone. The same card shows whether a backup of the volume's encryption header (the keyslots, never your data) is held off the instance, which is what lets the recovery key open the volume again if the header on the disk is damaged. Conversation history on such an instance is additionally encrypted inside the database, so a database file read outside the instance shows no message text.

Rate limits. security.rate_limits caps how much an agent can do:

  • per_tool: { tool_name: max_calls_per_minute } — cap a specific tool.
  • messages: { per_minute, per_hour, per_day } — cap inbound messages across all platforms. Omit a window, or set it to null, for unlimited.
  • per_platform: { telegram: { per_minute, … } } — per-connector caps.

Two things to know. Message limits are opt-in: the schema shows a default of 60, but limiting only activates once you set a rate_limits block explicitly. And they apply only to external inbound traffic — scheduled jobs, heartbeat runs and the agent's own background work are exempt, so a rate limit never throttles the agent's own initiative.

(requests_per_minute is a legacy alias for messages.per_minute. Prefer the messages form.)

These override the deployment-wide rate_limits: in config.yaml for that agent.

A note on boundaries. An agent reaches its own workspace, plus shared folders you declare and read-only skill sources. Other agents' directories are deliberately invisible to it — a "permission denied" there is the isolation working, not a bug to work around. Cross-agent work happens through tools that are individually approved, not through the filesystem.

docs.title: Revisions
docs.text: Automatic version history for the deployment's configuration and the files your agents work with, in the Revisions tab.

docs.title: What is tracked
docs.text:
History follows a deliberate allow-list, so a new kind of file can never slip in by accident:

  • config.yaml, organization.yaml, the approval rules, and every agent's agent.json5 (with its env values replaced by __vault__, so secrets are never stored).
  • Inside every agent's workspace and in installed skills, files of these types:
    • notes and documents: Markdown, text, HTML, CSV, PDF, Word, Excel, PowerPoint (and their OpenDocument equivalents), EPUB;
    • data and configuration: JSON, JSON5, YAML, TOML, INI, XML;
    • scripts and source code: Python, notebooks, JavaScript and TypeScript, shell, and other common languages (executable scripts keep their executable flag);
    • images, audio and video: PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, SVG, MP3, WAV, M4A, MP4, MOV, WebM and similar.

Never tracked: .env files, the vault, databases, session transcripts, logs, archives, hidden folders, dependency and cache folders (node_modules, virtual environments, __pycache__), another git repository inside a workspace, a customer-service agent's private per-customer memory, and configuration files whose name says they hold a credential (token.json, client_secret.json, credentials.yaml).

Commits are attributed to whoever caused the change (the agent or the human), so you can answer "who changed this, and what did it look like before". Changes are debounced (default 45 seconds) so a burst of edits becomes one entry.

If you have data-deletion obligations, set revisions.include_memory: false: memory files carry distilled personal data, and this keeps them out of history.

docs.title: Files that are held back
docs.text:
Some files are tracked but cannot be recorded as they are right now. Each one keeps the last version that was recorded (it is never recorded as deleted, so a push never removes it from GitHub), and the Revisions page lists it with the reason, until the cause is fixed:

Reason Cause Fix Too large Larger than revisions.max_file_kb: 50 MB by default. It can be raised to 100 MB, the most GitHub accepts for one file; above 50 MB GitHub warns on every push. Make the file smaller, or keep it elsewhere. Looks like a credential A text file (or an agent.json5 outside its env block) contains something shaped like an API key, an access token, a private key or a password inside a database URL. History is pushed to GitHub, so it never stores one. Move the secret to the Vault and reference it; the file is recorded again on the next change. Does not parse An agent.json5 that cannot be read, so its secrets cannot be removed safely. Fix the file's syntax.

Very large files make history grow: every version of a 90 MB video is kept. The Revisions page shows the history's total size, and the disk clean-up repacks it.

docs.title: Seeing what changed
docs.text: Select any commit on the Revisions page to see what it did: how many files it changed, how many lines were added and removed, which files were added, modified or deleted, and the diff of each file side by side or unified. A commit made by a pull from GitHub is a merge: its file list shows what the pull changed on this deployment.

docs.title: Syncing with GitHub
docs.text: The history can be copied to a GitHub repository you own, as an off-site backup and as a place to edit files by hand. The history on your deployment stays the source of truth; GitHub is a copy you push to and pull from.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
1. On GitHub, create a new repository. Make it private and leave it empty: no README, license or .gitignore. A repository that already has commits is refused the first time, and a public one needs an explicit confirmation, because the history holds your configuration and your agents' memory.
  2. Choose how the deployment signs in to GitHub. When GitHub is already connected on the Connections page, that connection is selected for you and there is nothing to paste; otherwise the access token is.
    • GitHub connection: reuse the GitHub account connected on the Connections page. It reaches every repository that account can reach.
    • Access token: create a fine-grained personal access token with Repository access set to Only select repositories (the new one) and the permission Contents: Read and write. A classic token with the repo scope also works. The token is stored encrypted in the vault under a reserved name: it is not shown on the Vault page, it is never written to config.yaml or the history, and agents cannot read it. A token can be limited to this one repository, which a connection cannot.
  3. On Revisions, choose Connect a GitHub repository, enter the repository as owner/name (or paste its URL), the token, the branch (default main) and the automatic push mode, then Connect and push. The whole history is pushed at once. The window then shows each step (checking the repository, recording a snapshot, uploading the history, saving the connection) with a progress bar and the upload's size and speed; a large history can take several minutes. Closing the window does not stop it: the GitHub sync card keeps showing the progress until it finishes.

What is pushed is exactly what the history tracks: config.yaml, organization.yaml, approval rules, every agent.json5 with its env values replaced by __vault__, and workspace markdown, including memory unless revisions.include_memory is off. .env files, the vault, databases, sessions and tokens are never in the history, so they are never pushed.

docs.title: Pushing
docs.text:
Push sends new commits to GitHub. Automatic push decides whether the deployment also pushes on its own:

Mode Behaviour Manual (default) Only when you press Push. Once a day At most once every 24 hours, when there is something new to send. After every commit Right after each commit (commits are already grouped: by default 45 seconds after the last change).

A push never overwrites commits on GitHub that the deployment does not have. When GitHub has moved on (someone edited a file there), the push stops, the page says a pull is needed, and automatic pushing pauses until you pull. You can also choose Force push, which replaces GitHub's branch with the deployment's history; the page asks for confirmation, because the commits only GitHub had are dropped from the branch.

docs.title: Pulling
docs.text:
Pull brings GitHub's changes into the deployment. Pulling is always manual. Check for updates only asks GitHub what is new, without changing anything.

  • When only GitHub has new commits, its files are applied as they are.
  • When both sides changed different parts, the changes are merged automatically.
  • When both sides changed the same lines, nothing is applied. The page lists the files in conflict; for each one, compare this deployment's version with GitHub's and choose Keep this box's version, Take GitHub's version, or Edit the merged text (the text starts with both versions between <<<<<<< and >>>>>>> markers; remove the markers before completing). Then Complete merge. Abort merge drops the pull and changes nothing.

After a pull the page lists what was updated, added and deleted, and offers to restart agents whose configuration changed (their new configuration applies from the restart). A pull is careful about what it writes:

  • Only files the history tracks are written. Anything else in the GitHub repository (a README, a .env, any other file) is ignored and listed, and the next push removes it from GitHub's branch.
  • env values in agent.json5 keep this deployment's real values. A variable that only exists on GitHub is left out, with a note to set it on the agent's Variables tab.
  • The revisions: block of config.yaml always stays as it is on the deployment, so a pull can never disconnect GitHub or switch history off.
  • Deleting config.yaml, organization.yaml, the approval rules or an agent's agent.json5 on GitHub is not applied: remove an agent from the dashboard instead.
  • Files with invalid YAML or JSON5 stop the pull before anything is written.
  • If an agent writes one of the affected files while the pull is running, the pull stops without applying anything; pull again.

docs.title: When several people sync at once
docs.text: Only one GitHub operation runs at a time for the deployment: a push, a pull, Check for updates, a merge, connecting, disconnecting, or the automatic push. If another admin (or the automatic push) is already running one, the page says which operation and who started it, and the buttons come back as soon as it finishes; nothing is queued behind it. Pressing Push when GitHub already has every commit sends nothing.

docs.title: Disconnecting
docs.text: Disconnect stops syncing and deletes the stored access token. The GitHub repository and the history on the deployment are both left as they are. Connecting again later needs an empty repository.

docs.title: Scheduler and heartbeat
docs.text:
Scheduled jobs live in the agent's schedule list and appear in the dashboard's Scheduler tab, where you can also create, pause, edit and trigger them.

schedule: [
  {
    name: "Morning revenue check",
    cron: "0 9 * * 1-5",
    timezone: "America/Costa_Rica",
    message: "Check yesterday's revenue and flag anything unusual.",
  },
  {
    name: "Weekly deep analysis",
    cron: "0 7 * * 1",
    message: "Review last week's numbers in depth and write the report.",
    model: "olano:pro", // this job only; the agent's own model is unchanged
  },
]

Schedules are standard cron. Every cron expression here (this list, a stored task, the Advanced field of the task form, a when: line in the heartbeat file) has five fields: minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week. The day of week counts from Sunday: 0 or 7 is Sunday, 1 is Monday, so 1-5 is Monday to Friday. Names work as well (mon-fri, mon,thu, sun). The Scheduler tab's weekday picker and calendar show the days a task runs on, and an agent that creates or reads a task is told the same days by name.

Schedules saved before this numbering was adopted were rewritten once into weekday names for the days they were already running on, so no existing task changed its days. If one of yours now reads, say, tue,wed,thu,fri,sat where you meant weekdays, it had been running a day late; edit it to mon-fri.

A job is a message sent to the agent at a time you choose — so anything the agent can do in a conversation, it can do on a schedule. Use thread_id to keep a job's history in one continuous conversation.

A model per job. model (provider:model, for example olano:turbo or anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6) runs that one job on a model other than the agent's configured one, so a cheap tier can do the nightly digest and a bigger one the weekly analysis on the same agent. Leave it out and the job follows the agent's model, including later changes to it. Each run is billed to the model that ran, and the run's conversation in the chat list shows which model it was; on a managed deployment a bigger tier spends credits faster. A model whose provider is not connected is refused when the job is saved, and a model that stops working later fails the run with that reason in the job's history rather than falling back silently. The same field exists on tasks in the Scheduler tab ("Model", with "Agent default" as the first choice) and on the scheduling tools an agent or AgentFather uses.

And a reasoning effort per job. reasoning_effort sets how much thinking the model does before answering on this job's runs, independently of the agent's own reasoning_effort: a nightly digest can run at low while the weekly analysis runs at high on the same agent. The value must be one of the levels the model the job runs on accepts (model when set, else the agent's configured model); the Scheduler tab's "Reasoning effort" field appears only for such a model and lists exactly that ladder, and every surface that saves a job refuses a level the model does not take, naming the ones it does. Leave it out to follow the agent's own setting. Higher levels cost more tokens and time per run; a level that stops being valid later (a model retired, a package changed) is dropped for that run with a log line rather than failing the job.

flowchart TB
    subgraph start["What starts the work"]
        direction LR
        S1["schedule list in agent.json5<br/>cron only"] ~~~ S2["Scheduler store<br/>the New task form or the agent itself,<br/>cron or one-time"] ~~~ HB["Heartbeat<br/>every 60 minutes by default,<br/>reads HEARTBEAT.md"]
    end
    start --> RUN["The agent runs, exactly as in a conversation:<br/>tools, files, approvals"]

What a run knows about the time. Every scheduled run's message opens with the current date, weekday and time in the job's own timezone (UTC beside it), and every model call the agent makes, scheduled or not, ends its instructions with today's date. A brief that says "weekdays only" is decided from that clock, never from the newest date the agent happens to find in its files. The agent still calls get_current_time for the exact time of day during a long run. Set LIONCLAW_CLOCK_TIMEZONE in the deployment's environment to have the date line name your business timezone beside UTC; LIONCLAW_CLOCK_STAMP=0 turns the date line off.

Late and missed runs. A firing is not always on the second: the runtime can be busy, or restarting, at the moment a job is due. A job that fires late still runs, for up to scheduler.misfire_grace_minutes (six hours by default, set in config.yaml), and its message says when it was due and how late it is, so a morning report that starts at 08:40 is written as a late morning report rather than dated to the wrong moment. A firing that fell inside a restart runs as soon as the runtime is back, as long as it is still inside that window (scheduler.catch_up_on_boot, on by default); a dashboard Run now never counts as late. Past the window the firing is recorded in the job's history as skipped, naming the reason, and a notification on the bell says which job was skipped or failed and links to it; the notification clears by itself on the job's next completed run. Heartbeat polls and Cortex background phases keep a short five-minute window, since their next tick is minutes away.

A run that never ends. Only one run of a job executes at a time, so a run that keeps going holds the job: every later firing is recorded as skipped: the previous run was still executing, and a job that fired once and then never again usually means exactly that. A scheduled run is therefore bounded by scheduler.max_run_minutes (three hours by default). A run still going at the limit is stopped, its history row says so, the bell carries a notice, and what it wrote before the cut is kept; the next firing runs normally. Set the limit to 0 to remove it. The Next column on the Scheduler tab shows the job's next fire time; a dash there on an active job means the runtime holds no job for it, which saving the task again repairs.

Fan-out. With multi-user mode on, for_each_customer: true runs the job once per end user, and the message can use {customer_key}, {platform} and {user_id}. Use action instead of message to run a named script from allowed_actions.

Two places jobs live. The schedule list above is one of them; the other is the scheduler's own store, which is what the Scheduler tab's "New task" form writes and what an agent creates when it schedules something itself. The Scheduler tab merges both and badges each row, so nothing is hidden — but the difference matters when you go looking for what is triggering a job. A schedule entry is cron-only and lives in the agent's configuration; a stored task can also be one-time and can be handed to a different agent later.

Asking an agent about the schedule. Any agent can read and change its own scheduled work in chat, and AgentFather can do the same for every agent in the deployment — across both places — so "what wakes the finance agent at 3am?", "pause that job", or "schedule a Monday summary for the support agent" are all things you can simply ask for. Changing, creating or immediately running another agent's job always raises an approval card first, because it makes that agent start working on instructions you supplied. Ask to see a job's full instructions before approving an edit: a listing shows only its name, schedule and the first couple of lines.

Heartbeat is different and simpler: the agent wakes up periodically (default every 60 minutes) and reads HEARTBEAT.md in its workspace — a plain markdown file of standing instructions. It is the low-ceremony way to say "keep an eye on this" without writing a cron entry. Control it with the heartbeat block per agent, or heartbeat: in config.yaml for the fleet.

docs.title: Subscriptions and monetization
docs.text:
Charge end users for access to an agent. Set it up on the agent's Monetization tab or in the monetization block.

Two payment routes, usable together: Stripe (set plan.stripe_price_id; empty means Stripe is off) and Telegram Stars (set plan.stars_amount; 0 means it is off). trial_days (default 3) gives newcomers a free window. channels limits the paywall to specific connectors; gate_groups extends it to group chats.

Payment provider secrets go in the vault, never in the config file. The plan fields here are what users see — your payment provider remains the source of truth for what is actually charged.

Monetization pairs naturally with multi-user mode (Multi-user: two different features): you need per-user isolation for per-user subscriptions to mean anything.

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text:
Two directions, both configured in the agent's webhooks list and manageable from its Webhooks tab.

Outbound — tell an external system what happened.

{
  name: "ops-pager",
  direction: "outbound",
  url: "https://hooks.example.com/olano",
  events: ["agent.error", "budget.exceeded"],
  secret: "${WEBHOOK_SIGNING_SECRET}",
  rate_limit_per_minute: 30,
}

Payloads are signed with HMAC-SHA256 so the receiver can verify they came from you. Delivery retries with backoff, and delivery to internal network addresses is blocked by default. Webhooks re-register automatically after a server restart.

Inbound — let an external system give the agent work.

{
  name: "stripe-events",
  direction: "inbound",
  prompt: "This webhook receives Stripe billing events. Summarise what happened, and if a payment failed, draft a dunning email.",
  respond: false,
  accumulate_thread: false,
}

Each inbound webhook gets its own unguessable ingress URL. Whatever the sender POSTs — JSON, form data, plain text — is appended to your prompt and handed to the agent, so you do not need to know or control the sender's payload format. That is the point: you describe what the data means and what to do with it, and the agent handles the shape.

  • respond: true runs the agent synchronously and returns its reply in the HTTP response. Use for something waiting on an answer.
  • respond: false (default) acknowledges immediately and works in the background.
  • accumulate_thread: true keeps one running conversation across all payloads instead of starting fresh each time.

Both directions keep a delivery history, and the Test button sends a sample (outbound) or simulates an ingest (inbound) so you can check the wiring before going live.
